Machine learning (ML) based detection of network attacks has shown effectiveness when tailored to a single organisation, but combining data from multiple sources is challenging due to data format inconsistencies, privacy concerns and commercial confidentiality issues. To address these limitations, this paper presents a novel federated learning framework for multi-organisation data sharing. This method allows several institutions to collaborate on training a robust ML model for detecting intrusions without exposing their networks, by sharing anonymised attack data only. A key innovation is the use of balanced stochastic gradient descent to ensure all participants contribute equally to the model. Furthermore, this approach is assessed using three publicly available datasets and compared to traditional ML techniques, and federated learning alternatives, in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Experimental results indicate that this scheme can achieve high overall accuracy in detecting attacks, even with data from two or three different institutions. Moreover, training duration is directly proportional to the amount of local data available, and accuracy improves significantly as more institutions collaborate. Finally, this method outperforms traditional ML techniques and a federated learning alternative, and reduces training time by dividing it into multiple iterations. The issue of scheduling a robot's tasks efficiently is a long-established concern in manufacturing. Solutions have commonly drawn on a variant of the classic Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), with a focus on achieving the quickest or most time-efficient task sequence. Despite their optimality, these methods face challenges in real-time execution, especially with larger problems. In fast-paced online planning environments where tasks are executed swiftly, the time taken to optimize task ordering becomes a substantial hindrance, even overshadowing the overall task duration. The optimal approach in such cases involves balancing solution quality with total task completion time, achieved by identifying the most suitable sequence within the task set. The proposed algorithm offers this compromise through an iterative process involving task generation, grouping, and sequence optimization. The results indicate significant reductions in execution time, with these improvements verified against a standard algorithm in both simulated and practical UR5 robot scenarios. The capacity of wireless networks is inherently restricted by interference, and there has been a lack of investigation into the correlation of interference, which has the potential to cause substantial delays in local transmission. This study addresses the query of whether randomizing the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer, using protocols like frequency-hopping multiple access and ALOHA, can mitigate the adverse effects of interference correlation. By deriving precise analytical expressions for the mean and variance of local transmission delays in both protocols, this study creates a correlation metric and determines the optimal parameters that minimize these delays. Furthermore, simulations demonstrate that these derived optimal parameters also minimize delays in other, non-correlated scenarios, and a comprehensive evaluation of the delay performance of different protocols under varying correlation levels is provided. Ultimately, this investigation establishes a fundamental framework for understanding the impact of interference correlation on local transmission delays in wireless networks. Furthermore, the derived analysis and simulation outcomes can guide practitioners in selecting the most suitable protocols to meet the specific requirements of their applications. Specifically, this study's findings can guide designers in choosing between frequency-hopping multiple access and ALOHA, and the proposed correlation metric can be extended to analyze other wireless protocols. Finally, the codes related to this study's research can be accessed via a link provided in the authors' bio section.

Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely replicate existing knowledge. Secondly, they combine pseudo-labels with actual labels using the same loss function, failing to acknowledge their distinct contributions to classification. To address these limitations, we propose InfoGNN, an innovative pseudo-labeling framework. InfoGNN focuses on labeling nodes with the greatest informative value, which effectively represents local neighborhoods through mutual information maximization. To counterbalance the risks of pseudo-label noise and class imbalance, we also incorporate a modified cross-entropy loss with class-balanced regularization in the model re-training process. Comprehensive experiments on six graph datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, which outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and robust self-supervised methods on graph-related tasks. Furthermore, we highlight the theoretical advantages of our proposed approach over conventional methods. Detailed source code is available at https://github.com/CSAILVision/InfoGNN.

In video processing tasks, precise identification of recognizable objects at a low computational cost enables real-time video analysis on devices. We present PatchNet, a highly efficient neural network model for tracking objects across adjacent frames in videos. Unlike traditional pixel-based approaches, PatchNet leverages patch-wise correlation features. This results in a compact network with minimal parameters, capable of real-time performance on modern GPUs. For instance, its inference speed on the NVIDIA Jetson TX2 is approximately 70 frames per second. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of PatchNet by utilizing it as a base model for two video analysis applications -- video stabilization and distortion correction. These applications involve re-identifying objects under geometric transformations. We achieved notable performance gains in comparison to the current state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, our video stabilization technique outperformed existing models by expanding the tracking range from 64 pixels to 512 pixels. Similarly, our video distortion correction model surpassed existing models by supporting a wide range of angular transformations with minimal computational requirements. We present a generic, classical modeling of electric circuits that describes conventional single-tone microwave optomechanics, where a mechanical oscillator functions as a mobile capacitor within a parallel RLC circuit. Analytical derivations are developed, incorporating fundamental aspects like the back-action force, input-output relationships, and key parameters such as the motional capacitance, effective mass, and mechanical FOM. The model is validated by comparing it with the outcomes from a established optomechanical simulation tool. Additionally, we apply this model to analyze the characteristics of a particular design featuring a 3D microwave membrane resonator. The analysis involves calculating the mechanical oscillator's parameters, such as its thermal motion, mechanical FOM, and the conversion efficiency of optical to mechanical energy. We introduce a visual representation system that translates Coq proof scripts into tabular forms, which can be exported as $\LaTeX$ or PDF files. Our tool aims to facilitate learning and proof review by providing an interactive visual representation of each step in a proof. Consequently, this system enables educators and reviewers to utilize the proofs without relying on the Coq program, thereby allowing them to be printed or shared in other forms, as opposed to the more conventional hypertext or markdown formats. Additionally, it provides reviewers with means to annotate and communicate the content. Moreover, as the proofs are fully $\LaTeX$ed, they can be customized with an infinite array of options. Our tool evaluates this in the area of teaching undergraduate students in mathematics. We observed that visual representations of these proofs distinguish between definition, lemma, and theorem levels, which may offer additional insights to educators and reviewers. Our experiment also shows that including interactive elements further enhances the visual representations, as they capture 85\% to 95% of the proof structure. Our evaluation suggests that this system could serve as a starting point for utilizing interactive visual representations in mathematics education. We demonstrate that the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms is limited under the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis for a specific degree 8 L-function. This is achieved by leveraging Watson's formula, which allows us to recast our investigation as a tractable problem related to L-functions, ultimately facilitating the application of Soundararajan and Harper's methods for deriving sharp bounds on the moments of the Riemann zeta function. Consequently, this provides the first such sharp bound on the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms. Notably, this approach can likely be extended to investigate moments of a broader class of Hecke cusp forms. 

This research relies heavily on Deligne's work regarding the periodicity of certain sheaf functions on curves over finite fields, as well as the findings of many other mathematicians, which have provided significant insights into the properties of L-functions. By combining these insights with the functional equation of the L-function, we are able to derive the desired inequality. 

The key innovation of this research lies in harnessing the data from the Fourier expansion of Hecke cusp forms, which Watson's formula makes accessible, to investigate the characteristics of the period function. This, in turn, enables us to make inferences about the distribution of the non-trivial zeros in the number plane. Ultimately, this provides a new understanding of the relationships between the Fourier coefficients of Hecke cusp forms and the behavior of the period function. 

The specific computational techniques employed in this research, which involve the evaluation of determinants and tridiscant integrals on unitary groups, likely possess independent significance. Furthermore, the general methods developed in this study to investigate the characteristics of L-functions, which are recast as entities involving measures, are anticipated to yield fruitful applications in the study of Hecke cusp forms. Additionally, the text includes detailed appendices that provide supplementary mathematical investigations, which may also be of interest to researchers in the field. 

The main results presented in this research can be summarized as follows. First, by combining Deligne's work and Watson's formula, we are able to derive new insights into the properties and relationships between the Fourier coefficients of Hecke cusp forms (specifically, their fourth moment) under the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis for an L-function of degree 8). Second, by leveraging the functional equation of the L-function, along with many other mathematicians' findings, we are able to derive new bounds on the period function.

In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation system, speeding up convergence often involves developing optimal preconditioners for the linear solver. However, standard termination criteria for the solver frequently cause excessive 'oversolving' by insisting on sufficient residual reductions. This paper presents an alternative approach to interior point methods that utilizes an inner termination criterion not dependent on the residual, as well as indicators for premature inner iteration cessation informed by IPM demands. It also modifies this criterion to accommodate Conjugate Gradient and Minimum Residual algorithms, and demonstrates substantial performance enhancements in computational experiments for quadratic optimization problems, which translates to considerable time savings in IPM solution. The code for this solver is included in a public repository: https://github.com/pkubin/InnerTerminationCGMR. Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrices to generate continuous, overlapping DNA sequences within a chromosomal region. By dividing a genome into fixed-sized segments and assigning them to multiple workers, the assembly process can be accelerated, with the ability to scale comprehensively. In addition to achieving a 5-fold speedup with 12 workers, the developed framework exhibits exceptional memory efficiency, surpassing existing solutions by at least 2-fold. Furthermore, the generated sequences are integrated into a compressed and partitioned graph format to minimize memory usage during the assembly process. A substantial 44% average reduction in memory consumption was achieved with minimal impact on assembly quality. In combination, these optimizations result in substantial time and memory savings, enabling the efficient assembly of large genomes on commodity hardware. In particular, this approach enables the assembly of a 200-Mb genome in under 25 minutes and a 1000-Mb genome in under 2.5 hours with 12 workers. The code is freely accessible on GitHub under the AGPLv3 license. Future research will focus on enhancing the assembly algorithm further, incorporating additional features such as read alignment and primary contig generation. To facilitate collaboration, the authors invite researchers to join a genomics assembly community on SourceForge. The proposed approach is versatile and can be applied to various assembly methods, with plans to extend it to other tools in the future. With further development, this framework has the potential to accelerate genome assembly and other graph-based applications in genomics and other fields. To demonstrate the assembly pipeline's effectiveness, two novel, assembled genomes of endangered species are presented, showcasing the importance of accurate genome assemblies in conservation efforts. The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model offers a computationally efficient solution to handle complex data analysis. Introduced as a parameter-free and robust method for high-dimensional regression analysis, the HDR Lasso has been proven to outperform other approaches in statistical terms. Mathematically, the HDR Lasso is equivalent to an optimization problem with an L1-regularized loss function that utilizes Jaeckel's dispersion function and Wilcoxon scores, making traditional lasso algorithms ineffective due to non-differentiability. Building upon existing research, we introduce a novel adaptive-sieving-based method, AS-JRL, to solve the HDR Lasso. This method comprises two primary stages: an outer iterative process and an inner optimization problem. In the outer process, we divide the data into adaptive sieves based on a sample quantile threshold, while the inner problem solves a sub-problem within each sieve via a modified gradient descent method. Through rigorous analysis and extensive simulations, we demonstrate the AS-JRL algorithm to be sparse, consistent, and computationally efficient with a time complexity of O(n log^3 n), outperforming existing methods in terms of speed. Numerical experiments validate the superior performance of AS-JRL across various noise types and dimensions. Additionally, we apply the AS-JRL algorithm to real-world datasets, successfully retrieving significant features in these data sets. Furthermore, we introduce a Fortran-based CPU implementation and a Java-based GPU implementation of the AS-JRL algorithm, demonstrating comparable results between CPU and GPU versions. Ultimately, we conclude that the AS-JRL algorithm represents a highly efficient and adaptive solution to the HDR Lasso problem. An older suggestion by Bars and Yankielowicz to match the theory's 't Hooft anomalies with those of free fermions is revisited, resulting in novel constraints for the large N limit. Furthermore, SU(N) theories with an additional Weyl fermion are studied, demonstrating a matching of 21 't Hooft anomalies with a Spin(8) gauge theory. This discovery hints at a non-supersymmetric expansion of the Pouliot and Strassler duality, while non-supersymmetric dualities involving vector-like matter in SO(N) and Sp(N) gauge theories, subject to Weingarten inequalities, are also explored. An old proposal by Seiberg to match the low-energy properties of SU(N) theories to those of free fermions, particularly for the non-singlet components, is revisited and shown to require a novel interpretation. Ultimately, candidate non-supersymmetric dualities involving vector-like matter in the same three gauge groups are provided. Last but not least, SU(N) theories with multiple Weyl fermions are examined, matching the low-energy properties to those of free fermions for specific fermion combinations and potentially leading to novel non-supersymmetric dualities. In conclusion, this research delves into various chiral gauge theories to analyze their dynamics, leveraging anomaly matching, Poisson equations, and Weingarten inequalities to guide the investigation. The visual appearance and auditory qualities of an object provide distinct insights into its properties.  In everyday situations, we easily identify objects by combining the information from vision and hearing.  This ability is referred to as multi-sensory integration.  This research investigates the practical application of multi-sensory integration in identifying fallen objects through the synchronization of visual and auditory cues.  A novel computer system has been developed to locate objects based on the correlation of their visual and auditory characteristics as captured in video and audio recordings.  A database of 13 different objects has been used in experiments for training and testing the system, with experiments conducted under two lighting conditions to simulate real-world scenarios.  The system was designed to operate in real-time, processing frames and audio samples in the order they are received, allowing it to function at high processing speeds.  Compared to traditional object detection methods, this system demonstrated enhanced performance in localizing objects, particularly in difficult-to-detect situations.  A video demonstrating the system's capabilities can be found online at the address: https://youtu.be/6B7Y1j0s4gY.  The source code of the system can be accessed via the link: https://github.com/Ahmed-Ali-Shehata/Fallen-Objects-detector.  This research aims to contribute to the advancement of computer vision, specifically in the areas of 2.5D object detection and asynchronous multi-sensory integration.  In addition, this research paves the way for various practical applications, such as autonomous navigation and navigation-assisted mobile robotics.  The effect of falling objects on humans can also be studied using this system, potentially leading to new findings. Past research has linked this phenomenon to the violent collisions among particles, causing a shared goal among researchers to understand the universal underlying mechanics. Past studies have employed diverse measurement units, making it challenging to pinpoint a universal scaling law. A groundbreaking study by Bruno et al. in 2011 discovered that, when adjusted for density and particle size, the shear rate at the thickening threshold remains surprisingly constant across various substances. Building upon this breakthrough, our research expands upon it by incorporating new data and quantifying the shear rate's slight variations. Furthermore, we derive a precise formula for predicting the shear rate at the thickening threshold, taking into account both density and particle size. Crucially, our prediction remains unchanged regardless of the given density, suggesting a universal underlying truth. Moreover, our simulation indicates that the shear rate at the thickening threshold is entirely independent of fluid density but directly proportional to the particle size, confirming the suspicions of many scientists. This study investigates how Google's personalization affects users' likelihood of discovering relevant information through their search engine. The underlying assumption is that users will only recognize the relevance of information they encounter if it appears in their search history or previous queries. To test this, the researchers employed two experiments, the first of which demonstrated that non-personalized Google users fail to notice up to 57% of relevant information when searching for a topic. The second experiment found that when personalized search results are displayed, relevant information beyond the first page is often overlooked, with the exception of users who frequently perform repeated searches on the same topic. The experiment yielded a figure of 51% of relevant information missed by these long-tail users. Conversely, users who rely on personalized search are less likely to click on pages beyond the first, with the experiment indicating that they miss out on as much as 44% of relevant information. Notably, the researchers found that long-tail users are more likely to miss relevant information when searching for diverse topics rather than focusing on a single subject. Based on these results, the researchers estimate that worldwide, Google's personalization may result in the overlooking of up to 2.3 billion relevant web pages each month. The study's findings suggest that dependence on personalized search comes at a cost, and may lead users to rely on other information sources, such as social media, to fill the gap in their knowledge. Further research is required to refine these estimates, and to explore the impact of other customized online services on users' information-seeking behavior. Potential avenues for investigation include Bing's personalization and the ways in which users interact with customized news feeds and social media content. By examining these questions, researchers may gain a more comprehensive understanding of the role of personalization in the digital information landscape. The study's data have been made publicly available, and the results have been shared with Google, which have confirmed the study's methodology and provided additional context. Ultimately, the researchers concluded that while personalized search may be beneficial, it is essential to inform users about how their searches are being customized, and whether relying on a single search engine meets their information needs. By raising user awareness, the researchers argue that individuals can take steps to supplement their search habits and make more informed decisions about how to find relevant information online. To promote these efforts, the researchers proposed several strategies, including educating users about search terminology and developing standardized interfaces for web search. Automatically creating programs from detailed specifications is a task called program synthesis. A novel framework for generating code based on flow charts is presented, where a deep neural network called GRCNN is trained to accurately interpret these visual specifications by identifying their graphical structures. By being trained end-to-end, GRCNN is capable of simultaneously predicting node and edge details in a flow chart. By analyzing the B dataset containing 1.8K flow charts and evaluating two distinct metrics, the top-performing model, GRCNN, achieved a remarkable 97% recognition accuracy for identifying connection relationships and also demonstrated strong predictive capabilities, specifically, a median relative error of 0.6% for estimating program logic connection sequences. Furthermore, detailed studies revealed that GRCNN's synthesis capabilities are enhanced by its ability to fully comprehend the specifications through its recognition of graphical structures. By employing human-in-the-loop methods, such as asking GRCNN to propose and then having a human reviewer refine its predictions, the synthesis accuracy of this model was increased from 59% to 71%. Additionally, an experiment showed that this model was able to generate actual Java programs from flow charts with the synthesized code matching 85% of the original code. This text explores multiple reduction techniques that facilitate the connection of Earth's climate models of varying complexity, emphasizing approaches that enable thorough reduction. It distills key mathematical concepts behind each method while showcasing several benchmark climate modeling examples for illustrative purposes. The primary methods examined include dynamical systems, multilinear spectral methods, proper orthogonal decomposition, and the geometric reduction of multiple-scale systems. While this paper concentrates on reduction methods, it also briefly touches on relevant techniques for modeling complexity, such as parameterization and model hierarchies. Ultimately, the paper seeks to contribute to further exploration of reduction methods in the dynamics community. Due to the vast number of climate researchers who are not familiar with reduction methods, this paper aims to introduce these methods in an approachable manner. In contrast to existing literature, which primarily focuses on the theoretical aspects, this paper places a greater emphasis on illustrative examples from climate modeling. Consequently, the paper's mathematical rigor may be compromised in favor of clearer exposition. Nonetheless, readers seeking in-depth mathematical rigor are directed to comprehensive papers and books listed at the end of this review. This includes works by Bubeck et al. that lay out the underlying theory of variational methods, and the respective Geometric Models of Atmospheric Dynamics by Majda and Gualtieri for geometric reductions. This review aims to provide an accessible entry point into reduction methods for readers well-versed in climate dynamics. Key outcomes are summarized in a concise manner, with extensive references provided for further reading. In particular, the paper references the works of Cessi and China in dynamical systems, Faranda et al. on multilinear spectral methods, and the works of Bubak et al. and Grima et al. on geometric reductions. This review also draws from own research, including the works of Bubak et al. and Grima et al. This includes the study by Grima et al. examining the multidecadal climate variability in the Atlantic region using multilinear spectral methods, and another study by Grima et al. which applied geometric reduction to a multiple-scale climate model. This review also relies on joint research with Andrew W. Woods in dynamical systems, and a collaborative project with Andrew W. Woods and Chris Hillier on model reduction. The groundbreaking discovery of gravitational waves emanating from a binary neutron star merger in August 2017 paved the way for a new era in multimessenger astronomy. Kilonovae, produced by the expelled macronova material, present an intriguing opportunity for astronomers to study not only neutron stars but also extreme nuclear matter through electromagnetic emissions following the event. The key to understanding these emissions lies in the relativistic atomic structure of the ejected elements. By utilizing the most up-to-date relativistic atomic structure principles, the necessary data for kilonovae generation has been generated, including energy levels, electron densities, and relativistic energies for the $4s^2 4p^6 5s^2 5p^6 6s^2 6p^6 7s^2 7p^6$ electron configuration of osmium isoelectronic ions. A comparative analysis with non-relativistic atomic structure models showed substantial discrepancies in the energy levels and radii, with relativistic corrections amounting to around 20% for low-lying levels and an average radii difference of about 10%. Compositional data analysis is a technique that deals with data sets consisting of vectors whose components represent proportions of a whole system. Researchers in the compositional data analysis field utilize linear algebra along with various visualization and interpretation methods. Although widely adopted in applications such as geochemistry and biochemistry, compositional data analysis remains underrepresented in standard statistical textbooks. This article focuses on the linear algebra fundamentals of compositional data analysis and offers a fresh perspective on the methodology through logratio space, including data visualization and interpretation. The authors' aim is to introduce this approach to a broader statistics community with an emphasis on accessibility for early-stage students and practitioners in data analysis. The linear algebra principles outlined in this article can be utilized to develop effective composition data analysis methods. The authors provide a comprehensive reference list that combines both established and novel techniques. Ultimately, the article's authors hope to inspire future research in the field by highlighting the potential of composition data analysis to address a wide range of problems in various scientific contexts. The exoplanet sample from CORALIE/HARPS (Mayor et al., 2011), which was discovered through Doppler radial velocity measurements, does not demonstrate the'sub-Saturn mass desert' that is observed in other populations (e.g., GTO Kepler planets, Peplinksi et al., 2018; the TESGA project, Armstrong et al., 2018; or the CESSI project, Jordan et al., 2017), which suggests a missing link in understanding planet formation and evolution processes. Analysis of the CORALIE/HARPS data reveals that planets with masses between 0.1 and 5 Earth masses and orbital periods between 10 and 200 days are detected in a manner that is free from detection biases. Interestingly, the sub-Saturn mass desert is not present in this sample, as the probability of this phenomenon occurring is less than 2%. Since the CORALIE/HARPS sample is one of the oldest and most extensively populated in the mass-period space, these findings indicate that the missing link in understanding planet formation and evolution processes is likely not a process that affects the detection of planets in this particular region of the mass-period space. Possible explanations for this phenomenon include the rapid evolution of the sub-Saturn mass desert due to tides or the presence of a second generation of planets resulting from the dissipation of protoplanetary disks. Future observations of this region of the mass-period space using the ESPRESSO and ELT/HARPS upgrades are required to confirm whether the sub-Saturn mass desert actually exists or not. Based on these projections, the likelihood of observing this phenomenon will increase to 75% if the signal is present and the detection probability will be lower than 1% if the signal is absent. Thus, these future observations will provide crucial answers regarding the evolution of exoplanets in this particular region of the mass-period space. References Armstrong et al. Dark matter consisting of bosons in an attractive potential may lead to the formation of solid-like structures, which results from the way these particles interact when they slow down. To investigate the properties of this type of matter, we need to consider the characteristics of the interaction between the particles as well as their mass. In this study, we focus on a specific kind of dark matter composed of bosons that interact with each other through a Yukawa interaction and form a solid-like substance. In this type of matter, when the system is slow, its low-energy states resemble a crystal lattice structure. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve various problems that demand sequential processing, but their broad applicability has been limited by several constraints. Previous research indicated that training RNNs can be computationally complex and may not always be feasible. Moreover, even well-trained RNNs can struggle to resolve tasks that require a high level of cognitive complexity. In order to overcome these obstacles, we introduce an innovative strategy that utilizes a single fixed sparse RNN to excel in multiple cognitive tasks. This approach is built upon three fundamental principles: (1) the use of a single and unchanging sparse RNN architecture, (2) relying on an unsupervised learning method called Autoencoders, and (3) an adaptive task-mapping system. Through experimentation, we demonstrate that this strategy is capable of solving a diverse range of cognitive tasks, outperforming existing state-of-the-art techniques while reducing training time by several orders of magnitude. Even under constrained computational environments, this method allows for seamless task adaptation, and our analysis shows that an extensive range of cognitive tasks can be learned within a relatively low time threshold of 30 minutes. This breakthrough enables the development of artificial cognitive systems that are more intelligent, efficient, and robust, potentially mimicking key aspects of human brain function. Our work lays the foundation for future research in this field, and we provide an open-source code for sparse RNN learning available at: \href{https://github.com/fatemahsaadatmarmo/sparse-rnn}{github.com/fatemahsaadatmarmo/sparse-rnn}. Additionally, the link to our interactive website is provided at: \href{https://fatimasmarmo.github.io/sparsernn}{fatimasmarmo.github.io/sparsernn}. This research presents an enhancement to the Symmetry-Plus (SP) approach, a powerful image registration technique that leverages computational group theory to expand comparison scope beyond traditional features. The SP method has shown excellence in registering MRI volumes, but its performance is largely contingent on accurately extracting robust features. While previous iterations relied on 2D SIFT features, this study seeks to elevate image registration by extracting features in a more comprehensive manner - specifically, by applying 3D SIFT features to extend comparisons to sub-volumes within images. Additionally, this study seeks to streamline feature comparison by eliminating the need to match individual features individually, instead using discrete symmetry groups to expedite the process. Thorough validation has been achieved by examining the robustness of the extended SP approach to varying parameters, such as rotation invariants, feature extraction criteria, and group order. Moreover, challenging datasets including human head MRI volumes and Kendall benchmark dataset have been used to demonstrate the robustness and efficiency of the extended SP approach, with results compared against state-of-the-art registration methods including ELASTIX, SITK, and DeepLearning. Consequently, significant enhancements have been achieved - specifically, a 300% improvement in dice score and a 100% improvement in consistency when evaluated on Kendall benchmark dataset with tight and loose criteria respectively. Code and data used in this study can be accessed via https://github.com/AbdullahMoussa/3D-SIFT-based-SP. Results suggest that feature-based approaches can still outperform learning-based ones in image registration, particularly in scenarios where few examples are available. Hence, this extended SP approach can be regarded as a robust, efficient, and feature-based solution to image registration challenges. With respect to particular components, while 3D SIFT features present advantages, they also incur additional computational burden - specifically, a 10fold increase in memory usage and a 15fold increase in processing time, with some variations depending on dataset used. Consequently, discrete symmetry groups can be regarded as an efficient means to expedite feature comparison, memory usage, and processing time. Finally, under examination were the resilience of the extended SP approach to rotation in image registration, featuring a comprehensive analysis involving 10 distinct orientations. Results indicate that feature extraction criteria hold more significance than rotation in image registration. Consequently, while assessment has been rotated (literally), the extended SP approach remains a reliable and efficient means to achieve successful image registration. We've carried out an in-depth examination of the photometry and one spectroscopic observation from SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, an unusual binary system with a 40.5-minute period. The analysis revealed the presence of distinct frequency components, namely 0.0163 d^-1, 0.0139 d^-1 (likely harmonics of the primary frequency), and 0.0059 d^-1, corresponding to 1 d^-1, 2 d^-1, and 3 d^-1, respectively. The triple-star nature of the system provides the most plausible explanation, attributable to the primordial material surrounding the binary system, giving rise to the observed frequencies and harmonics. Notably, however, our examination failed to uncover evidence supporting significant variations in the low-gravity H and He $z$ broadening feature. An alternative explanation is also presented: the observed non-uniform frequency spectrum might be the result of an irregularly shaped mass transfer stream towards the companion star, displaying irregular motion due to the binary system's constraints. The system's donor star, initially estimated to be 0.13 M_sun in mass, is proposed to be an oxygen white dwarf, given the observed period and mass, which would imply a system age of approximately 1.26 Gyr, consistent with other double-degenerate binary system dimensions. An accompanying radial velocity study is planned to further refine the system's frequency spectrum and allow for independent system age estimation. Lastly, our analysis confirms the system's two component masses to be approximately 0.13 M_sun and 0.19 M_sun, as the donor star undergoes substantial mass loss, reducing it from 0.17 M_sun in an estimated 5.8 Gyr. In this time frame, the donor star will diminish in mass, ultimately becoming a conventional low-mass white dwarf. An accompanying paper will provide an in-depth analysis of the system's observed full mass range, as well as its implications. Observations indicate the system is approaching an equal mass ratio, with the donor star undergoing mass reduction due to non-conservative mass loss. An estimated 10 more years remain before the system reaches equal mass distribution. In this paper, data extraction and analysis were facilitated using the JEDEye software package. The primary objective of this research is to examine aspects of the validity of the active galactic nucleus unification theory. Our focus lies on AGN host galaxies which, according to the unified theory, should not exhibit systematic differences depending on AGN classification. We used the SDSS catalogue up to a redshift of 0.2, and the Galaxy Zoo Project catalogue which classifies galaxies into two broad Hubble types, and classified AGNs using emission line diagnostics. Our findings reveal that elliptical galaxies have a significantly higher fraction of Type 1 Seyfert nuclei compared to other AGN types, and the transition from Seyfert 1 to LINER, Type 2 Seyfert, and composite nuclei corresponds to a rise in spiral host galaxy fraction. Moreover, we discovered a notable presence of spiral host galaxies among narrow-line objects, and the distribution of narrow-line object orientations within this host galaxy type exhibits more uniform variation. In contrast, the distribution of Type 1 Seyfert nuclei and their narrow-line counterparts show little variation in galaxy orientation. Our research indicates that the active galactic nucleus continuum radiation does not equally penetrate the gas in host spiral galaxies, and the spiral arms of these galaxies harbour the gas that nourish the AGN. Our results imply that the active galactic nucleus power is insufficient to expel gas from spiral arms, and the relatively short lifespan of an AGN cannot significantly alter its host spiral arm. Furthermore, the data suggest co-existence of a LINER or an obscured AGN and a normal galaxy, and the low ionisation mechanism within these galaxies can be explained by the presence of a low-intensity, obscured AGN. Our research paves the way for a new theory, and challenges the unified AGN model, specifically addressing active galactic nuclei and their host galaxies. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, a method which can
be marred by uncontrollable biases. To investigate a more effective method, we
proposed that depth estimation using untagged videos might be a better choice
for pre-training. Although this method lacks any meaningful scene details, we
assert that calculating the three-dimensional geometry of scenes is closer to
the goal of semantic segmentation than assigning broad image classifications.
To test our hypothesis, we designed and implemented an innovative technique,
AutoDepth, which leverages untagged videos to estimate scene depth. Our method
involves training a monocular 3D convolutional neural network using video stills
along with corresponding movement estimates derived from video sequences.
Our experimental findings show that pre-training both small and large models on
depth estimation yields superior performance when followed by refinement using
labeled data, while classification-based pre-training produced inferior results
for the smaller models. Nonetheless, the benefit of pre-training on depth
estimation was minimal for larger models already achieving high performance through
supervised training. Moreover, in contrast to expectations, we discovered that
pre-training on untagged video depth estimates led to marginally poorer
performance when evaluated on untagged video test sets, suggesting the
presence of uncontrollable biases in the acquired knowledge. To validate the
usefulness of pre-training, we also conducted exhaustive evaluations using
artificially created synthetic data, confirming that depth estimation can serve
as a meaningful prior knowledge source. To share our methods and outcomes with
the public, we have released both AutoDepth and the created synthetic depth
dataset. Additionally, our code, pre-trained models, and post-trained models are
publicly available at https://github.com/fatemehkarimii/AutoDepth.ToF.

The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that ensure consistency but often produce mechanical, uninspired narratives. In contrast, we introduce TCube, a neural framework that can describe time-series data in a universal way without being tied to a particular domain. TCube represents essential time-series elements using a knowledge graph, which is then translated into coherent, engaging stories by leveraging the strengths of pre-trained language models. Since there's a scarcity of labeled data for time-series, TCube incorporates a knowledge graph to make the translation process feasible. This innovative approach marks TCube as the first exploration of neural methods for time-series narration, according to our current knowledge. In our comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that TCube significantly improves the variety of words in the generated stories, while also maintaining correct grammar, by up to 65.38%. Moreover, an expert review of 21 professionals showed that 76.2% of them preferred TCube as a viable system for time-series narration because of its richer narratives, despite being auto-generated. TCube's open-source code and supporting materials are publicly available for anyone to reproduce our results and build upon our work. Additionally, a demo of TCube is available at https://tcube-time-series.github.io/. In the future, we plan to continue refining TCube by incorporating more domain-independent knowledge to the knowledge graph to make the translation process even more feasible. This could involve using machine-learned knowledge or even integrating TCube with other prominent knowledge bases like Wikidata. Moreover, we aim to expand TCube to support other modalities, such as visual and audio, to enable more immersive experiences. This could involve using available metadata or even making predictions to supplement the missing information. We hope TCube serves as a solid foundation for future developments in this area. In particular, we propose TCube as an essential tool for data storytelling in various domains and it could be useful for data analysts, scientists, and educators working with time-series data to create more engaging and easier-to-understand narratives, especially when presented with complex and intricate datasets. This could further lead to improved decision-making and communication among these professionals. These equations feature coefficients that experience moderate blow-up as sublogarithmic growth, represented by the function $|\ln t|^\gamma$ where $0 < \gamma < 1$. By applying a specific metric on the phase space, we can categorize these equations within a certain class of partial differential equations with controlled properties. Our findings reveal that the solutions for these equations exhibit a certain level of dependence on the initial data and may lose some regularity as time progresses. Notably, we are able to extend the work of Ralston, Fefferman, and Nakanishi, even though the coefficients in our equations may lose regularity at a slower rate. Our work also encompasses various special cases of partial differential equations, including equations with non-stationary coefficients, equations in multiple dimensions, and equations with complex properties. Furthermore, we are able to derive an estimate of the solution's dependence on its initial conditions, which may lose regularity as time progresses. This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese word segmentation using LSTM and GRU, this study tackles the more complex task of Japanese word segmentation which involves various character types such as hiragana, katakana, and kanji. These characters lead to significant orthographic variations and increase the difficulty of accurately segmenting Japanese words. To address this complexity, this study proposes an LSTM-based model for Japanese word segmentation, taking into consideration the essential global context. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed model attains exceptional accuracy when evaluated across different Japanese corpora. Notably, when testing on the Japanese WordNet corpus, this model achieved an f-score of 90.4%, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, when applying the model to more challenging corpora such as NIKL and JMD, the results demonstrated substantial improvements over previous methods. Specifically, the model showed an f-score improvement of 3.6% and 2.3% respectively. These outstanding results indicate that LSTM has the potential to significantly contribute to Japanese word segmentation tasks. Consequently, this study expects LSTM-based models to become the new standard approach for addressing this complex task. The ever-evolving nature of software development drives the need for developers to incorporate external resources, like APIs, into their codebase. This study investigates how frequently developers share external links on Stack Overflow and the impact of these links on the platform's knowledge base. Through an analysis of a large, weighted sample of 1.68 million question-and-answer posts, researchers uncovered a notable pattern of link sharing, totaling 16%, with just under half of these links targeting the same 2% of Stack Overflow users. Further examination revealed that links are often reused by multiple users to share external resources, such as GitHub repositories, YouTube tutorials, and blog posts, contributing to a growing problem of stale links on the platform. With a survival analysis, researchers estimated that 20% of these links become inoperable within the first year after being shared. The findings suggest a need for developers to utilize persistent identifiers, like DOIs, to maintain the accuracy and reliability of Stack Overflow's knowledge base. Potential research avenues, like employing machine learning algorithms or collaborative filtering to track and update external links, are also presented. Furthermore, the findings could guide developers in framing effective questions and utilizing the metadata associated with external links on the platform. Galactic rotation curves show an unexpected displacement, denoted by the displacement parameter $\alpha$. The extent of this phenomenon varies significantly among various galaxies, prompting a question about the underlying cause of this observed discrepancy. If the measured discrepancies are not solely due to observation errors, it implies that there must be substantial dark matter within some galaxies but not in others, which seems illogical. This study aims to address two primary concerns: first, how do common analysis methods for rotation curves affect the measured value of $\alpha$?  Second, how can the observed galaxy-to-galaxy differences in rotation curves be explained. Using realistic dwarf galaxy models, we simulate rotation curves and analyze them through common methods used in observational data, specifically including a weak lensing technique and an exponential fit approach. The results show that most standard analysis techniques yield a relatively small, consistent value for $\alpha$, which is around 1. The employed exponential fit can sometimes provide a second slope, enabling dark matter fractions and particle masses to be determined. However, these additional parameters are highly sensitive to the fitting model used and its complexity. Finally, the variation in rotation curves observed in galaxies can be attributed to uncertainties in astrophysical processes such as star formation and the gas flow that occurs during galaxy formation and evolution. Therefore, the parameter in question must be closely tied to baryonic processes. By applying the Bayesian inference method to our model, we conclude that a typical cosmological particle mass of approximately $10^{-13}$ GeV results in an approximately 10 times larger value of $\alpha$ and closely matches the observed galaxy-to-galaxy differences in rotation curves without requiring dark matter.  In our model, the observed variation in rotation curves is primarily accounted for by non-cosmological particle mass variations.  In contrast, the observed variation in rotation curves is difficult to explain using a single particle mass that is consistent across all galaxies, which implies that further astrophysical processes are necessary to fully explain the observed galaxy-to-galaxy differences in rotation curves.  Ultimately, the problem of diversity in galaxy rotation curves warrants further advancement in multiple fields including both astrophysics and particle physics.  Specifically, more accurate and nuanced simulations of galaxy evolution are needed along with experiments that can test particle masses using galaxy rotation curves as observational evidence.  By combining the insights from these fields, we can better understand the observed galaxy-to-galaxy differences in rotation curves.  In particular, our study indicates that the observed diversity in galaxy rotation curves is inconsistent with a simple dark matter hypothesis and instead requires an explanation

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from their errors. Despite initial expectations, however, its application in autonomous driving remains unfulfilled. This research project aims to tackle a few fundamental challenges within deep reinforcement learning, particularly its slow learning process and the likelihood of failing to generalize across diverse scenarios. Our investigation centers on autonomous driving as a real-world case study. To enhance the learning speed and adaptability of deep reinforcement learning, we introduce the concept of pretraining. Pretraining involves an agent undergoing a series of training sessions within a simulated environment before being transferred to real-world settings. A notable aspect of our study is the development of a comprehensive framework for integrated pretraining and testing of autonomous driving systems. This framework comprises a advanced driving simulator capable of handling a variety of roads and traffic scenarios. Additionally, we design an advanced agent architecture that integrates long-term planning with short-term decision-making, leveraging the strengths of both model-free and model-based methods in deep reinforcement learning. Model-free approaches enable the agent to adapt to unforeseen situations, while model-based planning ensures efficient navigation in familiar environments. A critical component of our generalization strategy involves selecting the most relevant samples from the pretraining environment and applying them to correct the agent's navigation skills in novel situations. To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted a series of experiments under different conditions, including the simultaneous presence of various objects on the road and in comparison with a deep reinforcement learning-based driving system without pretraining. These experiments resulted in a notable improvement in our method, with an average speed of 20 km/h faster and only 0.05% lower than the baseline in terms of lane deviation. To further assess our approach, we also analyzed the performance of a self-driving system during a 100-km long, real-world test drive. Following the initial adaptation period, our pretraining-based agent successfully navigated the road without human intervention, achieving a score of 4.5 out of 5 in a evaluation metric that combines speed and lane deviation. A video demonstrating the agent's performance in both simulated and real-world environments is available at https://youtu.be/7kK8S1mTLsY. To summarize, our investigation has led to the development of a generalised approach to deep reinforcement learning, with a notable application in autonomous driving. In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets. Unlike existing RNN models that rely on graded potential synapses for high accuracy, we introduce a novel approach using binary spikes which not only facilitates computation on spiking hardware but also enables synapses to assume a dynamic role within the network. We experimentally demonstrate that the resulting spiking RNN model can be trained to reach nearly perfect accuracy on small datasets and high accuracy on large datasets without requiring expensive synapse dynamics. Moreover, we find that these models are resilient to disruptions affecting both neuron and synapse parameters and can operate at a substantial fraction of their maximum spike rates, thus potentially paving the way for accurate AI classification in resource-constrained neuromorphic computing applications. We provide open-access to our model's source code and experimental datasets. Due to an error in our model's training process, our previous results appeared flawed and we recommend genetic algorithms as an accurate training method for binary synapses. This correction significantly expands our previous work by presenting a fully trainable spiking RNN model that can be trained using algorithms like Adam or SGD to reach high accuracy on complex datasets, thus upholding the promise of accurate and energy-efficient classification with spiking neural networks. We present a new model where the synapse dynamics are determined by the network itself, thus eliminating the need for expensive hardware. Our results show that this model achieves comparable accuracy to traditional neural networks with the added benefit of being resistant to disruptions and operating efficiently on spiking hardware. We experimentally verify our model on real spiking hardware, specifically the neuromorphic brain-scale chip called BrainScaleV6. This model's success significantly improves our previous work and we believe it has the potential to significantly advance the field of neuromorphic computing by allowing neural networks to accurately classify data while operating efficiently on spiking hardware. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. Our findings show that as the temperature increases, the radius of the star expands, and a strong magnetic field leads to a shrinkage of the radius. Additionally, we computed various thermodynamic properties such as energy density, pressure, chemical pressure, and causality condition for spin-polarized strange quark matter. A detailed analysis of our results demonstrates that spin-polarized strange quark matter can be a more dense and stable state of matter compared to non-polarized quark matter. Consequently, we anticipate that spin-polarized strange quark stars would be more dense and have larger radii than non-polarized quark stars. Utilizing our derived results, we calculated the mass, radius, and moment of inertia of spin-polarized strange quark stars, and our findings show significant variations depending on the magnetic field strength and temperature. A strong magnetic field produces more massive and larger-radius quark stars, and an increase in temperature leads to a decrease in mass and radius. Finally, we determined the parameters for the moment of inertia of spin-polarized strange quark stars as a function of temperature and magnetic field. Our results indicate that both temperature and magnetic field strength significantly impact the moment of inertia of spin-polarized strange quark stars. Ultimately, this research provides valuable insights into the structure and properties of spin-polarized strange quark stars under various environmental conditions. An analysis of our results may shed light on the underlying physics of quark matter and quark stars. A surge in personal device ownership offers an immense, yet largely underutilized resource of computational power, making it feasible to utilize it. To harness this potential, we developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing system based on JavaScript, running directly within web browsers. By integrating a self-contained sandbox environment, Pando isolates and secures both the client's personal activities from the distributed workload, as well as the distributed code itself. Key functionalities of Pando include a dynamic load-balancing system that allocates tasks to available browsers and browsable worker registries, enabling a decentralized approach that fosters trust among participants. To facilitate a practical implementation, we combined Pando with the Distributed Deep Learning Library, enabling a successful image classification demonstration utilizing a common desktop. This work aims to contribute to the advancement of volunteer computing as a robust and secure platform for a variety of applications and communities. A live demonstration of Pando is available at https://pando-vc.github.io/. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/pando-vc/pando. Additionally, a documentation of Pando is at https://pando-vc.github.io/docs/. Pando is currently open for community usage, and we welcome contributions that can be viewed on https://pando-vc.github.io/community/. Pando's performance has been extensively evaluated in a study, and can be accessed at https://pando-vc.github.io/evaluation/. It outlines the results of multiple experiments that supported the development of Pando, as well as an in-depth comparison with BOINC, showcasing Pando's notable advantages. BOINC is a prominent volunteer computing system with a long history of existence, and the mentioned study can be accessed at https://pando-vc.github.io/boinc-study/. Ultimately, our findings indicate that Pando excels at security, performance, and ease of use, and we believe that it holds potential to become the leading volunteer computing system moving forward. If you agree or disagree with our research, please feel free to engage in a discussion on https://pando-vc.github.io/discussion/. It would be great to have your input! In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data and model interactions, specifically introducing Flatee - an efficient federated learning framework across these environments, that substantially minimizes both training and communication times, while remaining robust against adversarial manipulation. By integrating techniques such as straggler detection, parallel training, early detection, and gradient batching, the authors successfully evaluate the efficacy of this framework, achieving considerable speedups - up to 2 times faster training and 6 times faster communication, all while remaining secure against adversarial attacks. Evaluation experiments, encompassing various scenarios like differing model sizes and communication disruptions, demonstrate the proposed framework's substantial performance advantage, empirically confirming its potential as a real-world solution. Lastly, the authors also showcase the adaptability of this framework, successfully implementing it on diverse platforms - Google Cloud TPU, Amazon SageMaker, and Microsoft Azure ML. Overall, this research presents a novel, performance-oriented approach to safeguarding federated learning model exchanges within various environments, addressing a limitation in previous state-of-the-art models and offering a general framework for efficient, secure collaboration among multiple parties. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for managing microservices deployed in Docker containers. Timeloops is a dynamic system-call filter enforcement framework that learns and applies precise time-based access controls to improve the security of microservices. The system utilizes a lightweight training process, based on regular expression matching, to create customized Deny/Allow policies for individual service operations. The efficient training time (on the order of microseconds) and compact policy size (less than 10 bytes) enable fast and scalable operation. Effective protection is achieved through integration with the Linux kernel, and a comprehensive evaluation demonstrates the performance and security benefits of Timeloops. By comparing it to existing systems, the results show that Timeloops outperforms other alternatives by a factor of 2-3 in terms of processing speed and achieves a processing speed similar to or higher than that of microservices components. Furthermore, Timeloops offers 2-4 times more robustness and security protection compared to other systems. The development of Timeloops has been facilitated by close collaboration between researchers and industry experts from top companies, and the source code is now available for public use at a specified repository address. Additionally, a detailed documentation of the training process has been provided. The effectiveness of Timeloops in real-world applications is illustrated through its successful integration in popular frameworks, such as Flask and Spring Boot, and a publicly accessible demo has been deployed to showcase its functionality. The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables and binary relations are examined in this study.  Specifically, we demonstrate that any such sentence, denoted as $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'$, utilizing the same number of variables and one symmetric binary relation, whose set of model cardinalities increases linearly with $\Phi$'s model cardinalities. Furthermore, we observe that the models of sentence $\Phi'$ are all bipartite graph representations.  Consequently, we deduce that, in order to resolve Asser's conjecture regarding the class's closure under complement, we may focus solely on examining sentences with at most three variables whose models consist of undirected bipartite graphs.  Additionally, we discuss the progression of related research since Bogdanovic's work in 1986.  Using our new framework, we reevaluate several known theorems and prove a few new ones regarding sentences with at least three variables whose models consist of undirected bipartite graphs.  In particular, we demonstrate that Bogdanovic's theorem, stating a sentence has a linear model size increase when modified to use three variables instead of one, also holds for sentences whose models consist of undirected bipartite graphs.  We also show that a sentence has a linear model size increase when modified to use three variables instead of two, though the three-variable sentence may require a distinct relation.  We discuss how these results relate to h-colorability systems and exhibit a complement to a known h-colorability system, resolving a problem initially posed by Bogdanovic in 1986.  We also discuss the closure under complement of classes of sentences whose models consist of undirected bipartite graphs for n variables, particularly highlighting the case where n equals one.  In this case, we resolve Asser's conjecture by showing the complement of any such class is in NP.  We also discuss additional research questions.  Specifically, we ask whether there exist sentences whose models consist of undirected bipartite graphs whose model cardinalities increase quadratically with the number of variables.  We also ask whether there exist sentences whose models consist of undirected bipartite graphs whose model cardinalities increase exponentially with the number of variables.  In examining these questions, we develop a simplified model that allows us to analyze linear system size changes in low-degree bipartite graph representations.  This model enables us to prove a theorem stating a sentence has a linear model size increase when modified to use three variables instead of one

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is often hampered by their limited resolution due to pixelation. Yet, the feasibility of relying on this method to rectify phase plate issues in TEM analysis is questionable. Given that high-resolution data is typically obtained through image segmentation, which involves magnifying specific regions, it's plausible that using these segments to directly project images could improve resolution without the need for pixelation reduction. Notably, the results showed that the programmable phase plate can correct certain aberrations more effectively than the conventional type, particularly in tasks requiring high spatial resolution. This finding suggests that the feasibility of employing programmable phase plates in TEM analysis is greater than previously thought. Furthermore, the experiments indicated that a single programmable phase plate can correct multiple types of aberrations, including spherical and higher-order astigmatism, through independent control of its electrostatic and magnetic fields. This capability, combined with the findings of previous studies on multipole correction, could enable the development of a general-purpose, multipurpose device for aberration correction in TEM analysis. This advancement could potentially lead to a major breakthrough in TEM analysis, enabling the resolution of individual atoms in the transmission electron microscope. By simulating a range of conditions, the researchers discovered new possibilities for its design and implementation, potentially leading to significant improvements in electron microscopy technologies. Ultimately, our findings were presented in a matrix representation as our primary theorem. Additionally, we provided a numerical example to demonstrate the accuracy of our derived equation. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. In the high temperature limit, however, the thermal capacity exhibits a temperature dependence characteristic of two-dimensional metals, with the coefficient influenced by interactions among Dirac electrons via a logarithmic correction. Furthermore, at intermediate temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a behavior reminiscent of "difficult metals," where the logarithmic correction is significant. In addition, we have used the derived correlation to examine the thermal screening length in doped graphene, revealing that at very low temperatures, the screening length exhibits a temperature dependence controlled by interactions among Dirac electrons, with a logarithmic temperature dependence. To facilitate experimental implementation, we have developed a plan to measure the thermal capacity of doped graphene using a magnetic lever arm, thereby capturing the material's full thermal budget rather than just the quadratic component that has been measured to date. In the process, we have identified a previously unexplored thermal channel, referred to as the "Fermi artery," which is a normal Fermi liquid component controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. Moreover, we have identified a previously unexplored mechanism, referred to as "Fermi artery collapse," which is a thermal screening effect driven by interactions among Dirac electrons via a logarithmic correction. Ultimately, we believe that the derived correlation and associated screening effects provide a foundation for understanding the unique thermal and electrostatic transport properties of 2D materials, which are currently understudied in the existing body of knowledge. Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to strategically crafted inputs that can manipulate their outputs, presenting potential security risks. This paper explores a new threat scenario, specifically Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks, where an adversary can deceive a classifier by intercepting and manipulating network traffic between a client and a server. To accomplish this, the adversary must create realistic data that mimics the actual traffic, allowing them to manipulate the classification process. By analyzing the limitations of current adversarial research and the potential of network traffic manipulation, this paper proposes a novel research direction - network traffic classification manipulation, and presents an empirical study of this threat model. An analysis of existing mitigation strategies for adversarial examples in relation to the MitM threat scenario is also provided. An empirical evaluation of the effectiveness of neural networks and GANs in mimicking HTTP traffic for two public datasets is conducted, revealing that neural networks and GANs can accurately classify up to 80% of traffic data with minimal error. Furthermore, this research demonstrates that an adversary can launch a MitM Attack by intercepting and manipulating network traffic, and presents potential applications and extensions for future research in this area. Our analysis focuses on whether such conspiracy theories are more widely shared by those who do not believe in climate change or those who do. Furthermore, we examine the most popular conspiracy theories, their variations with differing levels of climate change acceptance, and reveal that non-believers predominantly disseminate messages containing conspiracy theory-related keywords. Notably, all conspiracy theories are not equally prevalent. Our findings also highlight their implications for effective climate change communication strategies. Although scientists have utilized beams of numerous particles to make significant breakthroughs, creating and working with beams of antineutrons, specific hyperons and their counterparts has been notoriously challenging.
However, a recent high-tech research setup known as a super $J/\psi$ factory holds the potential to greatly improve access to these elusive particles. As a result, a huge number of $J/\psi$ decays occur annually, creating favorable conditions to accurately analyze these interactions using precision-tagging of co-produced particles. 
This state-of-the-art technology can facilitate groundbreaking studies of diverse targets and open doors for new particle and nuclear physics applications, such as studying antinucleon-nucleon interaction, properties of strange nucleons and nucleon-like particles, (anti)hyperon-nucleon interaction, exotic light hadrons and more, along with advancing our understanding of hypernuclei, calibration of computational simulations in hadronic physics and medicine, and exploring numerous other related topics. 
Moreover, this research setup can enable the development of second-generation high-technology experiments focused on unique $J/\psi$ production in proton-proton, antineutron-neutron, or other non-traditional ion collisions to uncover new insights in nuclear and particle physics. 
In conclusion, a super $J/\psi$ factory offers a vast array of opportunities for high-technology experiments that can greatly expand our knowledge of matter and its various forms. 
This article presents an in-depth analysis of the numerous possibilities these experiments can explore. 
Follow-up studies will concentrate on specific technical aspects, while present work aims to provide an overall framework for future research and technological development. 
It is essential to note that many proposed research avenues can benefit from existing or near-future experimental efforts, such as $e+/e-$ collider projects like CEPC, FCCee, ILC and CLIC.

The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes. Specifically, this approach extends the influential Mumford-Shah model, allowing for improved segmentation of gray-scale and vector-valued images affected by noise, blurriness, or missing data. Our model can be efficiently optimized using the alternating minimization algorithm, which converges under minimal conditions. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior segmentation results, particularly for blurry images and those with missing pixel values, outperforming existing state-of-the-art segmentation models. Furthermore, we showcase the effectiveness of this approach in performing boundary detection on spatiotemporal image sequences.
