Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. This research also provides upper limits on the masses of axions, assuming their non-observation through superradiance within certain ranges of black hole spins. The investigation further explores the potential for the detection of fractal structure in space-time through superradiance, analyzing a black hole of $10^7M_\odot$ as an example. Ultimately, we determine the upper limits on the parameters of Dirac-Bergman invisible axion particles and their relationship with magnetic monopoles. The information obtained within this research could be useful in the investigation of magnetic monopoles, ultralight bosons, and their connections to fundamental structure of space-time. This work is part of a broader research that examines superradiance as a tool for the exploration of black hole properties and potential indicators of black hole instability and decay, which could serve as a gateway to fundamental physics, including quantum gravity and its non-Newtonian properties. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of black hole instability and decay through superradiance could provide a link between theories of general relativity and quantum gravity. This work is also related to research on black holes as a potential detection tool for unique properties of quantum gravity, such as ultralight gravitons and other virtual particles with negative energy. Variations in the mass of these particles could be triggered by their decay into other particles, such as axions or fermions with very low masses. Creating intelligent, neuroinspired systems poses a significant challenge due to its underlying hardware complexities. To overcome these challenges, a thorough comprehension of its fundamental building blocks is essential, coupled with the development of straightforward and user-friendly prototyping tools. To address this issue, an open-source emulator was designed, utilizing the Brian simulator and seamlessly integrating with existing workflows. This emulator successfully emulated the behavior of spiking neural networks on a graph topology, with a variety of synaptic transmission mechanisms and neuronal dynamics, matching the performance of proven neuroscience models. Furthermore, it emulated the behavior of large-scale networks on single-core devices, with a network size of over 181,000 neurons, surpassing the capabilities of current conventional emulators. This emulator will facilitate the development of novel algorithms to tackle challenging computational tasks. Additionally, it will serve as a resource to showcase the wide range of applications possible within neuromorphic computing. We now have the opportunity to push the boundaries of what emulated neural systems can achieve. This study lays the foundation for a comprehensive understanding of neural microcircuit cognition by integrating proven neuroscience principles into a readily usable platform. It enables researchers to explore, explain, and derive key insights about neural circuits, ultimately paving the way for innovative neuroinspired algorithm designs. Conversely, this study's findings will guide neuroengineers in crafting hardware systems that are both theoretically grounded and practically effective. Finally, this integration of theoretical and hardware concerns will foster cross-disciplinary collaboration among bioinformaticians, neuroscientists, and hardware engineers. Emerging hardware systems such as the Loihi chip provide a catalyst for these developments. We believe that our results will serve as a prototype model, emulating biological neural systems in software before their biological counterparts are fully understood. This reverse engineering approach will likely shape the future development of real neural systems. In particular, we believe that our model will derive value from its ability to derive and demonstrate novel hardware features, such as triggerable spiking junctions, through the emulation of integral neuromorphic loops. This approach will derive additional benefits from its emphasis on transparency, as demonstrated by the consistent correspondence between brain source code and hardware target code. This emphasis on clarity can also serve an educational purpose, facilitating learning neural computing concepts through the examination of the simulator's source code. This study demonstrates the feasibility and efficiency of the Brian2Loihi emulator, providing a platform for neuroscientists and engineers to test ideas and explore the capabilities of neuromorphic computing systems. We anticipate that the emulator will be an essential tool for developing novel hardware

A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. By analyzing data from the Rapid Imaging Variability Coud\'e Spectropolarimeter, researchers found a pattern of decreasing source size associated with increasing source position in active regions experiencing type-I noise storms. It was discovered that the area of the source ($A_\perp$) correlates with the beam's electron density ($N_e$) and its divergence ($D$), but only when the beam's curvature ($\kappa$) is considered, reveals important insights into the storm's evolution. Data showing the correlation between $A_\perp$ and $N_e$ or $D$ suggests that during a storm in AR NOAA 1211, fine-scale magnetic field instability leads to an increase in $N_e$ and $D$, resulting in a significant enhancement of the storm's radiation power. The involvement of the magnetic reconnection process in this phenomenon is also considered. It was observed that the ratio of the storm's peak power to its area ($P/A_\perp$) serves as an indicator of the beam's curvature, which is likely influenced by the magnetic field's helicity, making this a promising method for evaluating the storm's effects on solar plasmas. The research paves the way for future studies on the influence of solar storm-like phenomena on the Earth's atmosphere. Based on the data, a new diagnostic method for evaluating the curvature of solar type-I noise storm source has been established. It was found that the curvature of storm sources in some active regions is consistently positive, while it varies between negative and positive in others. Furthermore, it was discovered that during a microflare in AR NOAA 12107, the area of the storm source increases, but only when considering the beam's curvature, which is negatively correlated with the storm's electron density and divergence. Using the Euclidean distance, researchers classified the curvature of storm sources as either curved inwardly or outwardly, depending on specific criteria. Based on this classification, it was determined that curved outwardly sources are associated with flares and strong magnetic field instabilities. Additionally, researchers developed a new statistical method to evaluate the significance of curved outwardly sources in various active regions. It was discovered that curved outwardly sources are more common in close proximity to flare epicenters. A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated design that merges an optical grating chip and a magnetic coil chip. This novel setup minimizes the size and weight of the trap, requiring only a single laser beam to capture a population of approximately 10,000 cold rubidium atoms. The improved MOT architecture has potential applications in devices such as gravimeters, atomic clocks, and quantum memory systems, offering a reduction in volume, weight, and complexity. The setup's performance has been thoroughly evaluated in terms of atom capture efficiency, magnetic coil efficiency, and overall system optical properties. The planar-integrated MOT exhibits exceptional planarity, with a typical height of less than 5 micrometers, and is encapsulated within a thin silicon substrate less than 500 micrometers thick. The effectiveness of this design has been confirmed through a detailed study of the atom cloud's temperature, number of particles, and overall velocity distribution. The planar-integrated MOT presents an innovative solution for miniature atomic physics applications. The setup's performance and design innovations are presented in detail, along with future development pathways for this cutting-edge technology. The planar-integrated design offers a pioneering solution for small-scale MOT systems, showcasing its potential as a versatile tool in atomic physics research. The setup's development and characterization serve as a model for designing and implementing miniature atomic physics systems. The described technique could be applied to various species of atoms and is compatible with a range of packaging technologies, including both wafer bonding and assembly using standard IC infrastructure. The primary challenge of minimizing the laser beam's size has been overcome through a combination of technical innovations and design enhancements. The resulting compact MOT is capable of capturing a substantial number of atoms, with a cold atom cloud characterized by low temperature, optimal velocity distribution, and sufficient particle density. The planar-integrated MOT is an exemplary design for atomic physics research, with a small size, low size-to-function ratio, and exceptional performance capabilities. The described design is highly adaptable and can be applied to develop miniature systems for magneto-optical traps, atomic clocks, gravimeters, quantum memory, and other advanced atomic physics research platforms. The setup's development and results can guide the design and implementation of these innovative magnetic traps. The characterization of the compact MOT reveals a temperature of approximately 170 microkelvin for rubidium atoms, with an atom cloud shape that closely resembles a Gaussian distribution, and a number of particles in the range of 10,000 to 20,000. The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established boundary conditions at a distant point, we examine this process within a limited sphere. We use a series of asymptotic solutions and a version of the Fickian diffusion equation to understand the behavior of particles near the black hole's event horizon. These solutions indicate a finite number of particles can cross the event horizon at any given time. At very small times, an almost spherical distribution of particles occurs, and our findings show the mass accreted per unit time is similar to the Bondi accretion rate. However, due to angular momentum, a kinetic cloud's accretion rate is reduced by a factor of four compared to a kineticless cloud, especially at very small times. Additionally, a modified version of the Fickian diffusion equation is proposed that accounts for particles not crossing the event horizon as quickly. This model indicates a "leakage" of particles that reduces the accretion rate by a factor of four. Considering a kinetic cloud as consisting of an inner part that's almost kineticless and an outer part with sufficient angular momentum, leads to a fundamental understanding of the accretion rate. The inner part determines the accretion rate, whereas the outer part contributes to angular momentum. Consequently, a kineticless gas would be the primary driver of accretion, and the accretion rate would be largely insensitive to the radius of the cloud. Therefore, a kineticless model is proposed that can be used to calculate accretion rates for more realistic scenarios. Such a scenario is comparable to a kineticless cloud that loses energy but no angular momentum, and remains bound to the black hole. As a result, observations of accretion onto black holes in our universe may provide insight into the kinetic properties of matter at very small lengths scales. Furthermore, a kineticless model has significant implications for our understanding of hydrodynamic accretion and processes involving kineticless matter, particularly in extreme environments such as black holes and neutron stars. Finally, a kineticless model could be useful in future studies of hydrodynamic accretion and kineticless matter, and may lead to novel and interesting phenomena in various contexts. In particular, a kineticless model could explain how a kinetic cloud's angular momentum is transferred to a kineticless inner part and a kinetic outer part near the event horizon. The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a thin, perfect mirror. As the atom faces the mirror, its initial velocity can either trigger emission or result in the absorption of energy. If the atom is initially at rest, no radiation is produced unless its position is measured, in which case the vacuum state gives way to a superposition of atomic states corresponding to de-excitation or to the absorption of radiation. Similar effects are observed when the atom is moving: radiation is emitted only if its velocity exceeds a certain threshold, and the probability distribution of emitted photon energy exhibits a characteristic "bulge on a hillside". The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for an atom initially at rest, but with a catch - only the atom and the radiation field are considered, with the mirror treated as a semi-infinite potential barrier. It is found that atomic (de-)excitation and photon emission can be triggered not only by the atom's initial velocity, but also by its acceleration, which is inherently connected with radiation emission. The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for an atom moving in a direction perpendicular to its initial velocity, and the observed effects are analoga to those encountered when the atom is moving in the direction of the radiation wave. The observed features of radiation emission, including a low-emission "bulge on a hillside", are common to all the scenarios considered, and it is argued that these features should be easily detectable in experiments involving cold atoms. In particular, it is proposed that radiation emission, low-emission "bulge on a hillside", and photon-induced atomic excitation should be studied in experiments involving not only atoms, but also electrons and uncharged bosons interacting with a thin mirror. It is conjectured that a correct understanding of these phenomena would require a quantum treatment of all three "particles", and that such a treatment would be in line with the general principles of quantum mechanics. It is further conjectured that a correct description of these phenomena would lead to a breakdown of the long-standing semi-classical relation between electromagnetic field and charged particles. It is finally conjectured that a correct understanding of these phenomena would result in a considerable revision of our current understanding of the processes involved in particle detection, atomic excitation, and photon emission. A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to test this hypothesis more effectively.  In this research, we identify the massive stars located near the dense cluster Westerlund 2 and examine their spectral types, luminosities, and spatial connections to the cluster.  The results indicate that despite dominating the near-cluster landscape, highly luminous OB stars are scarce.  The absence of extremely luminous OB stars in the region, along with the presence of several runaway stars near Westerlund 2, lead us to speculate that cluster disruption may be the key factor explaining the presence of this group of Ober in the region.  The properties of the Ober stars, including their velocities and spatial distributions, predict that some of these stars, such as HD$93162A and HD$95168, may have escaped the cluster in a velocity range of ~50-100 km/s.  The cross-matching of the catalogue with Gaia DR2 data reveals three hot stars with extragalactic velocities among the Ober group, which could be O stars originating from nearby dwarf galaxies. An alternative explanation for the extragalactic velocities of these hot stars involves their being runaway stars with extreme velocities, which could have resulted from binary interactions within the cluster. Additionally, the velocities of massive stars located near Westerlund 2, particularly those with masses above 10 Msun, suggest the presence of an asymmetric velocity distribution, which is consistent with a rotating bar-shaped structure in space. The most massive stars with extragalactic velocities or extreme velocities tend to be located further away from the centre of the cluster in a direction towards the massive star cluster, CLUMPFIND-3. A hypothetical explosion of a massive star in this region could release ~ 1.15E49 ergs of energy within the time frame of one year, which might be sufficient to explain the recently observed outburst in this area. Future observations in the cluster are needed to confirm the asymmetric velocity pattern, the origins of hot stars with extragalactic velocities, and the presence of extremely luminous OB stars in the region. The data are available at https://github.com/ivanarmahidalgo/Westerlund2/tree/main-data. This research has been carried out using data, code and software from the following resources: PyAlqub, PyRAA, RAAbuilder, raabuilder GitHub, TOPCAT

This pioneering method differs from existing binarization techniques, which primarily focus on enhancing visual quality, by integrating a text recognition module to optimize output generation. We validate the effectiveness of our model through comprehensive experiments on the aging of handwritten texts dataset, showcasing its superior performance across various evaluation metrics, particularly in the recognition of degraded texts. Additionally, our model demonstrates remarkable efficiency in terms of computational resources required. A significant finding is that a pre-trained model can achieve impressive results on the target dataset with minimal fine-tuning, emphasizing its versatility and practical applications. Lastly, our model architecture, source code, and associated datasets are freely available on GitHub for worldwide access. With its ability to enhance both visual quality and readability, our model has vast potential for document restoration and recovery tasks. Lastly, we will delve into the theoretical foundations of our model to provide a solid theoretical framework for the research community. We anticipate these advancements to contribute positively to the fields of document processing and Generative Adversarial Networks. We will soon make significant updates to our model, which we will freely share on GitHub, accompanied by a detailed explanation of our research progress. We intend to present our findings at renowned international conferences, including ICDAR2022 and DRR2022, where we will demonstrate the efficacy of our model in written document recognition tasks. We aim to publish our work in prestigious journals, including IEEE and Springer.

In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in diverse and rapidly changing channels. To overcome these challenges, this research proposes an innovative low-complexity estimation method leveraging deep learning techniques. By utilizing deep learning, the proposed estimator leverages the spatial diversity inherent in multi-antenna systems, enabling more accurate channel estimation. Furthermore, integration of temporal averaging enables enhanced interference suppression, resulting in the optimal outcome. By optimizing structure and input data, the proposed estimator achieves substantial reductions in model complexity, enabling its practical implementation on real-time systems. According to the simulation results, the proposed estimator surpasses IEEE 802.11p and least mean square (LMS)-based methods by approximately 30 dB in the minimum mean squared error (MMSE) metric. Additionally, the proposed method demonstrates superior 10% BER performance over industry-standard IEEE 802.11p. Notably, the complexity of the proposed estimator is within the practical limits of real-time implementation, further validating its efficacy. To verify its practical applicability, the proposed estimator was successfully implemented and tested on an USRP B200mini board. Due to its lightweight design, the proposed estimator is suitable for deployment on real-time systems. To verify its in-field accuracy, the proposed estimator was tested in a controlled outdoor environment, showcasing its superior performance under diverse channel conditions. To facilitate its practical use, the research team openly shares the source code on GitHub, enabling widespread adoption of the estimator. As a result, the proposed estimator sets a high standard for deep learning-based channel estimation, addressing the industry's long-standing challenge of channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. To achieve this, the innovation involves integrating low-complexity deep learning with the temporal averaging technique, overcoming previous estimators' limitations through structure optimization and input data selection. Consequently, the proposed estimator achieves exceptional performance, setting a new benchmark for industry adoption. To ensure transparency and reproducibility, the research team publicly shares the source code on GitHub, facilitating broad implementation of the estimator. To promote its practical use, the research team is collaborating with industry partners to apply the estimator in real-world scenarios. To facilitate understanding, the governance details are available upon request. To ensure public understanding, the research details are openly available on arXiv, providing a publicly viewable document.

Another related issue is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves converting low-resolution images into higher-resolution versions. This research targets a novel, automatic colorization approach, specializing in astronomical images and leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on tedious iterative processes. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our proposed algorithm rapidly achieves low error rates in the regression and classification of intricate datasets, such as the Griewank function and the MNIST database for handwritten digits. Its mathematical formulation allows it to accurately approximate highly complex nonlinear functions with a minimal margin of error, and it also facilitates the solution of Partial Differential Equations. The annihilation of error terms in conjunction with the Uniqueness Theorem for Fourier Series analysis underpins the success of this weight calculation method. Furthermore, our findings reveal that increasing the number of weights leads to lower error rates in a wide range of scenarios. In a comparative study using the MNIST dataset, our Fourier Series-based approach outperformed the conventional Backpropagation algorithm, resulting in a training error rate of approximately 4% and a testing error rate of about 10%. Notably, the weight calculation method derived from our Fourier Series analysis boasts the advantage of being highly parallelizable. Consequently, implementing it using Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) or Field-Programmable Array (FPGAs) devices would yield substantial speedup in computation time. In a parallel computation experiment using the MNIST dataset, our approach exhibited a 4x speedup compared to the Backpropagation algorithm when utilizing 8 GPUs devices. Therefore, this weight calculation method may hold significant potential for advancing the development of ANN-based applications. In a sense, this method can be viewed as a weight regression technique based on the Fourier Series analysis. Unlike existing ANN models based on iterative processes or gradient descent, this novel method allows for rapid weight calculation in a hyperparameter-independent manner. Consequently, it may lead to the development of truly data-driven models. Unlike existing Fourier Series-based regression methods, our approach enables the simultaneous calculation of all weights from a 1D input signal, thereby facilitating broad applications. This weight regression technique may hold potential for solving numerous nonlinear regression and classification problems, and it could also be used to approximate solutions to Partial Differential Equations and Navier-Stokes equations. In a sense, this method can be viewed as an extension of the Fourier Series analysis paradigm to the regime of ANN-based weight calculation. Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces called dual metasurfaces. These line waves have the ability to switch quickly between different states, making them suitable for use in compact devices that manipulate light at an optical scale. A recent innovation in line wave technology involves the Metasurface Holography concept, enabling the concurrent control of line waves and propagating modes. This has the potential to revolutionize the field by enabling complex spatial structures to be generated through the steering of line waves. This technology could be utilized to create various optical effects such as high-resolution focusing, phase modulation, and polarization conversion. This research aims to explore the theoretical foundations and applications of line wave Metasurface Holography. First, we establish the general framework for line wave holography and present a figure-of-merit to gauge its effectiveness. Next, we propose two ideal scenarios for line wave holography, one that can generate arbitrary two-dimensional focusing and another that can create three-dimensional focusing. Finally, we apply line wave holography to achieve two innovative functions: a nanoscale, compact lens and an optical element that can switch between focusing and polarization conversion. These innovative ideas are expected to be of great value in designing new optical devices at an nanoscale. This approach can be extended beyond optical applications and potentially used in other fields such as conventional radio waves and terahertz radiation. This gives line wave Metasurface Holography vast potential for use in various cutting-edge technologies. One of the most effective approaches to building intelligent robotic systems is Learning from Demonstration (LfD), a method that has shown considerable success across various applications. However, several challenges remain, such as designing architectures capable of adapting to unforeseen situations and integrating well-established techniques like multi-agent learning, collaborative human-robot interaction, and large-scale distributed computing. To address these issues, we introduce modifications to the LfD architecture in four key areas: 1) a unified cognitive architecture for integrating various LfD techniques, 2) multi-agent learning models for predicting human demonstrations, 3) a collaborative interaction framework, and 4) a distributed computing system. To evaluate the enhanced architecture's performance, we conduct experiments in two complex domains: predictive modeling and collision-free navigation. The results of these studies, involving human-robot collaboration in large-scale environments, are presented as a foundation for future advancements in this field. The developed architecture and associated code are accessible on GitHub for free use by the research community. Additionally, the related data can be found on our lab's website. Emerging technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and robotics are now more significant than ever in various applications, leading to a growing interest in advanced cognitive architectures for integrating these technologies effectively. As a result, we believe that multi-agent collaborative learning in large-scale human-robot settings will play a crucial role in further accelerating the development of robust and efficient robotic systems. To validate this belief, we demonstrate the practical implementation and successful outcomes of an enhanced Learning from Demonstration (LfD) architecture in this study. The architecture in question is remarkably versatile, allowing the integration of various cutting-edge LfD techniques, prediction of human demonstrations using multi-agent learning models, collaborative interaction through human-robot collaboration, and distribution of computing processes. The effectiveness of this architecture is proven through collaborative human-robot activities in two complex domains, including collision-free navigation and predictive modeling. To facilitate future advancements, we also contribute open-source code on GitHub for implementing the architecture and present related data on our lab's website. A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  To overcome this limitation, a specific alternative strategy was implemented.  Establishing the bias correction involves verifying the local asymptotic normality property and a specific Bahadur-Kiefer representation.  Developed within the context of a traditional asymptotic framework, this proposal appears to retain effectiveness in high-dimensional settings, as evidenced by simulation results.  While the approach is designed to be simple and versatile, certain modifications are necessary to account for the effects of irrepresentability and compressivity.  A primary advantage of the proposal is that it yields an unbiased estimate of the median regression mean absolute deviation; however, this can only be realized under specific large-sample conditions.  A test statistic based on the proposed estimator has been defined and demonstrates the ability to correctly reject hypotheses in certain instances.  Although the approach is not consistent, a specific threshold has been determined above which the test's power exceeds that of classical tests.  A comprehensive framework for implementing the proposal's ideas has been developed through the implementation of a publicly available R package.  Continuous efforts are being made to expand the approach to the context of quadratic regression. The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy. Furthermore, we introduced a straightforward
evaluation metric to assess a model's ability to maintain accurate entropy in
predicting a subject's associated objects, providing a more comprehensive
assessment beyond traditional F1 scores. Our experiments revealed that current
state-of-the-art models could be improved through multi-task training, resulting in
an average 1.1% improvement in F1 score and 1.3% improvement in our proposed
entropy-based metric. Detailed analysis also showed that multi-task training
induced less data bias in models, leading to more robust and reliable
performances. Additionally, our study explored multi-task training under
knowledge graph link prediction's confidence thresholding and data scarcity
conditions. In a remarkable finding, we observed that multi-task training could
be applied even to models developed through simplified approaches, such as BERT.
Overall, our research demonstrated the potential of multi-task training in
relation extraction models, urging future developers to experiment with this
approach. The code and model configurations employed in this study have been
made publicly available. 

\textit{Note: A preliminary version of this paper was initially published in 2020
under the title "Exploring Multi-task Training for Relation Extraction," in
Proceedings of the Second International Conference on Automation of Software
Engineering (ASE '20).}

In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structure of deep learning systems, deriving the tangent space for convolutional neural networks and developing a curvature metric that regulates overfitting. Furthermore, we generalize the geometric model to include new architectures such as graph neural networks, transformer networks, and vector neural networks. By reimagining deep learning through a geometric lens, we unlock a unified theoretical framework that can guide the design and development of deep learning systems. The proposed geometric model also facilitates a comprehensive mathematical analysis of deep learning, enabling the derivation of generalization errors and optimal solution distributions. Experimental validation demonstrates that training deep learning systems to achieve optimal geometric curvature yields improved generalization performance. Moreover, the geometric model enables the seamless integration of geometric regularization techniques from the field theory community, the information bottleneck approach from the learning community, and the geometric structure of deep learning systems discovered in our study, providing a comprehensive understanding of deep learning generalization performance. Additionally, we show that the geometric model can be used to derive lower bounds on the generalization error of deep learning systems. The theoretical framework developed in this study consists of five main contributions. Firstly, we establish that deep learning systems can be geometrically structured. Secondly, we show that the geometric structure of deep learning systems offers a unified framework for analyzing a broad range of architectures. Thirdly, we use the geometric model to study the generalization performance of deep learning systems. Fourthly, we demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the geometric model in improving the generalization performance of deep learning systems. Lastly, we provide insights into the fundamental characteristics of deep learning systems that can inform future research. The integration of geometric model-based deep learning training, which we terms deep learning with geometric regularization, outperforms numerous benchmark methods in multiple experiments. The success of our deep learning models is further validated by their exceptional performance in the ImageNet classification challenge. The geometric model and associated algorithms have also been made available for public use. Furthermore, we have open-sourced the code used in this study, enabling other researchers to replicate our results. A simple method is introduced to uncover the decision-making processes behind deep neural network classifiers, specifically jet substructure taggers. By tracing back the influence of input images to specific objects within them, our approach reveals how taggers select jets with distinct structures. We demonstrate that this method accurately matches the behavior of traditional jet-based clustering techniques, and we utilize it to examine the role of jets with high-purity grooming tools, like the Hadronic Near-InfraRed (HNIR). We find that HNIR focuses primarily on the region at the tip of the jet, and this is consistent with its original description. Additionally, we analyze an internal competition that arises within the network, where substructures within jets can be prioritized over others, and this includes the inner regions of the jet. We observe that this effect is more pronounced in the HNIR tool. Finally, we estimate the performance gain that could be achieved if networks were trained explicitly on key features of jets, such as their structure, and how objects within them are correlated. We find that this could potentially yield improvements of up to a 30% improvement over current baseline performance. These findings are consistent for several different jet substructure tagging tasks that we studied. Ultimately, we propose that the method we've developed could be adapted to uncover the underlying workings of a wide range of deep neural networks, and this includes classification networks, as well as those that perform tasks that are even more complex and varied. Additionally, we specify a method that could be used to train networks in a more informative way, and this could lead to notable improvements in performance. A publication outlining these results in further detail is available, and associated code, including network implementations, as well as additional propagation results, is available at https://github.com/crcv-ugent/ReProVe. This work is an extension of an existing publication. We acknowledge the support of the CERIT-ART infrastructure, as well as computing resources provided by IT4Innovative, in our research. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, the altered contour may require the use of complex-valued action clusters in the simulation algorithm, presenting a challenge for standard neural network applications that typically assume real-valued actions. Additionally, we find that with sufficient depth, convolutional neural networks can replicate the performance of fully connected networks, even with complex-valued inputs and outputs. This implementation enables the extension of within-function methods to systems with a large number of electrons. Using this method, we have obtained density data for the 2D Hubbard model at intermediate temperatures, which reveals the coexistence of superconducting and insulating phases. This phase coexistence is in agreement with existing literature and our results differ from those obtained using the constrained path or Lefshetz fixed-point formalism. This finding suggests that the sign transformation and within-function techniques can complement each other in addressing the sign problem. Furthermore, we have found that at half-filling in the 2D Hubbard model, the within-function formalism yields results comparable to constrained path results, especially for low temperatures. In contrast, for the 3D Hubbard model at half-filling, within-function results are closer to those obtained with the Lefshetz fixed-point formalism. To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains. Specifically, we investigate how to select the most effective languages for adaptation, the number of languages to include in a training batch, and the potential benefits of preemptively training on low-resource languages before adding new ones. Overall, our findings indicate that by targeting languages with the highest performance deficits, adapting a small, high-quality model can achieve improved results with reduced computational requirements. With a modest 7-day training period, our enhanced model demonstrates notable improvements in zero-shot learning tasks, yielding a 43.2% average performance boost for the two added languages. Additionally, we observe a 54.3% drop in adapter size, and our model achieves a 27.5% higher overall score than the baseline model on the GLUE benchmark. Notably, integrating Korean, a language with complex phonology and syllable structure, necessitates a longer adaptation period and more training data than adapting German. This process is self-organizing and thus requires a strong interaction, characteristic of materials such as $\bf TiSe_2$, $\bf TiS_2$, and $\bf TaON$. We have developed an ab initio method, combining a first-principles density functional theory framework with a first-order perturbation theory, to describe exciton condensation. This approach, when applied to $\bf TiSe_2$, shows good agreement with existing experimental and experimental results, including the excitonic potential, lattice distortion, and superconducting properties. A corresponding action for the excitonic pair was derived and found to be in harmony with experimental data. We have also observed that the obtained pair wave function displays a significant coherence and exhibits a quasi-long-range pair order with $\bf q$-vector approximately equivalent to $\bf 0.06\pi$ ($\bf 0.18\pi$) in the lattice constant. This pattern of quasi-long-range order directly contributes to the $\bf 2b$ ($\bf 2a$) lattice distortion observed in $\bf TiSe_2$ and $\bf TiS_2$ and explains the formation of a low-symmetry group with monoclinic characteristics. In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based systems for processing community members' incident reports, which necessitated a closer look at interactions between community members and dispatchers through these platforms. To investigate, researchers analyzed the system logs of LiveSafe, a community safety tool, combining quantitative and qualitative methods to identify patterns in the conversational flow. By developing a data framework that captured common incident-related information, researchers discovered dispatchers' proactive responses, such as asking questions, helped reveal this information. Furthermore, analysis of the system logs enabled researchers to identify the sequential prunability, which indicated the feasibility of reducing the number of messages exchanged between users and dispatchers. By applying the prunability model, researchers were able to design an optimized conversation protocol, which resulted in a 30% decrease in the total number of messages and improved human-computer conversation. Additionally, the proposed approach facilitated data collection with parallel probes and allowed human reviewers to verify the effectiveness of proposed changes. The proposed methodology facilitated the discovery of hidden facts of user-dispatcher interactions, which Original Research value ultimately led to the improvement of the LiveSafe system. The system, which was based on the findings, was eventually adopted by safety organizations across the US. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the random phase approximation. In the presence of spin-triplet Cooper pairs, we observe a paramagnetic response, characteristic of Pauli paramagnetism, when the superconducting order parameter's spin component aligns with the external magnetic field. This behavior is seen in all computed channels. Moreover, we find that the magnitude of magnetic susceptibility is proportional to the superconducting density of states at the Fermi level and exhibits opposite signs between the two spin components. This study also confirms that the superconducting state's time-reversal symmetry breaking is inextricably linked to the nematic order parameter, as expressed through the London equation's inelastic term. Finally, we have computationally determined the ratio of magnetic susceptibility to superconducting density of states, which we found to be in the range of $-\mu\hbar^2/D(\mu)$ to $-\mu\hbar^2/D(0)$, with specific values of $4.1\times 10^{-3}$ eV J/C and $3.2\ttimes 10^{-3}$ eV J/C, respectively. These outcomes contribute to a deeper comprehension of nematic superconductors' magnetic properties and may contribute to the measurement and control of nematic superconductors' magnetic properties. This work may also facilitate research into magnetic properties of other triplet superconductors through the inspection of their density of states.  Ultimately, we hope that our findings will guide experiments examining magnetic properties in nematic superconductors.  Specifically, we anticipate that our results will stimulate investigation of nematic superconductors' magnetic properties and their response to external magnetic fields. Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then select the samples with the highest entropy that the discriminator identifies as unlabeled for human annotation. Experimental evaluation on image classification and semantic segmentation datasets demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The proposed approach is implemented in the ALtoolbox Python library. For more information, visit our website at altoolbox.github.io. A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves sequences of random, multi-dimensional symbol strings whose associated probabilities can be learned through reinforcement learning algorithms designed for single-dimensional data. This paper explores one such multiple-entry reinforcement process, examining its long-term properties as the reinforcement process converges towards equilibrium under specific conditions. Our analysis reveals that, in the equilibrium state, the distribution of single-dimensional data converges towards a mixture of the underlying probability distribution and a Dirac delta function. Additionally, the mean rewards obtained by the reinforcement learning algorithm follow a specific asymptotic pattern determined by the underlying probability distribution, and this mean reward achieves its maximum value in a range that broadens as the reward function's convexity increases. Our findings can be applied to random matrix theory, yielding unexpected correlations between single-dimensional data and the eigenvalues of such matrices. These correlations hold significance in various real-world contexts, such as network traffic and image recognition. Our conclusions are validated through numerical simulations presented in this paper. Our work resolves an existing challenge in multi-entry reinforcement learning, providing a theoretical framework that can be adapted to various reinforcement learning algorithms and probability distributions with unique properties. One potential area of exploration involves extending our results to higher-dimensional data in physics, where rewards could represent physical quantities such as energy rather than probabilities. Similarly, our findings can be applied to machine learning models in computer science, where mean rewards could be replaced by accuracy metrics and convolution functions. Our research offers a general framework that can be applied to various models and algorithms in both science and engineering due to its broad applicability. Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework. Furthermore, by translating intuitionistic natural deduction into Computational Ludics, this study shows that the harmony condition retains its essential proof-theoretic meaning. Ultimately, this analysis offers a deeper understanding of the very concepts that have defined proof-theoretic research for decades. This new insight also sheds light on the relationship between specific notions of harmony, particularly when restricted to single-handed proofs, as examined in a companion paper. This research expects to contribute positively to ongoing research into proof fragments and notions of harmony. This material is an expanded version of the arXiv paper 2101.08521. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Additional benefits include improved robustness to noisy comparisons and enhanced exploration by the agents. We demonstrate the time savings from using our method can be up to 9 times more efficient than traditional approaches. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/VisAssistRL.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps, initially modeling treatment and outcome to incorporate potential confounders, then applying predictions to ATE estimators, such as AIPW, with potential alternatives being Machine Learning algorithms due to their non-parametric nature and capability to handle complex relationships. In order to improve the efficiency of two NN models with no parameter regularization except SGD, our simulations indicate the significant drawbacks that arise when AIPW is used. In an effort to improve this, the proposed nAIPW offers the same double robustness and orthogonality as AIPW and can achieve asymptotic normality under specific conditions. Additionally, when imposing L1 regularization on the first step NN models with convergence, nAIPW along with L1 ATE estimators proves to be consistent and asymptotically normal. Importantly, this new method demonstrates superior performance within both large and small sample sizes, yielding more accurate results when using L1 predicted ATE compared to the unregulated version. It is essential to note that the implementation of L1 regularization leads to suboptimal bias but this bias can be eliminated by making the prediction function invertible and taking its derivative. Consequently, with the application of nAIPW along with L1 predicted ATE, researchers can enjoy both efficient model parameter values and accurate causal effect estimates. In a real-world context, this is exemplified through data analysis of applicants to US graduate school between 2010-2014. Using Python's Black and Isort for code formatting, our results showcase the effectiveness of the proposed method. In order to ensure the reproducibility of our findings, the code used for this research is attached within this report. It is also publicly accessible through link. The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in the current research into lepton flavor universality violations in B-physics, warranting greater theoretical attention in the coming years. Enhanced data samples from Belle-II, as well as LHCb, ATLAS, and CMS, will be crucial in further investigating the topic. Additionally, insights from $\tau$ decays into its spin will be particularly beneficial. If experimental findings of new physics prevail, it is anticipated that new CP-odd phases will be required by naturalness arguments. Considering the relatively small $\tau$ mass compared to B-meson masses, it offers a highly advantageous scenario for in-depth lattice studies, which could significantly boost the precision in testing the SM and potential BSMs. In this context, studying $\tau$ decays into hadrons and $\tau$ nuclear interactions will be crucial. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of theoretical understanding, followed by an in-depth discussion of the advantages lattice simulations can offer. Lastly, relevant challenges and objectives for future research are highlighted. A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the general circulation of mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. The device effectively replicates two crucial factors contributing to cyclogenesis, namely the influence of rotation and temperature variations, in a simplified laboratory environment. The annulus is filled with glycerin water, which offers a distinct set of properties compared to traditional water, thereby enabling an in-depth examination of the setup's dynamics. The research involves both numerical and experimental investigations, focusing on the setup's response to different initial and boundary conditions. Specifically, the studies revealed that even small impurities can significantly disrupt the baroclinic wave instability, leading to chaotic system behavior. This research is primarily presented to address questions surrounding a benchmark experiment designed to test the reliability of numerical models in complex geophysical contexts. The findings can also be applied to assess model validity and guide the development of more accurate geophysical models. The research is further relevant to investigations exploring the dynamics of atmospheric systems, such as cyclones and anticyclones, and similar geophysical flows, which exhibit quasi-geostrophic baroclinic wave dynamics. The studies offer a fresh perspective on the dynamics of glycerin, which can stimulate research in this area. Lastly, the researchers outline the steps required to establish a benchmark test, emphasizing the importance of straightforward results to validate geophysical models in the future. Conversely, some intriguing phenomena observed during the experiments remain unexplained to date and may contribute to novel theoretical and conceptual advancements in geophysical dynamics. Ultimately, the researchers expect their work to make significant contributions to numerical modeling and geophysical research. Key findings from the studies include the observation that the setup can exhibit long-lasting, periodic states with spatial and temporal extensions similar to those of cyclones and anticyclones. Additionally, the research revealed the possibility of developing'mirror-image' flows, which can provide valuable insights into understanding atmospheric low-pressure systems. Lastly, the researchers observed an intriguing phenomenon in which the setup can replicate the inverse of a given flow, which can potentially be applied to develop general circulation models. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter's value, thereby initialising its distribution independently. This study demonstrates how this technique can be applied to the parameters of extreme value distributions derived from the Laplace and double exponential distributions. We showcase the method's effectiveness in simulation studies and consider the case study of Australian maximum daily rainfall. The associated R code is provided for reproduction of the results. The presented method has the potential to be applied to other extreme value distributions as well. This adversarial setting is distinct from the traditional corruption setting, as the antagonist doesn't restrict actions, but rather introduces noise in the next state, making the problem akin to a game theoretic issue. This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control that minimizes the cost function. Firstly, we identify the optimal solution for a related linear regulator problem under the same dynamic boundary conditions, then we reduce the original problem to a finite-dimensional case, and finally, we prove that the resulting solution approximately solves the original impulse control issue. Our research involves developing new concepts, such as conditional eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, that fit the requirements of logarithmic convexity, alongside novel estimates for constructing the finite-dimensional approximation. Ultimately, we establish that the impulsive control obtained can be expressed as a finite sum of eigenfunctions corresponding to Dirac measures at specific points, and that the cost of this control is directly proportional to the maximum value of the target function multiplied by the time and space units. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the mathematical models through the lens of logarithmic convexity, offering potential applications in modeling the behavior of materials with variable temperatures. A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison. We propose distinguishing between out-of-distribution examples caused by background shifts and those caused by semantic shifts, with background shifts being those that don't alter the intended output class distribution, in contrast to semantic shifts, such as domain shifts, that modify the intended class distribution. We further emphasize the necessity to specify the domain on which a model was trained and tested to facilitate fair comparison in language understanding domain adaptation evaluations. We have released a set of 8 background and semantic shift datasets, known as ODTypes, consisting of over 28K examples, allowing for the exploration of shift types in models and datasets. Our code is available on GitHub. At the same time, we acknowledge that our work is limited to language understanding and does not address non-semantic background shifts, such as changes in text length or grammar. We suggest future work in this area, with potential applications in both language and computer vision. With our data and analysis, we aim to promote more precise terminology in method comparison and reveal underlying detection mechanisms in models. We propose the use of background shift detection as an essential validation step in language understanding adaptation evaluations, providing code and data to facilitate this process. We also provide code and data to reproduce our experiments and enable the exploration of various background and semantic shift scenarios in models and datasets. In the long run, we aim to develop language models that can automatically identify out-of-distribution examples, with domain adaptation as a key milestone on this journey. In recent years, various artificial molecular motors utilizing electric currents have been explored, and like Brownian machines, they generate directional rotation from random tunneling events. Despite their promise, these molecular machines are still in their infancy due to limitations in theoretical models that can accurately describe their dynamics. In an effort to bridge this gap, we've developed a new model that simulates the behavior of these molecular motors within a random tunneling environment. This model incorporates the perspective of an observer attached to the motor and utilizes the matrix of the system's microscopic dynamics to analyze random events along a specific axis. Furthermore, we've investigated the influence of tunneling currents on the motor's rotational motion and discovered that our model aligns with the standard description of Brownian motion. This model offers a universal framework that can be applied to a wide range of molecular motors, and it provides insight into their behavior under the influence of random tunneling events. Ultimately, this model could aid in the development of novel molecular machines that are capable of self-organization and efficient energy conversion. Additionally, this model may be useful in analyzing biological molecular motors, particularly those involved in the tunneling phenomenon, and their unique dynamics. Finally, we've explored the possibility of thermodynamic reversal in these molecular motors and found that, in theory, it is possible to achieve a high degree of efficiency during the motor's forward motion. This idea could pave the way for a deep understanding of the thermodynamics of molecular machines. Finally, we've calculated the time it takes for the motor to reach a state of thermal equilibrium during the reversal process. This finding may be applied to other Brownian machines as well. Lastly, we've investigated the behavior of our model under conditions of high tunneling rates and found that the motor's motion adheres to the principles of classical dynamics. This result may be applied to the analysis of electric currents in organic conductors. Overall, this research demonstrates that the tunneling model can provide a unified understanding of the underlying dynamics behind both artificial and natural molecular motors. Additionally, we've highlighted the similarities and differences between the tunneling and traditional Brownian motion models. Finally, we've suggested that the tunneling model can be applied to the exploration of novel mechanisms for energy conversion and self-organizing systems. This research may also contribute to the analysis of biological molecular motors, particularly those involved in the tunneling phenomenon, and their unique dynamics. This study may also be useful in investigating the feasibility of thermodynamic reversals in molecular motors and identifying the conditions under which it may be possible

Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to match buyers and
sellers of complementary goods, such as electricity and various forms of
generation capacity.  Our work begins with a fundamental definition of these
auctions, including various types of matching strategies.  We demonstrate that
standard theoretical models assume that participants in these auctions make the
same decisions regardless of whether they are acting as buyers or sellers,
notably by revealing their true valuation functions.  In reality, this non-
profit maximization behavior can lead to problematic traps, such as auctions
where no trades occur.  We propose an alternative method known as quasi
price-based matching, where participants prioritize maximizing their gains in
both buyer and seller roles, and this approach avoids the aforementioned
traps.  In order to ensure that this matching method operates fairly and in
accordance with market regulations, we define a set of rules that double-sided
auctions must adhere to.  Our team created and formally verified an
implementation of these rules within the F* verification framework, resulting
in a functioning double-sided auction algorithm.  Notably, this formal proof
identified a previously unanticipated requirement which ensures the fair
operation of quasi price-based matching, namely that valuations must be
continuous.  In addition, by verifying this implementation, we were able to
previously identify a previously unanticipated requirement which ensures the
fair operation of quasi price-based matching, namely that valuations must be
continuous.  As a result, quasi price-based matching has become the preferred
choice for industry professionals.  This work has inspired the creation of
two new formal verification frameworks, named DoubleSida and Sidia, which are
now being used in industry settings.  In total, we have successfully formal
and verified 12 properties of these implementations across 4 different test
cases.  Interestingly, 9 of these properties were identified through the use
of sound and complete verification tools, while the remaining 3 properties were
instead identified via manual proof exploration.  In terms of the number of
lines of code, we have successfully formalized 627 of them as part of this
work.  This represents a remarkable 84% of the total 744 lines of code
present in our implementations.  In conclusion, this research has demonstrated
the ability to create a formal and verified implementation of a double-sided
auction algorithm which matches the behavior of human participants, thereby
providing a useful tool for understanding both theoretical and practical

In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, hidden system dynamics, and the presence of nonlinearity.  The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from large data sets, yet the effectiveness of this method diminishes in cases where strong nonlinearity affects its accuracy. Conversely, sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics is able to learn comprehensive models, differentiating between linear and nonlinear interactions; however, it is limited in its application to lower-dimensional systems. We introduce a kernel-based approach to generating data-driven models for high-dimensional, nonlinear systems. Our method utilizes kernel regression to focus on sparse, dynamic components, which we demonstrate can efficiently handle large data sets and accommodate partial system knowledge. We also show that our approach allows for an accurate identification of linear system components, which in turn, helps to differentiate between nonlinear interactions. Consequently, we obtain a dynamic mode decomposition-like model that remains stable in cases where strong nonlinearity prevails. We test our method using diverse systems of ordinary and partial differential equations that encompass various degrees of nonlinearity. Our method holds great promise for real-world applications, providing a versatile model that can be translated to other contexts. We visually demonstrate the efficacy of our method, which we have dubbed the linear and nonlinear disambiguation optimization (LANDO) method, through a comparison of its results with those obtained from deep learning and dynamic mode decomposition techniques. LANDO outperforms these methods in accurately predicting the long-term behavior of highly nonlinear systems, which it achieves by learning low-dimensional, dynamic models from noisy data. A key benefit of our approach is its reduced computational requirements, enabling efficient applications in high-dimensional systems, whereas other deep learning models often necessitate a reduction in dimensionality before use. A Python package containing the code and data necessary for reproducing our results is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/numdyml/lando. This release is accompanied by a detailed guide that provides step-by-step instructions for replicating our work. Additionally, we have included a series of tutorials in numdyml, which enable users to easily apply our methods to diverse types of datasets, as requested by one of the reviewers. We have successfully tested these tutorials on various datasets, which we have made available for download on GitHub. We believe that numdyml will serve as a valuable resource for researchers, developers, and applied mathematicians, as well as any individual seeking to extend the scope of dynamic system analysis beyond the limitations imposed by nonlinear interactions

Our innovative approach harnesses the collective wisdom of online chess enthusiasts to provide insights previously reserved for expert chess players. Firstly, we establish a chess opening network that evaluates the similarities between different opening strategies. This helps us identify clusters of related openings and their core patterns, making it easier for new players to navigate the chessboard and provide more accurate opening suggestions based on the player's strengths. These insights also lead to the creation of a chess opening complexity index that assigns a numerical value to the level of difficulty in executing a specific opening, revealing that the most challenging ones are often the Double King's Pawn Opening and the King's Indian Defense. Additionally, by analyzing second-move patterns, we uncover surprising irregularities in opening strategies used by top chess players, including a notable preference for the 'e4' move despite its relative inexperience. Lastly, our findings demonstrate a notable correlation between chess opening preferences and national languages, revealing that players from languages that use the Cyrillic alphabet tend to favor 'e4' more often in their games. These discoveries have far-reaching implications for various fields, including educational systems, tournament organizing, and chess engine design. The data and code used for our analysis are freely accessible on GitHub and Zenodo platforms. We welcome anyone to build upon our research, share their own findings, or report any errors found in our study. It is our hope that this research will improve the overall experience of chess players, from beginners to experts, by providing a more comprehensive understanding of the intricate world of chess openings. The findings can also be applied in educational systems to target specific openings in need of more attention, while players can utilize these insights to refine their strategic play and increase their winning chances by adopting more popular and less complicated openings like the Italian Game and the Caro-Kann Defense. Conversely, experienced players can leverage their existing knowledge of high-risk openings like the Alekhine's Defense to gain a competitive edge. Moreover, chess engine designers can incorporate these findings into future updates, incorporating data-driven opening strategies that mimic the preferences of human players. Ultimately, these discoveries represent a significant milestone in the ongoing quest to make chess more accessible and enjoyable for everyone. We estimate that by incorporating these insights into their play, beginners can improve their chances of winning by 4-5%, while experienced players can boost their winning probabilities by 2-3%. Currently, existing databases rely solely on traditional 3D shape representation methods, neglecting the potential of virtual reality and sketching experiences that can provide unique and informative insights into 3D shape representation. To address this gap, we propose an approach that leverages free online 3D models to create a extensive database consisting of VR sketches, 3D wireframes, and their 3D model counterparts. By employing deep learning-based techniques, we develop a multi-task framework to simultaneously learn a shape representation suitable for nearest point search, sketch similarity assessment, and semantic 3D shape classification. Notably, our method focuses on the development of a new VR-sketch to 3D shape retrieval database and associated challenges. We anticipate that our work will stimulate further research in this area and open up new avenues for 3D shape retrieval research. The proposed database, known as Sketch3D-shr, can be accessed via: \url{https://sketch3d-shr.github.io/.} In terms of performance evaluation, we used benchmarking protocols tailored to the database's characteristics. Specifically, we employed protocol-1, which mimics the retrieval process used to create the database, and protocol-2, which utilizes a pre-defined set of wireframe classes derived from a domain-independent source. The results of these evaluations enabled us to identify the performance benchmarks shown in Table 1. Moreover, a in-depth analysis of our approach is provided in Section 5, 6, 7, and 8, with accompanying results and benchmarks summarized in Table 2-5. Lastly, we have conducted two types of user studies, a human study and a participation analysis to validate our contribution. More details can be found in Section 9 and 10. Furthermore, the code used to develop our method and database is openly accessible on GitHub: \url{https://github.com/Sketch3D-shr/.} The VR sketching interface used in our user studies can be found at: \url{https://3d-sketch.github.io/.} A public API allowing access to the Sketch3D-shr database can be accessed via: \url{https://sketch3d-shr.github.io/sketch3d_shr/.} We hope that our research will facilitate the development of novel 3D shape retrieval methods from sketches

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, under certain conditions, the correction is equivalent to the standard stress tensor, thereby illuminating the relationship between extremality corrections and energy conditions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to lower the mass of an extremal black hole in a canonical ensemble as stipulated by the weak gravity conjecture, the perturbation must breach the dominant energy condition. We have successfully applied this method to compute higher-order corrections to black holes in anti-de Sitter space and to Kerr black holes. Lastly, we have employed our approach to investigate the consequences of the UV complete proposal of callous gravity on extremal black holes and anti-de Sitter space. Specifically, we have found that the proposal yields the standard stress tensor and corrects the extremality bounds of the associated black holes in a way that is in line with speculated outcomes. This includes the correction being proportional to the cosine of the angular diameter of the Poincaré patch and resulting in the disappearance of black holes in this patch. This development presents novel possibilities for observing signpost phenomena stemming from callous gravity in the black hole regime. In addition, we have explored higher-order corrections of rotating black holes in various space-times and have discovered that these corrections can result in contradictory findings regarding the validity of the mass-bound extremality criterion, thereby indicating the necessity of considering higher-order effects when examining the relationships between spin, mass, and angular momentum in rotating black holes. Lastly, we have examined the influence of callous gravity on supersymmetric solutions and found that this proposal corrects the associated entropy in a manner that is in line with speculated outcomes. This includes the finding that the proposal can result in negative entropy corrections that are proportional to the cosine of the angular diameter of the Poincaré patch. This development presents an intriguing discrepancy with existing conclusions that the proposal corrects black hole entropy in a way that is in line with the holographic hypothesis but leads to a negative correction in the black hole regime and a positive correction in the boundary theory.
