End-effect models utilize a straightforward statistical representation of policy effects, which serve as a substitute for more computationally intensive predictive models. When combined with a reward structure, they form the foundation of a streamlined variational free energy minimization system. However, the primary challenge is balancing the upkeep of this simplified effect model with the policy's continuous updates. Interestingly, when the target distribution is uniform, our approach facilitates learning an efficient exploratory policy consistent with the principles of intrinsic curiosity. Moreover, when paired with an external reward, our method yields faster training times than traditional off-policy techniques. A thorough evaluation of our approach is conducted using diverse policy networks and rewarding structures in multiple robotic settings. Moreover, our end-effect model-based learning method offers notable computational efficiencies and continuity in complex robotic scenarios. Nonetheless, its limited capacity means it cannot recall its historical effects over an extended period of time. Consequently, its long-term effectiveness may decline, which could pose significant issues in long-term robotic learning applications, as demonstrated in a comprehensive setup. This research is motivated by a desire to integrate cutting-edge deep reinforcement learning techniques with the principles of active learning, intrinsic motivation, and efficient sample usage. Furthermore, we have conducted an in-depth examination of our hypothesis, as well as the extent to which our results can be applied to real-world scenarios. We have devised the first fixed-parameter algorithm to determine whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout, capable of handling parameterizations up to vertex deletion. This is also the first known solution for the upward embedding problem, which is fixed-parameter algorithmic. Building on this result, we've developed new parameterized solutions for constrained upward-planarity, including vertex splittability up to O(log N) iterations and vertex contraction up to 2 iterations, both of which were previously unsolved problems in the field. In addition, we've obtained a new tractable version of vertex splittability under the deletion parameter, which is useful in graph layout applications. These novel algorithmic solutions expand the current toolkit for graph layout, providing efficient solutions that could be useful in graph drawing applications where certain vertices can be hidden or simplified. This research provides the first known fixed-parameter algorithm for the single-source shortest paths problem with regard to vertex deletion in digraphs. This result is also contingent on an innovative application of the Harnal-Bess and Ohtsuki-McDiarmid theorem framework, which is a recently discovered method for analyzing graph parameters in relation to vertex deletion. This algorithmic innovation could have implications in digraphs, particularly in understanding which parameters remain affected and which remain unaffected by vertex deletion in single-source shortest paths digraphs. This research is also contingent on the development of new planar layouts, which can accommodate O(log N) splits and 2 contractions, both of which can be represented in upward planar layouts. These novel layouts could have useful applications in graph drawing, as they can accommodate vertex deletions while maintaining an upward planar representation. In particular, we've devised an algorithm to determine whether a digraph can be represented using O(log N) levels of upward planar layouts, which can accommodate vertex splits. This result is contingent on understanding which parameters remain affected and which remain unaffected by vertex deletion in single-source shortest paths digraphs, which is a novel contribution of this research. This contribution is based on an examination of the relationship between vertex deletion and the upward planar spanning forest problem in digraphs. This problem is not only fixed-parameter algorithmic but also provides a new fixed-parameter tractable version under the vertex deletion parameter, which is a useful result in graph layout applications. This research is also contingent on understanding which parameters remain affected and which remain unaffected by vertex deletion in upward planar embeddings, which is a novel contribution of this research. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms, but the optimal memory strategy remains unknown.
We propose MemoNav, a navigation model that leverages multiple memory types and selects the most informative memory through a designed attention process.
By integrating a memory selector, MemoNav outperforms previous methods on the MiniWorld platform, achieving up to an 8.5% increase in success rate and up to a 60% decrease in path length. 
Additionally, MemoNav demonstrates robust training capabilities, with its abilities generalizing well to unseen environments and objectives. 
The source code for MemoNav is available at https://github.com/DeepMind/MemoNav. 
A video showcasing the model can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZuU6yYy4k4Y. 
The model has been added to the DeepMind GitHub repository at https://github.com/DeepMind/world-exploration. 
We hope MemoNav serves as a foundation for future research in image-based navigation with multiple memory types. 
The model's performance can be improved by applying attention techniques to its encoder and decoder components, a possibility we intend to explore in subsequent studies. 
For example, attention could help the model focus on specific paths during navigation or crucial images when searching for objectives. 
In contrast to other memory-based models, MemoNav does not suffer from performance declines when memories are obscured or corrupted, a key advantage in practical navigation scenarios where such situations often arise. 
The model achieves this resilience through its attention-driven memory selection process and the incorporation of diverse memory types, a strategy we plan to build upon in future studies.

To increase cellular capacity, operators initially implemented 4G LTE small cells (Femto Cells) by reusing the same licensed spectrum. However, these cells' capabilities were insufficient to support future applications like virtual reality and augmented reality. As a result, operators have increasingly deployed unlicensed LTE-MTC in the 5 GHz band to support such demands. This paper summarizes the past (Femto Cell era) and present (LTE-MTC era) of small cell deployment, highlighting their shortcomings. It also explores six possible paths to the future (5G/6G SCF) and presents a new architecture that can support the reconfiguration of network function, AI-assisted data collection, and direct device communication over FROT. Additionally, simulation results show that the proposed SCF architecture can achieve better performance compared to current technologies. Finally, a demonstration is planned to test the proposed SCF architecture in a real-world setting. This research aims to provide in-depth insights into small cell evolution, including their theoretical foundations, and serves as a foundation for future developments in this field. This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems. We begin by exploring the operator growth dynamics in isolated SU(1,1) symmetric systems. We then generalize our approach to multipartner scenarios, where we utilize a standard entanglement measure to analyze entanglement dynamics. Interestingly, our results for two-qutrit systems reveal a distinct difference in entanglement between even and odd system operators. We connect these findings to information content, revealing a notable disparity. Next, we investigate operator growth in SU(2) symmetric systems under the influence of a external probe. Our analysis indicates that growth dynamics in these systems can be classified as either subdiffusive or diffusive in nature. We have found a significant relationship between these diffusive rates and the operator entanglement dynamics within these systems. Lastly, we have discovered a surprising correlation between the maximum information capacity and the operator entanglement dynamics within these systems. Our research provides a deeper understanding of operator growth dynamics in Lie-symmetric systems from a quantum information perspective. It also reveals new insights into the diffusion of operators in these systems. Furthermore, our study highlights key differences and similarities between operator growth in Lie-symmetric systems and the well-known quton model. Our analysis provides a thorough exploration of operator growth characteristics, enabling future applications in quantum machine learning and quantum information applications. Our research paves the way for further investigations into quantum information phenomena in Lie-symmetric systems. It also encourages the utilization of quantum information tools to study quantum phenomena in Lie-symmetric systems. In doing so, our study bridges the gap between Lie algebra and quantum information theory. Our results may also be transferred to other types of symmetric systems, such as rotating black holes. We have discovered that operator growth in Lie-symmetric systems can be probed through quantum information experiments. In the future, we aim to study quantum information experiments that probe these growth patterns. Our results may also reveal new insights into quantum error correction and quantum computing applications. The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. The paper provides information about the breakup mechanism of the Hoyle state by employing a novel experimental technique. The investigation of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay of the Hoyle state, rather than through the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ ground state, can be performed through an advanced analysis of the energy distribution of the three $\alpha$ particles from the decay. Using beta-delayed charged-particle spectroscopy on $^{12}\mathrm{N}$ via the Texas Active Target Time Projection Chamber, a highly sensitive measurement of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay ratio can be made without interference from overlapping events. The analysis using a Bayesian approach reveals that the direct decay fraction is less than 0.043% at the 95% confidence level. This value is in line with previous studies and the measurement's accuracy can be improved using more sensitive measurements. Such an experiment provides a method to investigate nuclear structure without disrupting the measured target, enabling further studies on delicate structures. The findings of this investigation will be useful in determining the $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ Hoyle state's deformation and $\alpha$-condensation properties. The current measurement's outcome is compared to different theoretical models, and future experiments will be conducted to make more precise measurements. The direct 3 $\alpha$ decay analysis also includes a statistical method to quantify the medium effects on the decay and the clustering properties of the Hoyle state, and the analysis reveals that the breakup mechanism of the Hoyle state is not purely an uncorrelated 3 $\alpha$ decay but rather has a minor interference from the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ ground state due to the free-nucleon e+ factor in the decay. Based on this analysis, the e+ factor can be eliminated, and the measurement of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay ratio can be made without interference from overlapping events. Additionally, the analysis using a Bayesian approach reveals that the direct decay fraction is less than 0.043% at the 95% confidence level and that the Hoyle state's clustering structure can be described as a weakly interacting system

In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels equipped with feedback and state information, which becomes available to the encoder in a predictable sequence. This encompasses a broad range of channels, including memoryless channels with independent and identically distributed states (referred to as the Shannon strategy), channels with Markovian states that offer the ability to access past states (known as look-ahead access) and energy harvesting. The capacity of these channels with feedback is described in terms of the directed information between auxiliary variables and the channel outputs. Additionally, we propose two distinct methods for determining this capacity: a method involving the development of an infinite-horizon average-reward dynamic programming system and a method utilizing auxiliary directed graphs called Q-graphs. These methods are applied to various illustrative examples, with one example involving a channel with a single input state, which exhibits a connection to the optimal Shannon strategy. Furthermore, our approach is shown to be capable of handling channels with complex state structures and non-uniform distributions. Examples of such channels include a convolutional channel and a phase-shift keying (PSK) channel. Ultimately, we establish that the proposed techniques can be efficiently computed for channels with look-ahead access to state information. Conversely, when state information is only available to the encoder in a random and unpredictable sequence, we demonstrate the development of a modified dynamic programming system and auxiliary Q-graphs methods to determine tight outer bounds to the capacity region. Examples of channels without state information include a binary erasure channel with feedback and a binary input, memoryless output, Gaussian channel with feedback. These methods are shown to be capable of determining the exact capacity region in cases of channels without state information where the state sequence is either perfectly predictable or completely unpredictable. Examples of such channels include a binary erasure channel with feedback, a discrete, memoryless channel with feedback, and a Gaussian channel with feedback. Lastly, we establish the accuracy and efficiency of these newly proposed methods. In particular, these methods are shown to be more efficient than other existing methods for channels without state information, such as those described in elements 1 and 2. These results are further confirmed by examples, such as a binary erasure channel with feedback and a binary input, memoryless output, Gaussian channel with feedback. These examples illustrate the superiority of these newly proposed methods in determining the capacity region when state information is either available or completely unpredictable. Ultimately, we establish the commonality of these methods to various channels without state information, channel inputs with a limited range and outputs with a discrete distribution. Examples

A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that under specific Rashba coupling and Zeeman field strengths, we can observe s-wave superconductivity in a Rashba Hubbard model with multiple doped electrons, characterized by spin 0, parity +1, and Chern number 1. This superconducting state is chemically stable and remains so even when the Rashba coupling strength varies. Furthermore, we found that both Zeeman field intensity and temperature affect spin-triplet Cooper pairs' pair field in a similar manner to traditional superconductors, ultimately rendering the spin singlet nature of the superconducting state unstable under these conditions. Additionally, we discovered that under strong Rashba coupling, the superconducting state can coexist with a Zeeman-driven antiferromagnetic state at a specific critical electron density. Importantly, this spin-singlet topological superconductor's topological nature remains intact when exposed to various Rashba coupling strengths and magnetic fields. Following the application of a charge vector, our results indicate that the superconducting state can also be achieved in a weak coupling regime with a Zeeman field intensity > than a critical threshold. This research demonstrates the possibility and stability of spin-singlet topological superconductivity under various conditions. Consequently, this may lead to the development of topological quantum technologies using Rashba Hubbard systems. Ultimately, we conclude that Rashba Hubbard systems can exhibit topological superconductivity under both strong and weak coupling conditions, thus expanding the domain of topological superconductors featuring unusual spin-orbit coupling. This finding presents novel avenues for generating topological superconducting materials naturally via doping and spin-orbit engineering in two-dimensional systems. Lastly, we propose topological quantum computing schemes utilizing Rashba Hubbard systems as a promising and versatile class of topological superconductors. This may enable the development of more robust and versatile quantum processors than previously thought possible with unusual spin-orbit coupling systems. Consequently, this may lead to significant advancements in quantum computing technology. Conversely, our results may also present challenges in generating topological superconductors due to spin-orbit disorder, thus introducing issues for topological quantum computing applications.

The task required participants to write subtasks aimed at automating the process of verifying factual information and finding supporting evidence within tabular scientific data. The subtasks included a classification task to identify structured information in tables, a classification task to confirm or deny a specific fact, a classification task to choose the cell providing the best evidence, a classification task to select the relevant column containing the evidence, and a free-text writing task to describe the column containing the evidence. The data consisted of a collection of 1,000 academic papers from the fields of biochemistry and medicine, containing over 26,000 tables. The evaluation used an in-house human evaluation process to assess performance. The data and task information are available at https://github.com/cs-mining-ua/SEM-TAB-FACTS. They're based on assumptions discussed later on. These equations aren't an original contribution but rather a reference guide for those working with simplified numerical models of groundwater flow.

I began with Darcy's Law, revisiting the conservation equation for vertical averaging in groundwater flow. Following that, I explored approaches for numerically solving the flow equation. Then, I considered scenarios where the hydraulic conductivity varies solely with depth, simplifying the steady-state flow equation in these cases. Lastly, there's a brief examination of the transient flow scenario. 

It's worth noting that these equations don't account for factors like vertical flow, multiple aquifers, and varying thicknesses of the aquifer. Also, the equations presented are not suitable for complex simulations but rather aim to facilitate straightforward, numerical computations. 

Finally, there's a section outlining assumptions underlying these equations, accompanied by a discussion on the implications of these assumptions. 

These equations are primarily intended for introductory students of groundwater flow but may also be of limited use to experienced researchers and scientists. 

I hope this review meets your expectations! Please feel free to suggest any corrections or improvements.

  Darcy's Law
  -----------

  Darcy's Law describes the one-dimensional horizontal movement of a fluid as:

  Q = -UA \* i

  where:
  Q = total fluid flow rate (m^3/s)
  U = fluid velocity (m/s)
  A = cross-sectional area of flow (m^2)
  i = hydraulic gradient (m/m)

  Or, in terms of head, it can be written as:

  i = -U \* (dh/dx)

  where:
  i = hydraulic gradient (m/m)
  h = fluid head (m)
  x = horizontal distance (m)

  h = h_s + 2/3(s/2 + w)

While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. As a more effective approach, inquiry-based learning has the potential to promote student autonomy in testing decisions. Our study aims to empirically verify the effectiveness of this method by comparing it to the traditional feedback style, focusing on the impact on student testing behavior and academic performance. By conducting an experiment involving 96 students, we gathered and analyzed data on various testing activities to determine the benefits and drawbacks of both methods. Our results indicate that students using the inquiry-based approach are more likely to create valid testing plans, efficiently use their time, and demonstrate better testing skills. Furthermore, this style appears to have a more significant impact on student performance when compared to the traditional method. To validate our findings, we analyzed the data using the Nonparametric Rank Test and Magnetic Linear Regression models. Based on these results, we conclude that the inquiry-based learning style is a more effective way to educate students in software testing. To further improve this style, we suggest adjusting certain parameters, such as the feedback threshold and conceptual relevance criteria. In the future, we plan to replicate this study with a larger participant pool and examine the long-term effects of this learning style. By combining the inquiry-based learning style with professional tools, instructors can provide students with valuable insights that promote structured testing habits and prepare future software engineers for real-world testing scenarios. In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming a necessity. However, existing methods often balance the breadth of coverage in model interpretation against the depth of theoretical accuracy. This work proposes a novel approach that utilizes concept analysis to pinpoint specific model decisions and an integer programming system to validate these assumptions within a dataset. By leveraging this dual strategy, we aim to shed light on why a DNN made a particular classification choice for a particular sample, and like other rule extraction methods, our method also suffers from the risk of over-fitting and under-fitting. Unlike other approaches, such as rule ensembles or zero-shot learning, this system does not pre-define the rules; instead, it determines the coverage of model explanations. Moreover, our method can accommodate both binary and multi-class models, and we demonstrate its efficacy using the German Credit and Mushroom datasets. While our results show that extracted rules exhibit a satisfactory level of accuracy in predicting target attributes, we also encountered issues of over-fitting and limited coverage, highlighting the inherent challenges of explaining complex DNNs. Notably, our method necessitates a preliminary dataset preparation step, involving dividing data into training and validation sets, and experimenting with different parameter configurations to achieve optimal results. Overall, our approach provides a unique blend of model understanding through concept analysis and a rigorous, data-driven approach to extracting meaningful rules. Although it doesn't necessarily capture the intricate, non-linear patterns inherent to DNNs, it does offer a high degree of accuracy in explaining single predictions. Leveraging the strengths of both rule extraction and model debugging, this method contributes to the ongoing quest for deeper machine learning model transparency. With continuous advancements in DNN technology, our approach may serve as a useful tool for assessing model reliability, validating model decisions against human intuition, and promoting data cleaning by identifying inconsistencies within datasets. Moving forward, we intend to expand our method to support more complex models, such as multi-layered DNNs and ENN models. Additionally, we plan to develop a more user-friendly implementation of our approach, and experiment with it using real-world datasets. Furthermore, we aim to extend our method to support explanation generation at the attribute level, and explore its applicability in areas such as data mining and customer relationship management. Lastly, we plan to investigate the feasibility of our approach in domains involving sensitive or confidential data. By addressing these research questions, we hope to contribute meaningfully to the evolving field of explainable AI. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. We analyze multivariate time series data with consideration of heavy-tailed randomness to capture extreme events more accurately. To this end, we developed a multivariate extension of the auto-regressive fractional integrated moving average model, incorporating two types of non-stationary behavior: linear and nonlinear. To facilitate model estimation, we proposed an efficient two-step method, involving initial estimation of univariate components followed by joint optimization of the remaining parameters. Through extensive Monte Carlo simulations, we evaluated the accuracy of our estimator and uncovered surprising results: the method exhibits consistent estimation biases, particularly when model components exhibit complex non-stationary behavior. To address these biases, we derived exact confidence intervals for key parameters under specific heavy-tailed distributions as well as a general approach for other distributions. To further improve inference precision, we explored the performance of this estimator in the context of within-sample partitioning. Ultimately, we applied our method to two real-world data sets related to stock market returns and economic indicators, utilizing a combination of exact and Monte Carlo inference methods to analyze these datasets. Internet Service Providers have long requested that Content Providers contribute financially towards improving the quality of Internet services. This research examines profit-sharing agreements between a single Content Provider and multiple Internet Service Providers, with the Content Provider agreeing to split profits in exchange for enhanced network quality by a certain deadline. Each Internet Service Provider has the option to terminate agreements and claim their share of profits if the agreed-upon quality is not met. We present a Bivariate Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Program to optimize negotiations between the Content Provider and Internet Service Providers, aiming to maximize both parties' profits. Notably, variations in market power among Internet Service Providers and Content Providers significantly impact negotiation outcomes, and our model is validated through simulations involving real-world scenarios. Results demonstrate that when Content Providers hold market power, negotiations yield higher profits for all parties, and these profits are mostly concentrated among larger Internet Service Providers. Conversely, when Internet Service Providers dominate the market, negotiations result in lower profits for all, and these profits are mostly concentrated among smaller Content Providers. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that when market power resides with the Content Provider, negotiations are mainly beneficial to all Internet Service Providers. Lastly, our study provides significant generalizability, and our findings are not limited to profit-sharing scenarios, but can also be applied to other agreements between Internet Service Providers and Content Providers. Ultimately, our research offers valuable insights for negotiations between these parties in the context of network quality negotiations. With ongoing market shifts toward platforms like YouTube Premium and Spotify Free, our study's relevance extends to these services' very real negotiation scenarios. Yielding valuable insights into optimizing profits in cases where agreements can be terminated if agreed-upon quality standards are not met could prove especially helpful. Given the market-leading positions of companies like Netflix and Amazon, our research also offers substantial practical generalizability to these industry giants. Additionally, our study is not confined to just profit-sharing agreements, but can be applied to a broader array of Internet Service Provider and Content Provider agreements. Given its theoretical nature, our work is anticipated to contribute meaningfully to research in this field. In the context of a quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic three-dimensional manifold with a boundary that approaches infinity, its foliations at infinity are closely tied to its stable foliation. When a given non-Fuchsian hyperbolic surface is deformed while maintaining its conformal structure, the measurements of its foliations at infinity capture the essential topological features of the changing geometry. Our research involves calculating the natural symplectic form associated with these measurements as this surface is deformed. We demonstrate that this calculation yields a closed 1-form whose integral is constant when the surface is deformed along a path within the Fuchsian locus. We also show that this constant is zero in the principal foliation at infinity, which is a key component of the Measured Luscher-Taylor theorem describing foliations at infinity on hyperbolic three-dimensional manifolds. Ultimately, our findings generalize the Luscher-Taylor theorem to quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic three-dimensional manifolds. Additionally, our research implies that any deformed surface with a finite hyperbolic geometry along a path within the Fuchsian locus will have a foliation at infinity that is tame and realizable. We also provide a geometric characterization of the foliations at infinity that are invariant under the stable holonomy of the conformal boundary. This characterization extends a result initially found by David Dumas. Our work has further implications, with cohomology vanishing across an entire parameter space associated with surface deformations and an infinitesimal version of the Farey rotation, which inverts the mapping between the orbit of a surface under the farey rotation and the orbit of its foliation at infinity under the tea rotation. Our findings also reveal new properties for the farey rotation, including it being a free, orientation-preserving action on the space of surfaces with a conformal structure. We demonstrate as well that the farey rotation is topologically equivalent to a circle action and further show that any surface with a conformal structure that is Fuchsian can be equipped with a foliation at infinity that is tame and realizable. Our research identifies new invariant measures on the space of surfaces with a conformal structure and further shows that any surface with a conformal structure that is Fuchsian can be equipped with a foliation at infinity that is tame and realizable as well as taut. This paper presents an accurate method for calculating the mean return of an investment portfolio. The approach considers a investor making one random investment choice without knowledge of the items, leading to a frequency distribution of returns. We demonstrate the convergence of this distribution to a mixture of two power laws, resulting from the combination of a power-law distribution of asset values and a normal return distribution. We also observe that this method can estimate the return of an investment portfolio as the harmonic mean of the returns of its individual assets. This calculation method is comparable to the arithmetic mean for uniformly distributed assets. We further apply this method in order to analyze the returns of the S\&P 500 index and the Greek stock exchange's composite index. Our new estimation method suggests lower expected returns for these indices compared to the arithmetic mean. We also use this method in order to validate the Feldstein-Horioka mystery, i.e., the positive correlation between asset returns and GDP per capita. However, we also model the error and find that this correlation is likely the result of biased estimation due to the presence of noise. We further propose an alternative estimation method that eliminates this bias, resulting in a power-law distribution of return-growth ratios for the S\&P 500 index. This method is similar to one recently proposed by Cizauskas et al. We also use this method in order to analyze the returns of a sample of 100 companies. Our results indicate lower expected returns for companies with smaller market capitalization. We show that this result is likely the result of incomplete exposure to the stock market on the part of these companies. We further apply this method in order to estimate the return required by investors for companies with known risk profiles. We show that our estimation method is more accurate compared to the widely used modern portfolio theory. We further demonstrate the applicability of this method to any type of investment portfolio. As such, our method has broad applications in the fields of finance, economics, astrophysics, geophysics and botany. It can also be used in order to analyze the returns of companies according to their industry, the performance of their CEOs, the returns of hedge funds and other investment tools. Furthermore, our method can be employed in order to develop more accurate models of investment portfolios by taking into account the power-law distribution of asset values. In this context, the power-law distribution can be the result of a variety of mechanisms, including preferential attachment, network effects and self-organization. This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on bidding tactics and outcome profitability. Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in both settings fall within a narrow revenue-maximizing range. We initiate a study of local defining ideals of Hessenberg varieties, specifically focusing on regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type A, utilizing an affine coordinate chart based on the maximal element of the Weyl group corresponding to GL(n,ℂ). Key findings include the following. Firstly, we prove that the local defining ideal associated to a given Hessenberg function within this specific coordinate system can be decomposed into vertices. Furthermore, combining our result with existing work on generators, we demonstrate that this set of generators constitutes a Gröbner basis for this ideal under a suitable monomial order. Lastly, applying our analysis, we derive an explicit splitting of a key region of Flags(ℂ^n), effectively decomposing its local defining ideals across all indecomposable Hessenberg functions. The significance of our work lies in its connection to the complex geometry of Artin, with an additional connection to the recent simplification of the Burau representation of the braid group Brn. Lastly, our analysis also yields a detailed description of the local defining ideals of regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type A. The approach employed in our research draws from various sources including combinatorics, geometric vertex decomposition, and the concept of Gröbner basis in algebra. Neural Painters, utilizing a GAN-based approach, generate brushstrokes that are assembled into paintings. Despite GANs' superiority in AI-generated art, their training can be exceptionally challenging. To address these difficulties and accelerate Neural Painter training, we employed Transfer Learning, achieving a notable time reduction from days to just hours without compromising visual quality. Our findings are presented in this study. Additionally, to enable more efficient training, we optimized Neural Painters using multiple stroke directions, resulting in higher visual quality and diversity in generated brushstrokes. We also examined the effect of Noise Normalization on GAN training, revealing its significance in maintaining visual quality. To facilitate reproduction of our results, we provided a simple, open-source training implementation and an interactive demo allowing users to see the painting generation process in real-time. These resources showcase the GAN training process from a GAN-naive perspective, offering insights into the GAN training community. We tackle current, striking discrepancies in flavor anomalies observed within the $K$ and $B$ meson systems, specifically addressing CP-violating Kaon decay and lepton-flavor universality violation in $B$ meson decays, all within a single, unified framework. This new theory introduces three vectorlike compositing domains that allow for the efficient creation of new heavy states, thereby enabling sizable CP-violating interactions between standard model particles and these heavy states. Consequently, this yields predictions that align with observed values for the $K^0:\bar{K^0}$ mass difference and the $\Delta F=1$ anomalies in $B$ meson decays without necessitating unusual scalar or vector mediators. The proposed model also predicts a minimum mass for the heavy states of around 10 TeV and sets a minimum mass for the lightest CP-even scalar state of around 1 TeV. The proposed model remains consistent with the observed values of $B_s$ and $\tau$ lifetimes as well as the $B$ meson $d^2g$ anomaly, offering a coherent understanding of the observed anomalies within the standard model using vectorlike compositeness. Finally, this model predicts new signatures that could be searched for at the LHC, specifically multiple jet signatures and signatures involving both jets and hadronically decaying photons, which could be investigated using reconstructed jet mass and dipion mass analyses to verify the model's predictions. Based on our calculations, it appears that the upcoming HL-LHC run should be capable of verifying the model's predictions. A critical aspect of the model's vectorlike components is their natural ability to efficiently produce long-lived particles, which could be detected using long-baseline neutrino beams or by reexamining existing $B$ meson search data. This model remains consistent with standard model predictions for these processes, adjusting for differing heavy state masses. Lastly, this model offers a predictive framework for potential future discoveries at future neutrino facilities and FASER2, specifically within long-baseline neutrino physics. Certain long-lived particle masses should be observable at these facilities, while others may require more advanced facilities to detect. A brief exploration of these potential discoveries is included. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their focus on abstracts and prior knowledge. To develop effective solutions, we created a large dataset of 12,500 question-answer pairs drawn from research papers in the fields of computer science and biomedical sciences. Unlike existing datasets, which consist mainly of fact-based questions, our collection includes a high proportion of complex, informational questions that require a deeper understanding of the subject matter. We evaluated several neural network models for a task called Question Anchoring, which involves linking relevant sections of the document to such informational questions, but found the models to be less capable of answering these questions compared to the existing state-of-the-art. We plan to make our dataset available under a free license, enabling further development and improvement.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they significantly enhance readability by reducing character count, they can also complicate comprehension, particularly for readers unfamiliar with acronym definitions. To address this, the Acronym Disambiguation Task aims to match abbreviations with their relevant meanings. To support researchers in this field, a new dataset was introduced in 2020. Building upon the foundations laid by the proposed dataset, our technique leverages a BERT-based model to determine acronym definitions. This paper presents MadDog, a web-based interface providing access to the acronym dataset, enabling users to submit unfamiliar acronyms and receive accurate definition matches through our developed annotation model. Additionally, madDog offers a knowledge base that includes comprehensive definitions for over 3.4 million acronyms, sourced from Wikipedia and multiple online dictionaries. This knowledge base can be utilized as an effective pre-trained model for acronym definition detection, showcasing the diverse applications of acronym-related information. To facilitate research accessibility, MadDog's source code and web application are openly available for public use. experiments conducted on the introduced dataset demonstrate promising results, with our model achieving a 71% median rank for acronym definition identification. Furthermore, our system outperformed other competing models in definition accuracy and research efficiency. evaluation tests revealed the efficacy of the MadDog system in defining unfamiliar acronyms, with users confirming its effectiveness in the acronym disambiguation task. Moving forward, we plan to enhance our acronym knowledge base by incorporating definitions from books, research papers, and user-provided annotations. In the near future, we aim to expand our MadDog system to encompass other related tasks, such as word identification and part-of-speech classification. Using the acronym definitions collected, we can develop a model for the classification of domain-specific phrases. This proposed work has significant potential to contribute to research in the acronym disambiguation task. Additionally, we plan to explore the feasibility of leveraging BERT-based models to identify definitions in outdated texts. With its capabilities to process long contexts, BERT may aid in the revival of dormant acronyms. It is interesting to note how MadDog's diverse knowledge domains can facilitate the revival of acronyms. Furthermore, we anticipate the discovery of novel applications for acronym definitions, such as identifying synonyms and related phrases. Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the most notable manifestations of quantum physics. Historically, quantum interference has been observed in charge transport; however, recent findings indicate that it also significantly affects thermal properties. This insight enables the precise manipulation of heat within microscopic devices through phase-coherence. This study showcases how exploiting phase-coherent edge states in quantum Hall systems allows for the realization of exceptional thermoelectric properties and efficient heat rectification. A multi-quantum point contact tunneling setup with multiple interference paths was used to demonstrate that these systems break electron charge symmetry. As a result, an electron can pass through with a specific charge configuration, but the opposite occurs when it traverses in the opposite direction. This trait triggers unusually robust thermoelectric responses and heat rectification effects when electrons interfere with each other. These findings emphasize the importance of considering complex interplay between quantum fluctuations and interference in determining the electron's local spin and charge configurations. This understanding paves the way for innovative applications in heat management and energy harvesting at the nanoscale. Additionally, this work provides a fundamental framework for understanding the connection between quantum physics and heat within dimensionally confined systems. This perspective may foster the development of new perspectives on quantum physics that extend beyond established principles. It may also encourage re-examination of common low-dimensional quantum systems due to their potential to exhibit exceptional thermoelectric properties and heat rectification effects. These phenomena often rely on intricate interplay between electrons and their local environment. A thorough investigation of these systems may reveal previously overlooked insights that can be exploited for the design of advanced thermal devices. These findings could also prompt a deeper exploration of the fundamental links between quantum physics, heat, and charge, which may hold significant value for the advancement of quantum technology in the future. It is anticipated that this research will stimulate an increased focus on developing novel thermoelectric materials based on quantum interference and heat rectification effects. These efforts may ultimately lead to the creation of highly efficient heat management systems at the nanoscale. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of distinct, uniquely designed primers defines a distinct storage container called a *primer box*. Multiple data objects, categorized by the same primer pair, are hierarchically organized within a single primer box, allowing for simplified data management and revisions. To optimize data storage capacity, our design incorporates multiple levels of hierarchical organization, allowing data objects to be grouped into larger sets. Upon detection of a primer binding error, a correction strategy involving the resequencing of related primer boxes minimizes data loss and reduces recovery time. Furthermore, our design includes an advanced indexing system, enabling rapid data retrieval via a primer-based hash table, and allows for the tracking of data revisions through a tree data structure indexed by primers. Our experimental results, based on real-world data, demonstrate a primer-specific sequencing order, resulting in a 30% reduction in total resequencing costs. Additionally, our hierarchical model facilitates seamless data evolution, yielding an average reduction of 90% in resequencing costs and allowing for the revision of a substantial data portion with under $100 in resequencing expenses. Our proposed approach outperforms the best-known alternative, reducing resequencing costs by a factor of four while maintaining a primer box error rate five orders of magnitude lower. Ultimately, our findings reveal that, under specific assumptions regarding sequencing costs, the optimal approach would call for a substantial portion of 38% of DNA storage being dedicated to data revisions. Our work presents a novel, general framework for DNA storage systems, providing a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between sequencing costs, error rates, and system efficiency. Our study offers a systematic approach for designing and evaluating DNA storage systems, enabling a thorough analysis of the trade-offs inherent in these systems. At the same time, our findings illustrate the complexity and constraints inherent in DNA storage systems, particularly as they pertain to data revisions and error correction. Finally, our results provide meaningful insights into the parameters that optimally balance sequencing costs and error rates in these systems. To achieve this, we employed a detailed analysis of DNA storage efficiency, examining key parameters at multiple levels of system evaluation, such as storage capacity, sequence order, and primer box design and organization. Our work provides a thorough understanding of the efficiency of DNA storage systems. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples from photonic systems. Due to their inherent two-dimensional nature, experimental implementations of topological nodal lines are more accessible than their three-dimensional counterparts. In oscillatory media, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can give rise to outgoing waves, which are crucial for synchronization across entire systems and are prevalent in many biological and chemical processes. These waves, typically triggered by pacemaker-generated activity, serve as a means of transmitting information at a constant speed over extended distances. This research utilizes advanced analytical tools to explore the determinants of wave velocity, focusing specifically on singular perturbation and phase reduction techniques in the context of two distinct types of oscillators, one built on bistability and the other featuring time delay in negative feedback mechanisms. By examining the various mechanisms contributing to slow-frequency fluctuations in oscillatory systems, this work aims to enhance understanding of how systems encode and transmit information over long distances. Given the widespread application of analytical methods in the featured scenarios, this study also aims to demonstrate the feasibility of these methods in uncovering and interpreting key results. Ultimately, the analysis provides a means of accurately estimating the speed at which pacemaker-generated waves propagate, a parameter that may be further optimized through a demonstrated strategy in the case of delayed negative feedback. This research is expected to contribute significantly to the field due to its broad relevance to the effects of delay on oscillatory systems, a topic that has only grown more prominent during the COVID-19 pandemic. A fundamental concept, entropy, has significant implications in both classical and quantum physics and computer science, leading to diverse applications across theoretical and practical domains. The focus is on determining approximations within a factor $\gamma > 1$ of the Shannon entropy in probability distributions and the von Neumann entropy in mixed quantum states. The key contributions are two algorithms that use quantum queries to accurately estimate entropy, where the first is a modified version of Bruttain and Sattler's previous approach and yields an approximation within a factor $\sqrt{n}$ of Shannon entropy with $\widetilde{O}(\gamma^n \sqrt{n})$ queries, whereas a refined analysis reveals the original entropy estimation was $\widetilde{O}(\gamma^n n^{3/2})$. Additionally, an adapted solution from Bruttain and Sattler's paper provides an approximation within a factor $\sqrt{\log n}$ of the quantum entropy with $\widetilde{O}(\gamma^n \sqrt{\log n})$ queries. Importantly, for both algorithms, the number of queries grows sublinearly in $n$ when $\gamma < n^{1/m}$ and $\log n < n^{1/p}$ for $p = 2, p+1$, demonstrating sublinear query complexity. The study further includes two more algorithms designed to estimate entropy in Markov chain mixing, with one yielding an approximation within a factor $\sqrt{\log n}$ of the mixing time with $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n \log n})$ queries, where the mixing time is estimated to be $\ge n^{3/2} \log n$ and $\ge n \log n$ with high probability, respectively. The other algorithm provides an approximation within a factor $\sqrt{\log n}$ of the quantum entropy with $\widetilde{O}(\gamma^n \log n)$ queries. Importantly, for both algorithms, the number of queries grows sublinearly in $n$. The main contributions stem from enhancing entropy estimation, mixing time estimation, and combining these concepts to estimate quantum entropy. Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), have been analyzed by recent studies using machine learning techniques to forecast diagnoses based on CTNs, a task known as International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding. Annotating medical data can be particularly labor-intensive due to the required level of specialist knowledge. This study presents an innovative approach to supplement a sparsely annotated collection of Icelandic CTNs using semi-self-supervised machine-learned imputation. By initially training a neural network on a small number of specialist annotations, the model is then applied to a large dataset, generating diagnoses for every CTN based on its most similar clinical CTN. This imputed data is used in place of non-annotated CTNs in model optimization, in addition to incorporating expert assessments as additional data in training. In comparison to traditional fully supervised methods employing only annotated data, this semi-self-supervised method has yielded better results in recent studies for forecasting diagnoses based on CTNs, achieving an overall mean absolute error of 0.73 ICD-10 categories and reporting moderate to strong effect sizes (d = 0.56, Cohen's $p$). This achievement has been accomplished without increasing computational resources, and without compromising model interpretability. Most notably, this semi-self-supervised approach has shown considerable generalizability, performing within 10% of the best known method in the domain, and boasting a code factor of 0.80. This approach is suggested as a feasible solution to the problem of sparse data in medical text annotations, and its validity in the medical domain. In particular, this semi-self-supervised approach may serve as a useful low-resource solution for domains with abundant data. A theoretical model of this approach is also provided, in addition to relevant code and data that replicate results. This work is the winner of the Challenges in Natural Language Processing 2021 competition organized by the International Conference on Machine Learning. A short version of this research was presented at the conference. Longer versions can be found at arXiv:2101.02890 and arXiv:2103.06521. This research is based on data from Iceland's National University Hospital, and has received funding from the Centre for Registered Data Analysis. This research is in accordance with relevant guidelines. In particular, PLOS One's guidelines for reporting results were considered. This research is in the public domain, and can be accessed at https://github.com/cefactr/ICD-Clinical-Text-C

Specifically, we will expand upon their definition and explore various properties of this class of ideals, particularly those involving the Linial complex and other key concepts. Additionally, we will establish a connection between almost Cohen-Macaulay binary ideals and ideals with linear resolution, which is a more stringent criterion. Crucially, our work will be centered around the graph theoretic aspect of these ideals. By examining the vertices of the Linial complex associated with an almost Cohen-Macauline binary ideal, $I$, we will derive a condition, denoted by $\Delta(I)$, which essentially captures the maximal degree of the facial simplex's vertex count. The main contribution of this note can be summarized as follows: Given an almost Cohen-Macauline binary ideal, $I$, with its Linial complex denoted by $\Phi(I)$ and vertex count parameter $\Delta(I)$, we will demonstrate that $I$ has a linear resolution if and only if $\Phi(I)$ satisfies the $\Delta(I)$-condition across all its facial simplexes. Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, achieving an impressive speedup due to a lower asymptotic complexity of $O(N^{3/2}K^{1/2}\log P)$ compared to the classical method's $O(CKP)$. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, and 3D shape from image data, even in complex real-world scenarios. To further adapt our method to deep learning, we propose an efficient regularization technique that leverages frequency-domain properties to counteract the biases introduced by optimization-based training data generation, allowing our model to generalize well beyond the trained data. A comprehensive evaluation showcases the effectiveness of our method on various tasks, demonstrating its potential to offer state-of-the-art performance in image-based 3D inference and material recovery applications. In an array of nonlinear oscillators with random frequencies and purely conserved interactions, global phase coherence is demonstrated to occur within finite networks and further examined as it collapses through the generation of localized periodic and chaotic waves following a parameter adjustment. For weak nonlinearity in the system, these global phases exhibit a temporary state of stability, akin to that observed in nearly conservative systems. The obtained results are also compared to the outcome of a simplified phase model where the oscillations' amplitudes are eliminated under an adiabatic process. The outcomes of this reduced model match the findings from full system simulations, revealing a robust mechanism for achieving global phase coherence. Moreover, this reduction provides a general approach for the design of array networks supporting global phase coherence. Ultimately, this theory offers a potential pathway to a new class of self-organizing holographic displays. This collaborative approach in visual analytics aims to facilitate seamless interaction between humans and machines, according to established standards and best practices. To achieve this, we propose an intelligent system that provides domain experts with relevant suggestions for data exploration, grounded in current knowledge and tailored to the user's specific needs. This paper introduces Lotse, a practical framework for insight guidance in visual analytics, and showcases its effectiveness in generating actionable recommendations that improve human performance when conducting complex data analysis. We achieve this by leveraging a comprehensive ontology that structures existing knowledge in the domain and a suggestion engine that offers multiple ways to provide guidance. To ensure optimal relevance, the system can adapt to a user's individual preferences and the specific task at hand. Our framework not only complements human intuition but also supplements existing recommendation methods with additional perspectives derived from domain expertise. As such, it can serve as a valuable asset for developers creating guidance systems, and we illustrate its usefulness with a practical example from the domain of biomedical research. To further demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we conducted a series of experiments, and the results of an evaluation by domain experts confirm that Lotse offers more relevant and diverse guidance compared to state-of-the-art baseline methods. Given its flexibility and modularity, Lotse can be applied to a wide range of domains and domains of interest, and we outline the plans for future development and improvement. Ultimately, this framework aims to empower domain experts with actionable guidance to enhance their insight and understanding when working with complex datasets and performing in-depth data analysis. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances design flexibility by taking into account coil placement during the modular coil design process, leveraging planar control coils and integrability objectives to improve quasisymmetry and nested flux surface quality. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by optimizing a coil set based on the NCSX design, which not only broadens the stellarator's design space but also reduces its size. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three different heating methods employed to study temperature distribution patterns. The findings indicate that the uniformity of the temperature distribution is directly related to the methods used for heating. Moreover, good correlation was observed between the temperature readings obtained by MRI and those measured with traditional temperature probes. This study validates the use of MRI imaging as a precise and non-invasive means of studying temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors. This novel technique offers promising prospects for optimizing the operational conditions of these systems. The time scale of temperature fluctuations captured in this study ranged from 10 seconds to 1000 seconds, covering fluid dynamics timescales and offering valuable insights into the interactions between gas and solid components. This research provides a new approach for scientists to study fluid dynamics and heat transfer within gas-solid systems using MRI imaging. Based on these findings, several applications and areas of further research have been identified. Initially, investigations will focus on the relationships between temperature distribution, gas and solid viscosities, and their impact on the pressure drop across the reactor. Additionally, further studies will explore the effect of key parameters such as catalyst particle size, shape, and distribution on the temperature distribution in the reactor. Lastly, MRI imaging will be employed to analyze heat transfer patterns within gas-solid systems, with a particular emphasis on non-Newtonian fluids. This research has opened the door for numerous future studies that can leverage the non-invasive capabilities of MRI imaging to gain a deeper understanding of the complex interactions within gas-solid systems. Furthermore, advances in this technique will enable scientists to study a broader spectrum of parameters including fluid dynamics, heat transfer, and rheology with unprecedented spatial and temporal resolution. The incorporation of MRI imaging will enable researchers to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying processes within gas-solid systems, ultimately fostering novel theoretical models and predictive algorithms. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. Experimental results validate the selective acoustic transmission properties of our design, with promising implications for the mass production of acoustic metagratings using this advanced 3D printing technique. Additionally, its capabilities extend beyond ultrasound, potentially applying to other types of high-frequency waves. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize adaptably to new tasks after being trained on multiple problems. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including novel environments that simulate realistic task scenarios. The paper introduces L2Explorer, a cutting-edge framework that enables researchers to test their continual learning strategies through a series of increasingly difficult challenges. L2Explorer is distinguished by its advanced generalization capabilities and its ability to simulate diverse scenarios that are difficult to program manually. When compared to existing approaches, L2Explorer's state-of-the-art model, developed using experience replay and curiosity-driven learning, exhibits exceptional performance, with notable gains of 14.6% and 12.5% on two assessment metrics. Furthermore, the researcher conducted an in-depth examination of the impact of dataset size on lifelong learning performance, revealing that, contrary to prevailing assumptions, larger training datasets may not consistently yield better results. Our future work will focus on exploring other dataset properties and their implications for lifelong learning strategies. Additionally, the source code and the L2Explorer environment are openly source, allowing researchers to repeat and build upon our findings. A video demonstrating the environment is also available. With travel restrictions in place, non-essential trips to high-risk countries have been discouraged. In medical contexts, various assessment methods often yield beneficial insights when combined, a process called information fusion. Through the integration of optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) data with optical coherence tomography (OCT) data, we discovered a substantial enhancement in the accuracy of retinal disease diagnoses. Specifically, by incorporating OCTA information, the average classification accuracy of glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy increased by 15% and 12%, respectively. Furthermore, a comparison with established deep learning models revealed that our proposed method achieved superior performance with reduced computational complexity, making it a more suitable approach for clinical applications where resource constraints apply. The effectiveness of this double-stream strategy prompted the exploration of its applicability to other multi-modal medical diagnosis tasks. The source code and OCTA-OCT fusion results can be found on our GitHub repository. The findings of this study are scheduled to be presented at the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition in 2021. The proposed method was tested on public glaucoma and DR datasets, yielding promising outcomes that demonstrate its potential for broad medical applications. The proposed method enabled a 15% and 12% improvement in accuracy with the incorporation of OCTA and OCT data alone, revealing its potential for a range of medical diagnoses. The 15% improvement from simply using OCT data alone indicates a substantial enhancement in diagnostic capabilities. The code has been shared on our public GitHub repository for the purpose of facilitating future research and development. The recent advancements in deep learning models have significantly impacted the field of medical image analysis, ultimately leading to the development of precise diagnostic systems. Despite these advancements, specific retinal diseases often go undetected due to the limited information available from a single imaging technique. By integrating the capabilities of multiple imaging methods, we aim to overcome these limitations and develop more precise diagnostic systems for a range of retinal diseases. The proposed method has been successfully applied to the classification of glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy, yielding state-of-the-art performance with reduced computational complexity. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. This paper tackles a long-standing problem in hardware optimization by developing an approach that uses a smaller number of hardware components to implement MCM. By extending and modifying existing work on optimal MCM circuits, this research proposes three new hardware optimization problems: one for each of three, four, and more than four hardware components. Due to the complexity and non-convex nature of these problems, a proposed iterative algorithm uses approximate multiplier values to gradually minimize the hardware cost. The proposed approach is also extended to accommodate several hardware constraints such as precision limitations and input range restrictions. Our research assesses whether the cosmic background of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation is negligible in comparison to the cosmic microwave background, primarily due to the black holes' low mass. This is caused by the emission's power law suppression of lower-energy frequencies. Although higher-mass black holes have lower-energy peaks, the intensity of Hawking radiation is still not sufficient to explain the observed signals. In an alternative scenario, we find that massive black holes may be able to emit radio waves as gas is drawn towards them, which could potentially account for the observed excess in ARCADE2 and LWA1 experiments. This process could deliver a non-thermal spectrum extending from p GeV to p GHz with comparable intensities. As a result, we propose that further investigation into extragalactic radio sources is warranted to determine whether this emission mechanism is responsible for the observed excess signals. In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.  Notably, while initial studies found size and position information to be valuable for object categorization in static scenes, our results indicate that size and position are likely derived by the network from video data featuring moving objects, thus suggesting the exploration of depth in categorical tasks.  This finding is consistent with cognitive theories stating that humans utilize size and position to perceive objects and suggests that size and position are inherently interconnected, much like memories, and thus cannot be independently learned or utilized.  This research provides the first evidence of recurrence in recurrent neural networks being exploited to collect relevant object features that are essential for object categorization in cluttered environments.  This study also offers a method for diagnosing and interpreting the role of recurrence in various tasks.  Finally, this research highlights the similarity between state-of-the-art artificial networks and cognitive models, thus suggesting that recurrent neural networks can serve as a useful model for understanding human object categorization abilities.  This study also provides guidelines for designing object categorization tasks that take into account the theoretical limitations and capabilities of recurrent neural networks.  Additionally, this research has implications for evaluating the performance of object categorization networks in controlled cluttered environments. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$. This outcome arises because correlations hinder the bulk-boundary correspondence, thereby invalidating the chiral symmetry in the absence of correlations. We verified these findings through the application to two concrete models: the correlated non-Hermitian Hofstadter model and the correlated non-Hermitian Fibonacci chain. The reduction in topological classification may also be observed in Hermitian systems, as demonstrated by the examples mentioned above. We therefore conclude that correlations pose an intrinsic obstacle to both non-Hermitian and Hermitian topological systems. To overcome this limitation, we propose an experimental method using artificial gauge fields to reduce correlations in non-Hermitian systems. We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad provides a viable way to handle partiality within univalent type theory, and we also demonstrate that a predicative and constructive Scott model is achievable. Notably, we avoid reliance on choice or quotient inductive-inductive types, unlike other approaches to dealing with partiality. Furthermore, we show that a significant portion of the standard univalent PCF development can be expressed within an entirely predicative and constructive Scott model. Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$. 
The resulting cancellation, for specific values of $s_1$ and $s_2$, 
leads to new, non-degenerate Eisenstein series, 
described by combinations of the one-parameter families $\Delta(\tau,m+n)|\cdot|^{s_1+s_2}$ and $\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$. 
Utilizing the Langlands reciprocity law, analogous cancellations occur in the local contexts of local fields $\mathbb{Q}_p($or equivalently $\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for almost elliptic Eisenstein series. 
In those situations, cancellations result in new, non-degenerate Eisenstein series, 
described by combinations of the one-parameter families $\Delta(\tau,m+n)|\cdot|^{s_1+s_2}$ and $\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$. 
In those situations, cancellations in the unramified cases are confirmed by unramified local Eisenstein series computations. 
In the ramified cases, cancellations are confirmed via the middle-degree Fourier-Jacobi lift, 
specifically by comparing the central value of the twisted Eisenstein series with that of the twisted automorphic representation. 
Ultimately, these findings can be summarized as specific instances of broader conjectures outlined in Ginzburg, Rallis, and Soudry's work. 
As an additional result, cancellations in the ramified cases are confirmed via an alternative approach by leveraging 
Gelbart and Rallis's work on Eisenstein series combinations and the Fourier-Jacobi lift. 
In a broader scope, this research can be seen as a further expansion of the findings presented in Ginzburg, Rallis, and Soudry's work.

To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users often consider undesirable, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. We introduce an innovative signature-based algorithm to calculate the nondegenerate locus of a given polynomial system through iterative transformations, providing a practical approach that can be utilized with generic, extension-based solvers like Singular's solveDEQ command. Moreover, the algorithm accommodates solvers with normal form capabilities, such as MMacSympy, as an alternative. Extensive examples showcase the efficacy of the proposed algorithm in obtaining the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system.
