Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, we found that approximately 20% of the $e^{+}e^{-}$ pairs originate from a non-hadronic source. Due to experimental limitations, we were unable to determine the invariant photon yield beyond $p_T=5$ GeV/$c$. Nonetheless, by using a transport model to simulate the remaining hadronic sources, we estimated that up to 40% of the photon yield at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ may not be accounted for. Consequently, we conclude that a considerable portion of Cu$+$Cu collision photons remain in hadronic form. Moreover, our findings indicate that the percentage of direct photons in Au$+$Au collisions at 200 GeV might be lower than previously reported. Ultimately, our research underscores the necessity for future $e^{+}e^{-}$ measurements at lower $p_T$ values to further elucidate the supplemental photon yield in heavy-ion collisions. In addition, we discussed the feasibility and importance of an in-flight $e/$-$p$ beam dump experiment to determine the direct photon yield at $p_T$ values below 2 GeV/$c$. This experiment could potentially be conducted at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider using the existing Holey Target experiment setup. Consequently, we would gain a deeper understanding of the supplemental photon yield in Cu$+$Cu collisions at $p_T>\sim 1$ GeV/$c$. To further explore this concept, we estimated the sensitivity of an in-flight $e/$-$p$ beam dump experiment equipped with a TPC at $p_T$ values below 2 GeV/$c$ and found that it would provide a direct measurement of the total photon ($a_1$ + direct) yield, thereby enabling us to investigate the supplementary photon yield in Cu$+$Cu collisions at $p_T$ values between 1 and 5 GeV/$c$. In an attempt to address these issues, a glsl anti-aliasing shader was developed to enhance the appearance of line joins on vector maps, while a AA render buffer was designed to accelerate anti-aliasing processing and reduce the computational load. As a result, the enhanced glsl anti-aliasing shader and AA render buffer enabled the classical line joins on vector maps to exhibit a crisp, clear appearance with minimal computational overhead. Moreover, the combined AA rendering method demonstrated a considerable time-saving advantage of up to 50% compared to the traditional AA rendering approach. Ultimately, the proposed anti-aliasing technique comprised an efficient spatial anti-aliasing rendering algorithm featuring glsl anti-aliasing shader and AA render buffer components that yielded a striking visual effect and a substantial computation load reduction.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. Importantly, our results indicate that this method can successfully approximate functions with steep gradients, achieving more precise approximations compared to existing methods. With its superior convergence rate and robustness, this new interpolation method serves as an effective tool for solving partial differential equations via the finite element method. Specifically, it is well-suited for modeling flow in porous media and designing efficient finite element methods. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches rely heavily on hand-engineered features, which are less effective than learning-based methods but fail to achieve similar levels of accuracy.
We have developed a comprehensive dataset of weather classifications, consisting of 8 distinct categories and including labels for background scenes, enabling the development of a novel data augmentation technique.
Our proposed solution incorporates a residual network with pre-trained 3D convolutional layers, utilizing feature maps from a two-stage feature extraction framework to extract meaningful features.
Our model has achieved an impressive mean accuracy of 96.5% across all classes, with an overall mean IoU of 87.6% for intra-class accuracy evaluation. Experimental results indicate that our model surpasses competing methods by a significant margin of 7.4%. Furthermore, our model demonstrates exceptional background suppression capabilities in raw RGB images. Using the proposed data augmentation technique, we have successfully validated the generalizability of our model through vehicle-mounted camera tests. Additionally, our model has shown promising results on the development of weather-aware systems. To ensure the high quality of our model, a comprehensive evaluation process has been performed. Detailed source code and the developed dataset are available for public access, along with a demonstration of our model's background suppression capabilities in unpredictable weather conditions. Our model can be utilized for weather detection tasks in various applications. With continued improvement, this detection system has the potential to further advance the development of weather-dependent intelligent transportation systems. Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have turned to data-driven methods. However, current methods typically require extensive model learning through simulations or offline processes, which often fails to adapt to novel scenarios or real-time grasping challenges. In this research, we propose an innovative online algorithm that uses the Koopman operator theory to update and refine a dynamic model in real-time. By integrating the updated model into a Model Predictive Control (MPC) structure, our approach enables seamless control implementation. Through experimental evaluations of a three-fingered soft gripper, our results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in adapting models and controls to diverse grasping tasks, even when the underlying system dynamics are unknown. Specifically, our methodology achieves a notable success rate of 97% in a challenging grasping task within a unknown dynamic system, surpassing the performance of traditional model-based approaches. Additionally, our approach's flexibility and general applicability are showcased through online learning experiments with multiple finger extensions, as well as in a dexterous four-fingered gripper. Our research showcases the potential of data-driven methods to tackle the complex control issues surrounding soft grippers and suggests a promising future for these technologies in a variety of applications. Videos and code are publicly accessible at https://ssoft-grasper.github.io/soft-grasper-web/. This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Firstly, we establish the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional over Lie algebras representing differential operators on a circle. We then identify the requirements for the irreducibility of tensor products between quasi-finite highest weight modules and modules free over $U(\frak h)$. Additionally, we show that these tensor products are isomorphic only if their corresponding base modules are equivalent, before expanding our findings to cover general Lie algebras representing differential operators. Lastly, we leverage our previous findings to determine the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional in certain special cases. We anticipate that these findings will contribute significantly to a comprehensive understanding of the categories ${\mathcal O}^+_{\frak g}\cap {\mathcal Sh}_{\frak g}$. Furthermore, we expect these results to be extended to cover quasi-finite highest weight modules over more advanced Lie algebras representing differential operators. Lastly, we preview the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional in the context of the Lie algebras representing differential operators on a circle and a square.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. To achieve this, we
propose a novel data collection method that combines an open-domain dialogue
foundation set with a smaller role specification dataset, allowing our system
to adhere to its assigned role in conversations initiated with role-aware prompts.
Our open-source system, which leverages large-scale language models, outperforms
baselines in both role consistency and conversation quality, and exhibits
competitive performance in natural conversation, empathy, and overall chat
quality. Additionally, our approach shows promising potential for systems to
maintain assigned roles in open-domain dialogue. Further details are available
on our project website: https://github.com/Chen-551/RoleOpenDial. (Equal contributions)

A reliable and efficient communication system known as the signaling game has been established as a fundamental aspect of human interaction. Emerging semantic communication seeks to enhance this framework by incorporating a semantic layer into the traditional communication structure. To further develop this concept, we propose an innovative approach that combines neuro-symbolic causal reasoning and signaling games to design a more resilient communication system. Specifically, we will examine how word meanings emerge in a complex communication scenario involving multiple human entities. The complexity of this problem stems from the interplay between words with unclear meanings and the unreliable exchange of messages among individuals. By integrating causal reasoning and a semantic communication framework within a game-theoretic context, we can analyze the long-term communication strategies employed by humans and provide a semantic connection that facilitates efficient and strategic communication. An example case study will be conducted to demonstrate how word meanings can evolve through a communication process known as the "iterated signaling game." Furthermore, we will examine the similarities and differences between two distinct game-theoretic models: one that relies solely on statistical patterns in word usage and another that incorporates the underlying causal relationships between words. Experimental results will showcase how the causal structure of word relationships affects the emergence of stable concepts, highlighting the potential for shared understanding in human communication that goes beyond statistical patterns in word usage. Natural language models often struggle with unknown words, whose presence can distort the probability distribution and lead to inaccurate predictions. One approach to mitigate this issue is to assign a default probability density function, such as uniform or Dirac's function, to unknown words. However, this method can result in suboptimal outcomes. Another approach involves omitting unknown words from the model's probability distribution, but this may compromise model performance. In contrast, combining latent variables with naive Bayes is a better way to handle unknown words, as it utilizes the context's influence more effectively. This model is similar to the one proposed by Li and Cover in 1996, which is an extension of naive Bayes for language models that incorporates the unstated frequency distribution of unknown words based on context, and our analysis shows that this model is an optimization of the original frequency distribution equation. We tested this model on multiple datasets and found it to be more accurate than models that assign a default probability density function or omit unknown words. Our results indicate that this model performs at least as well as a fully trained model with complete knowledge of words' frequency distribution. We also explored the model's generalization capabilities by simulating varying levels of training data and observed a significant improvement in performance with each increment of training data. Based on these findings, our model is an effective solution for natural language models that encounter unknown words in their data. We also developed hybrid models that combine our approach with other advanced language models, such as recurrent neural networks and long short-term memory for better output. These hybrid models performed even better, with improvements ranging from 14.2% to 64.1% over the basic model. Our work includes code that can be accessed through GitHub. We also calculated the theoretical bounds of our model's performance and successfully matched those bounds in our experiments. These findings confirm that our model is optimal. Our model offers multiple applications, including but not limited to, language modeling, text classification, sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging, parsing, word-sense disambiguation, and automatic text summarization. In addition to word prediction, this model can also be utilized for classification tasks by combining it with other classifiers. We also investigated the model's run-time efficiency and observed a rapid decrease in processing time with each increment of training data. Our model's high performance, combined with its ability to handle unknown words effectively, makes it a valuable tool for natural language models. Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional techniques. Recent examples include STAMP and NARM models, which, however, did not perform as expected on Zalando's Fashion-Similar dataset in comparison to a basic collaborative-filtering method. Our proposed strategy targets improving item ranking by leveraging the encoded session information through an attention network and demonstrates the potential through Candidate Rank Embedding in re-ranking. Experimental results demonstrate a considerable enhancement over the baseline on metrics such as Recall, MRR, and Click-Through-Rate in an online setting, and we further observed improvements when applied to STAMP and NARM models on two public real-world datasets for the task of next-click prediction. Specifically, these gains include a 4.5% increase in MRR and a 1.7% increase in hit ratio at a 90% recall threshold in the Fashion-Similar dataset. We have made the code publicly available for replication of these findings. Additionally, we have tested a related ranking method and observed promising outcomes, which we plan to explore further in future research. Our novel approach is motivated by the observation that current state-space models and graph models have difficulties in effectively capturing long-term dependencies within sessions. Consequently, the extracted session features from these models might not be adequate for the recommendation task. On the other hand, the attention mechanism present in many contemporary state-space models has the ability to concentrate on long-term information, but it typically benefits items already near the top of the rank list, leaving shorter-term information focusing on lower-ranked items. Thus, there is an underexploited potential in optimizing the rank itself rather than just the embedded session space. Our proposed solution involves the implementation of a re-ranking network that leverages the top-ranked items' embeddings as input, which are extracted using a two-stage approach comprising an initial coarse filtering stage followed by a finer re-ranking stage. In particular, the Coarse Filter employs an attention mechanism-based state-space model to generate embedded session representations that are then used in an unsupervised manner. These embedded session representations are then fed to the finer re-ranking network for the re-ranking task. Notably, the Coarse Filter attends to items that are typically higher ranked and less sensitive to long-term session information, while the finer re-ranking stage focuses on optimizing the final rank. A theoretical framework combines the principles of active nematics to accurately predict our findings. In this framework, we explore the formation of an active droplet, a localized structure that emerges within the active colloidal molecule's activity gradient. Our research reveals two distinct droplet types - a droplet with uniform droplet core and a droplet with a droplet core with a droplet tail - as well as the existence of an active droplet phase transition. This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: firstly, determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions (collision avoidance reformation), and secondly, effecting this reformation while minimizing the time and energy spent by the drones. To resolve the first challenge, a novel approach utilizing a centroid-based dynamic formation structure is presented, allowing the swarm to dynamically adapt its shape in response to external stimuli. To address the second problem, a registration algorithm drawing parallels from computer science is implemented to minimize energy expenditure during reformation. Through energetic evaluations and simulations, this method proves more efficient than existing solutions; for instance, compared to constant altitude collision avoidance, this approach reduces energy consumption by up to 70% when the number of drones reaches 20. Successful experimental validation of the proposed framework has been carried out using a testbed consisting of Nexus drones. Furthermore, simulations have been conducted to assess its performance under a range of scenarios, including scenarios with moving obstacles and varying numbers of drones. As a result, the developed technique exhibits superior performance in terms of collision avoidance time, with an average improvement of 30-90% compared to existing methods when the number of drones reaches 20. Key variants of the proposed approach have also been identified, indicating that the incorporation of more sophisticated collision detection methods and dynamic reformation strategies holds significant potential for further development. Based on these results, the estimated time required for human intervention following collision avoidance reformation has been minimized, with an average improvement of up to 66.7% when the number of drones reaches 20. To summarize, this study has led to the creation of an efficient and dynamic drone formation structure, featuring optimized collision avoidance reformation capabilities and reduced energy expenditure, thereby ensuring the prolonged functioning of the swarm. These findings have been empirically validated through both experimental and simulated research. As such, the presented approach holds significant potential for real-world application within areas such as aerial photography, where efficient and coordinated formation flying is often required. In the future, the focus will be on expanding the proposed framework to enable more complex reformation strategies. Additionally, the incorporation of external stimuli and obstacle navigation techniques will be developed to further enhance the performance of the swarm. Lastly, the estimated time required for human intervention following collision avoidance reformation will be statistically analyzed through the application of nonparametric tests. To this end, relevant software packages, such as MATLAB, Simulink, and DroneKit, will once again be employed in the implementation

In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures to establish necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principles. This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving a delayed consumption optimization problem from a cash flow and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints. Our study's results are significant to contemporary research on stochastic optimal control for differential equations experiencing delays due to complex noise dynamics. Additionally, the method of differentiating functions of measures contributes to the development of mean-field optimal control of differential equations, which is a topic of growing interest. RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with vehicles on the road. However, vehicles' mobility and relaying capabilities pose challenges in predicting network performance. In this study, an analytical model of vehicle-admitted assistance by an RSU is developed, focusing on relay mode, admission control, and relay power adjustment. Mathematically derived outcomes for K, an optimal value for M, and average energy per bit are obtained. Simulation results indicate that relaying by vehicles admitted by RSUs can enhance network performance, with an RSU acting as a central controller achieving this outcome. Additionally, this study investigates the impact of various parameters on relaying-assisted success probability and network performance. Furthermore, simulations using mmWave and Ray 6 channels show that vehicle relaying can benefit network performance in urban and suburban settings. Ultimately, this study concludes that vehicle relaying admitted by RSUs can serve as a viable option to enhance the success probability of downlink communications in vehicular networks. Details on the model's development, including derivations and simulations, are available upon request to the author. Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that combines natural language processing with an analysis of editing behaviors to label sentences without human input. By training the system using a large corpus from Good Articles, it outperformed human annotations in predicting editing behavior and accurately identified low-quality sentences on articles without humans intervention. Additionally, our method saves costs by providing a viable alternative to manual labeling, whereas the trained models can be utilized for text domains beyond Wikipedia's scope. Furthermore, our research suggests that editing behaviors contain more informative value for labeling purposes compared to the text itself, indicating that Wikipedia's quality control is heavily influenced by consistent policies rather than text content. Ultimately, our model is ready to be deployed for automatic labeling on articles, especially in domains where similar patterns in editing behaviors can be observed. To facilitate this process, we also released a neural network and relevant data through open access for other researchers to use. With this advancement, we are one step closer to efficiently labeling data and developing machines that can enhance article quality on Wikipedia. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on the ResNet-50 architecture and a range of image classification datasets, which show that it's equally effective whether or not the original data is accessible. The code for this method is available on GitHub at https://github.com/0oPhang.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.2±0.2) ×10^-4. The measurements made in the mass spectra of the $\bar{D}^0\bar{K}^0$ and $\bar{D}^{*0}\bar{K}^0$ systems are also presented. The findings are consistent with the Standard Model predictions. The second decay mode's significance was determined to be 3.4 standard deviations. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, demonstrating improved performance over traditional reinforcement learning techniques. Additionally, our method shows promising promise in a real-world robotic scenario. The code for this project is openly accessible on GitHub. Thorough experimentation validates the novelty of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, verifying its distinction from prior research in cooperative learning, imitation learning, and emergent knowledge settings. Furthermore, our findings address the critical challenge of peer agent diversity in co-imitation learning, showcasing its potential to substantially undermine performance. Thorough evaluation through comparison with established benchmarks, including multi-level benchmark systems, reveals our Co-Imitation Learning framework to be consistently superior to traditional reinforcement learning techniques. Moreover, our research presents a series of design choices for peer diversity in co-imitation learning, including the influential effect on performance it can have. The efficacy of our Co-Imitation Learning framework is further substantiated through its application in a complex robotic navigation scenario. Thorough experimentation demonstrates the superiority of our method, highlighting its distinction from a variety of relevant research, including co-imitation learning, imitation learning, and emergent knowledge settings. By applying the Polarization metric, we developed a method to calculate the Polar code's Error-Correcting capability and derived an efficient algorithm to obtain the Polar code's check nodes. This algorithm has a low computational complexity of O(log(2N)), where N is the code's length. Additionally, we provided a dynamic programming approach to determine the Polar code's survivor indices, which can be calculated in O(log(2N)) time. Furthermore, we developed a hybrid architecture for the Polar code decoder, which incorporates partially-parallelized Polar decoders, to achieve a balance between area, power consumption, and latency in VLSI design. Moreover, the hybrid decoder architecture offers a reasonable trade-off between area power and latency. Specifically, under a fixed area constraint, our design reduces power consumption by 10-20%, while also reducing latency by 30-40%. A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically identify and utilize specific points on objects for calibration, eliminating the need for any prior knowledge. A novel algorithm transforms real-world object points into a standardized coordinate system, allowing for accurate prediction of robot end-effector positions from 3D point data. Our method is fast, supporting over 10 calculations per second, and capable of handling diverse objects and tasks. Results show that our system exhibits only slight positioning errors compared to traditional methods, with an average position error of less than 2cm. Furthermore, our calibration is remarkably robust, with minimal error drift over time. To verify its effectiveness in diverse scenarios, calibration was performed in multiple environments using various objects, including a 3cm diameter rolling sphere and a 10kg box. A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods. This is evident from the results of our simulation, which also reveal that the test performance can be refined by incorporating variables other than those within the K-neighborhood. As a result, this novel approach enables the detection of treatment interference in networks with a small number of connected units. We demonstrate its utility using data from a study on the impact of local treatment on units connected in a triangle graph. Additionally, its extension to more complex networks is discussed. Software code for replicating the results is available on GitHub.

Our analysis covers an expansive 4820 square degrees of the sky, cataloging 40 million galaxies, translating to a density of 8.4 per square arcminute. Introducing ShapePipe, a cutting-edge pipeline leveraging Ngmix for precise galaxy shape detection and metacalibration for accurate shear calibration, the study reaches an optimal precision of 1.55%, surpassing the planned 2% prediction for the four-point correlation function analysis. Shear and density profiles show promising agreement with existing predictions and observations, showcasing ShapePipe's effectiveness. Using ShapePipe, the study discovered the point mass function and four-point correlation function with minimal residual biases, paving the way for future investigations. The UNIONS+CFIS data combination through ShapePipe has reached a precision of 0.75%, yielding promising results for ongoing and upcoming analyses. For hypersurfaces, this condition can be fulfilled if and only if the singularity is k-rational. Additionally, the k-rational/Du Bois properties in the case of local complete intersections are equivalent to those for k-rational/Du Bois hypersurfaces, provided the codimension does not exceed one. Furthermore, combining recent findings by [FLP20] and [FLP20b], we establish that k-rational singularities of local complete intersections are also k-Du Bois, thus resolving an open question posed in [FLP20]. Lastly, this resolution has significant implications, extending certain theorems related to k-rational singularities to the realm of k-Du Bois singularities. Notably, among the concrete applications is the proof that for k-rational hypersurfaces, the k-Du Bois locus coincides with the log smooth locus. The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this contribution, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop Feynman integrands, exemplified through the case of planar and non-planar 2-loop box integrals. The causal representation is then evaluated using numerical methods, enabling the direct computation of causal Feynman integrals. Notably, we find that numerical values of causal Feynman integrals can differ significantly from their conventional counterparts. The conventionally-defined integrals are often redundant, with their structure containing non-physical information that must be eliminated to obtain meaningful results. The causal representation provides a universal framework for encoding Feynman integrands, and offers a potential solution to the problem of numerically evaluating multi-loop integrals in a physically valid manner. The implementation details of this approach, including numerical evaluation and book-keeping concerns, are critical for practical applications and are therefore carefully considered. The numerical results presented in this contribution are accurate to all orders in the coupling constant. The material presented here serves as an extension and expansion of the original work detailed in Eur. Phys. J. C 80 (2020) 1, featuring an extensive set of numerical results, along with additional insights gained from examining the causal representation in detail. Specifically, we have obtained the numerical value of the planar 2-loop box at order $O(q^2)$ as $44\pi^2 + 19$. The corresponding non-planar 2-loop box was evaluated as $52\pi^2 + 24$. The numerical evaluation of the 2-loop box $Q_2$ up to $O(q^2)$ yielded $-17+20\pi^2$. The set of numerical results for both planar and non-planar 2-loop boxes stands in contrast to conventional findings, and highlights the distinct character of the causal representation. It is crucial to note that while this approach may offer advantages in numerical computations at higher loop orders, additional non-physical information must be accounted for at $O(q^2)$. The impact of loop-tree duality is far-reaching, and the causal representation is a key manifestation of this effect. This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on the Heisenberg operator basis. The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. In studying this, researchers investigate whether this analogy accurately describes the collective behavior of quantum Hall states and other chiral topological systems. By analyzing the Haldane model, which simulates different environmental conditions, they examine the consequences of two scenarios: one with variable gravity and electrostatic forces, and another with variable temperature and chemical potential resulting from interactions with surrounding electrons and phonons. The study reveals significant differences between these scenarios, particularly regarding the helical Mott insulator phase, where variable gravity causes a substantial entanglement entropy increase, whereas variable temperature only slightly affects it. Furthermore, the researchers found that the system's energy density is not directly proportional to its entropy, a deviation from this expectation being a hallmark characteristic of the phase in question. Regarding the topological Haldane model, which describes a different set of states, the researchers found that the system's response to anisotropic gravity is uniform and proportional to its entropy, connecting variability in gravity to a corresponding variability in heat conducted along the direction perpendicular to the energy flow. The discovered relationships between these variables have implications for experiments measuring chiral systems' properties. The study uses a general theoretical framework that can be applied to a broad range of systems, providing a deeper understanding of their behavior. The researchers identified a particular type of critical point, where the system's response to an external stimulus is the same regardless of the stimulus's direction, and described how this critical point behaves when exposed to external pressure, resulting in a critical phenomenon known as scaling. The study uses numerical methods to analyze the system's phase diagram and the transitions within it, and observes a type of critical behavior known as deconfinement, where the system's components become less tightly bound as it approaches a critical temperature. The researchers found that the critical temperature is directly proportional to the pressure applied, and speculated that this may be universal behavior for chiral systems. The study delves into the system's low-energy excitations, discovering that these vary depending on whether gravity is present, with numerous non-interacting fermions replacing entangled anyons under certain environmental conditions. The researchers found that one-component of these low-energy excitations behaves like a charged particle under electrostatic force, and that their low-energy energy levels can be calculated using a type of scaling theory, which holds even when the system is at its critical point. The study uses these findings to reevaluate the system's collective behavior in the presence of long-range electron interactions

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred over more complex ones, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity. Our findings suggest that the popularity of these methods can be attributed to their implicit control over geometric complexity, and we showcase their effectiveness in a set of well-established benchmarks for deep learning. Additionally, our research reveals that geometric complexity is closely tied to generalization performance, and we introduce a geometric complexity metric that can be easily computed during training, serving as a valuable additional metric for evaluating model performance. Our code is publicly available.

With this full dataset at hand, the new approach achieves tighter constraints on the $C_9$ Wilson coefficient, yielding $C_9^{\rm GWT}=(4.7\pm 3.7_{-2.2+1.2})\times 10^{-5}$, closely aligning with the Standard Model prediction of $C_9^{\rm SM}=(4.2\pm 1.0)\times 10^{-5}$, thereby significantly enhancing our understanding of this critical quantity. This method is anticipated to significantly contribute to the study of semileptonic $B\to K$ decays at future beam dump experiments where a significant suppression of hadronic activity enables the uncovering of new physics in this process. Additionally, this method may be adapted for analysis of $B^0\to K^{*0}\tau^+\tau^-$ decays although this will necessitate the evaluation of numerical integrals affecting the unbinned likelihood method due to the increased complexity introduced by the $\tau$ mass. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of NLP models in recent years, including those for automated essay grading.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in addressing this problem.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of data augmentation methods for automated essay scoring using transformer-based models, specifically examining the difference between using the BERT and BERT-LSTM models in comparing the accuracy of augmented and non-augmented models.  We found that the BERT-LSTM model distinguished between the accuracy of augmented and non-augmented models, indicating a positive impact of data augmentation when using this model.  Additionally, our results showed that the BERT-LSTM model performed better than both the BERT and LSTM models alone in predicting human scores based on both individual and aggregate annotations of essays.  Notably, our findings suggest that data augmentation leads to improved model performance when using the BERT-LSTM model, highlighting the practical value of this technique in automated essay grading.  Finally, our study indicates that the BERT-LSTM model exhibited improved robustness against variations in length compared to other models examined, despite its fixed positional encoding mechanism, which positions the first token representing a special token at position 0.  This means that models may adapt to different sentence lengths in pre-trained models, which could have significant practical implications in automated essay grading and other domains. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings. Furthermore, our findings highlight the significance of considering both present and future effects when making policy decisions that involve intergenerational mobility. In particular, distributing opportunities equally may not always maximize the overall well-being of all individuals. The distribution's fairness depends on the specific circumstances, such as the opportunity-giving body and the level of restrictions on social mobility. This recognition enables derivation of the Pauli exclusion principle for bosons without relying on relativistic quantum mechanics. Furthermore, recognizing the origin of exchange statistics from parity symmetry leads to a natural extension of this principle to relativistic quantum field theory, where the spin-statistics connection remains a parity-driven phenomenon, and the exclusion principle for bosons still has a non-relativistic quantum mechanical basis. Finally, this understanding yields a novel interpretation of the C, P, CPT symmetry transformation effects on spin and wavefunction parity, resulting in a simple physical explanation that matches established results. This abstract encapsulates the main thesis of a corresponding physical semantics lecture.

Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been done using several patterns of final particle arrangements.  Together, these findings indicate that same-type boson interactions occur at a level that is not much different from standard model predictions, with cross-section estimates ranging from 20 to 62 fb, at a 95% confidence level.  Additionally, these results result in constraints on certain beyond-standard model theories involving electroweak symmetry breaking, where certain models predict anomalous couplings between bosons that have minimal effects on standard model predictions, with couplings up to 0.065 TeV$^{-1}$ being ruled out at a 95% confidence level.  Finally, these results result in the first measurement of triple boson ratios to verify standard model predictions for their relative production rates.  These results yield a ratio of same-type boson production to mixed boson production that matches the standard model's prediction with an uncertainty of 8%, nor has a notable discrepancy been found in this verification process.  Future analyses using upcoming data could increase precision in these measurements by a factor of ten.

This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, which has evolved significantly since its initial creation. This research paper addresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus offers enhanced tokens representing Hebrew words, improved annotations with higher standards, and a comprehensive selection of UD categories suited for contemporary Hebrew. Unlike previous initiatives, this new project combines data from various sources, including forums, social media platforms, blogs, and news articles, to create a highly representative UD Hebrew treebank. This research paper details the corpus construction methodology, explains the rationale behind token and category choices, and describes the annotation scheme. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs. To facilitate practical implementation, we also develop an optimization framework for optimizing degree-degree correlations, allowing us to create LDPC designs that surpass traditional ones under specific constraints. Numerical results verify the effectiveness of our approach. Due to the complexity of analyzing degree-degree correlations using the density evolution method, we develop a simplified model based on degree-degree Correllation Spectrum Analysis. This analysis, inspired by methods used to investigate quantum systems, enables us to accurately predict ensemble properties, including the minimum degree distribution, average degree, and Trivedi Function, all of which are crucial for evaluating LDPC code performance. An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with a substantially lower number of variables compared to conventional MPSF formulations, which are typically based on flatness-based formulations. This means that SL-MPSF can efficiently handle larger-scale systems with more complex structures, which was demonstrated through numerical testing of two distinct systems. This includes a simple aircraft flight control system and a large-scale mass spring-damper oscillator model. These experiments highlight the advantages of SL-MPSF in terms of improved spatio-temporal system design and performance evaluation capabilities. Furthermore, SL-MPSF outperforms flatness-based MPSF methods in terms of computational efficiency and scalability. These findings suggest that SL-MPSF could provide a valuable and practical solution for safety-critical control applications. To better understand the formation and evolution of such structures, we have developed a numerical model integrating 1D hydrostatic accretion with customizable cooling, magnetic fields, and thermal conduction. Our simulations revealed the critical importance of self-gravity in accumulating mass from a larger area, unlike filamentary structures. We found that magnetic fields play a significant role in regulating cloud stability, but only affect its growth rate. Thermal conduction weakens the hydrostatic balance but allows for a more extensive accretion radius. Our results indicate that the evolution of cooling clouds is determined by a delicate balance between inflow and outflow rates, and we propose a theoretical model to describe this balance. Moreover, we observed a unique hysteresis cycle in our model, where the cloud's size depends on the accretion rate and pressure, leading to contrasting growth patterns in the inner and outer regions of the accretion flow. Ultimately, our study underscores the interconnectedness of processes regulating gas accretion and cooling, suggesting a unified perspective is needed to comprehend the dynamics of cooling clouds. A remarkable relationship exists among these amplitudes, where one is proportional to the others. Calculations of their spectra reveal a common framework, where one is composed of the others, thus explaining a long-standing conjecture made by Gross in 1988. To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods based on underlying device technology, which we refer to as the "air interface." This can be achieved by incorporating more intelligent and adaptive methods that take into account various data transmission parameters, such as power consumption models. By promoting greater autonomy in network management, these methods can enable MNs to be fully automated, allowing for easier integration of M2M communications and enabling MNs to be viewed as standardized, self-contained systems. We propose specific procedures for realizing autonomous MNs with minimal environmental impact, which we demonstrate using 5G LTE as a case study. These procedures facilitate the exchange of information between network entities, enabling control of energy consumption and quality of service parameters. To ensure seamless operation during the transition from non-autonomous to autonomous mode, these procedures are designed to work in tandem with traditional air interface resource allocation methods. Furthermore, these procedures promote energy efficiency by enabling MNs to switch between different operational modes and adjust transmission power in a power-controlled state, which in turn affects the MN's overall spectral efficiency and bit rate. We investigate the potential benefits and implications of these procedures, revealing that autonomous mode can lead to reduced system data rates during periods of minimal mobile traffic, but may also result in decreased spectral efficiency compared to non-autonomous modes, which we aim to mitigate through the design of these management procedures. To address these concerns, we propose the use of two specific procedures: the "Power-Controlled Autonomous Schedule Procedure" and the "Energy Efficiency Optimized Schedule Procedure," which prioritize minimizing system data rate and spectral efficiency, respectively, while demonstrating the possibility of quantifying the extent to which these objectives conflict. To facilitate a comprehensive evaluation, we also develop and apply two alternative scenarios, which we derive from a prior study on MNs and confirm to be effective in the context of MNs. Upon examination of the results, which show that the current spectral efficiency of 5G LTE is insufficient for supporting autonomous MNs with minimal environmental impact, we confirm the necessity of incorporating additional intelligent and adaptive methods to take advantage of the full potential of 5G LTE. Moving forward, we suggest that future research be focused on further evolving these management procedures to meet the evolving needs of mobile and IoT applications. Ultimately, this will enable the realization of fully autonomous MNs with minimal environmental impact. We present our findings in a concise manner, using clear and straightforward language to ensure ease of understanding and replication

The objective of zero-speech synthesis involves creating speech without transcription, relying on acoustic units as the basic unit of information. Typically, trained models in this area first identify the transcription and then use a trained model to generate the speech. This study focuses on the speech synthesis component, using a large database of human-recorded sentences to train the model. Since transcriptions are already available, a novel approach is taken where the model is trained to select the most relevant units based on priority levels assigned to the acoustic units. Priorities are determined through a unit-to-unit similarity comparison, calculating the average distance between the dominant spectral features of corresponding units. This comparison is performed without the need for further transcription, using a similarity metric that can work with unsupervised acoustic units, such as mel-frequency cepstral coefficients. This study evaluates different models trained on this simplified transcription, comparing the results to a model trained using standard transcriptions. The quality of the generated speech is assessed using a range of metrics, including mean opinion score, mean squared error, and word error rate. The results show a noticeable difference in the generated speech quality when using the proposed transcription method, with a significant gap in performance compared to a model trained on standard transcriptions. Nonetheless, the speech synthesized using the proposed transcription method demonstrates improvements over a baseline system using unsupervised mel-frequency cepstral coefficients as the transcription. Additionally, the proposed method is shown to be effective when using a more basic model based on hidden Markov models for speech synthesis. This study provides evidence that prioritizing acoustic units based on a comparison of dominant spectral features is an effective strategy for speech synthesis, ultimately leading to improved speech quality. Furthermore, this approach is shown to be effective in systems using hidden Markov models for speech synthesis. Moving forward, the authors plan to explore priority determination based on non-parallel data, such as unsupervised melodic patterns, to further enhance speech synthesis quality. Given its reliance on a comparison of spectral features for transcription, this method is suitable for domains where visual data is limited or unavailable. Conversely, when visual data is readily available, more advanced features such as linear frequency cepstral coefficients or spectral quality factors could be used to further improve speech synthesis quality. Ultimately, the proposed system is seen as an evolutionary step for speech synthesis, providing a simplified transcription method that yields high-quality results. This approach is expected to be particularly beneficial in domains where transcription costs are high or visual data is limited, providing a more efficient alternative to traditional systems. Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinear optimization problems efficiently. Both individual stages and inter-stage connections are addressed using a data-driven approach that incorporates a specific assumption-based approximation for more efficient optimizations. This proposed method, combined with data-driven assumptions derived from actual ground interactions, yields significant reductions in optimization times, typically under 2 seconds, allowing for real-time applicability to small drones like Quadcopters. This proposed method has been successfully applied to optimal regrasp planning for multi-limbed robots, yielding notable improvements over current single-step optimization techniques. Crucially, both proposed method parameters and data-driven assumptions can be adapted for various robot types using readily available data, facilitating easy generalization to diverse multi-limbed robots. This proposed method's performance in complex scenarios, along with its potential for real-world application, is showcased through a variety of simulation and experimental results presented in this research. This includes successful application of the proposed method on a Quadcopter equipped with under-actuated grippers featuring four degrees of freedom, resulting in successful regrasp planning following initial training with simulated data. This facilitated the successful execution of a regrasp challenge at the 2019 Drone Grand Challenge. This work is expected to lead to significant advancements in optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion, enabling these robots to operate in a variety of challenging and complex environments. We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar pendulum and a mass-spring-damper system, with the spring constant representing resistance to movement. The position of the pivot changed under the influence of external forces like friction, inertia, and gravity, resulting in an intriguing combination of geometric and dynamical complexities. The spectrum of the system's nonlinear oscillator exhibits scaling properties and depends on the angle of carrying, leading to period and frequency changes as the pivot passes through typical carrying angles. The system exhibits a Hopf bifurcation with increasing friction, leading to stable small-amplitude limit cycles for certain parameter ranges. We verified the effectiveness of our model through comparisons with experimental findings. Additionally, we analyzed the relationship between our model's parameters and the carrying angle of the cup. We also explored the effects of incorporating frequency-dependent friction and unsymmetrical bouncing behaviors. The study gives insight into the sipping phenomenon and the dynamics of a pivoted oscillator with an irregular restoring force. Furthermore, it provides a framework for investigating unsymmetrical pendulum behaviors under various driving mechanisms. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, which achieves a $O(\sqrt{K}\log(K))$ regret. Furthermore, we examine a specific practical application involving wireless networks and demonstrate through experimentation that our proposed method outperforms current state-of-art techniques, even in scenarios where the data distribution remains unchanged. The experiment results show that DR-DSGD achieves a significant improvement over existing methods of up to $10$ times. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/alirezamomennasab/dr-dsgd. Additionally, a technical report containing more detailed analysis and additional results is available at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.4853/RR.4420.0. Our research was supported by NSF grant CNS-1731666. We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma. Finally, we predict the collision energy required to observe the hydrodynamic attractor principle, which implies a collective, hydrodynamic behavior, in collisions involving smaller systems such as protons and nuclei. This system-size threshold is expected to be in the energy range of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 6.5-7$ GeV.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric that measures system safety in the presence of destabilizing influences, such as saturation and filter error, which ultimately enables comprehensive compensation and performance restoration. It is acknowledged that within a safety zone, certain thresholds can be tolerated for these destabilizing factors, prompting the need for corrective action only when the system's status poses a significant threat. Numerical simulation examples effectively demonstrate the proposed strategy's merits. One significant finding is that while the BFC technique can mitigate filter errors, it is incapable of addressing actuator saturation. In contrast, the BPC method not only compensates for both issues but also offers improved performance advantages over the traditional backstepping control (BC) method in the absence of constraints and filter errors. Experimental validation on a hexapod robot is also presented to validate the proposed strategy's real-world applicability and performance. This experimental work highlights the importance of properly scaling the high-level BPC controller due to its sensitivity to measurement accuracy and filter errors, which can be mitigated by implementing a scale-adaptive low-level supervisor. Consequently, this paper confirms that the BPC method achieves superior performance outcomes, suppresses excessive controller demands, and ensures safe operational practices. It is noted that the proposed controller design does not violate any necessary or sufficient conditions but rather operates within the established safety boundaries. This study offers a fresh perspective on constrained nonlinear control, encompassing a novel safety assessment metric, to balance performance and risk management for a specific system class. This work can be seen as a control design for a specific system category with significant real-world applicability, including hexapod robots, rather than a general control design for all nonlinear systems. This distinction is made clear to avoid generating theories that may not translate to practical applications. We show in this work how the principles of gauge invariance are maintained in simulations of light-matter interactions based on tight-binding models. By examining the commutator of the Hamiltonian with the vector potential, a dipole approximation is derived that ensures the invariance of the system's wave function under the influence of the vector potential. This allows for the accurate description of strong light-matter coupling within these models, and we verify this invariance for realistic atomic and atomic-scale nanostructures. Additionally, we discuss the importance of invariance for simulating Rabi oscillations and other phenomena associated with strong coupling. Furthermore, we derive conditions for ensuring invariance in more complex models, extending beyond the restrictive assumptions of tight-binding. This invariance criterion can be applied to a broad range of models, enabling the description of complex light-matter interactions with consistency. Examples of such applications include simulations of materials composed of multiple atoms and those under the influence of non-local electric fields. By establishing this invariance, a reliable framework is established for simulating light-matter interactions across a diverse range of systems. Invariance is verified for a range of phenomena, including two-electron Rabi oscillations, atomic coherences in emitters, and electric dipoles not aligned with the light's polarization. This verification confirms the theoretical expectation that light-matter coupling follows gauge invariance. Moreover, we demonstrate the precision of our invariance approach by comparing it to more approximate methods, such as the rotating wave approximation. This comparison highlights the precision gained by maintaining invariance in simulations, particularly for excited states that do not adhere to the strict assumptions of tight-binding. Ultimately, we conclude that invariance is a necessary condition for accurately describing light-matter interactions within simulations. This finding releases a significant limitation on the scope of tight-binding models for quantum optics applications, allowing these models to describe complex phenomena that were previously inaccessible. By maintaining invariance, a versatile tool is established for simulating accurate pictures of light-matter interactions across a broad range of systems. This will facilitate broader applications of tight-binding models in quantum optics and condensed matter research. Related to this, we explore the implications for superconducting qubits based on box-like models, revealing the invariance for multi-qubit systems coupled to the same drive field. To address potential variability in object appearance and structure, we draw on geometric models from computer-aided design. This allows us to define a novel 3D geometric representation, referred to as the CAD model, and leverage it for shape estimation. However, since precise geometric models are often impractical, we aim to find optimal and robust methods for shape recovery using partial and noisy 2D and 3D keypoints. By framing this issue within a probabilistic framework based on graph inference, we derive optimal solutions through the application of variational inference and message passing algorithms. Notably, our proposed method achieves superior performance on PASCAL3D+ and KITTI3D for object pose estimation, and outperforms state-of-the-art geometric model-based methods for shape estimation, while also being more efficient and flexible. A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under one protocol. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to optimize sample size and allows information sharing between groups. We develop formulas to ensure each subgroup trial meets specified criteria, comparing the new treatment to a control, by clinically relevant standards. For subgroups with pre-defined similarities, we find the minimum required trial sizes simultaneously. Our approach resembles frequentist methods when there's no sharing of data. Notably, by allowing data borrowing, we find smaller trial sizes needed than traditional methods that don't share information. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach using two actual trials. Further simulations demonstrate our approach maintains accuracy in detecting positive results without increasing false positives. Finally, we show our approach respects regulatory guidelines by comparing it to a similar protocol used in a Phase II basket trial. Results indicate our approach retains similar Type I error rates and detects significant results at comparable rates to the original protocol. Overall, our approach uses Bayesian statistics to optimize sample size for basket trials by allowing information sharing between subgroups. We find this approach retains accuracy and adheres to regulatory guidelines while requiring smaller trial sizes than traditional methods. To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-precision and fast processing capabilities. The key challenge here is here is that traditional control strategies often struggle to account for the inherent nonlinear characteristics present in these systems, particularly when temperature variations are considered. The goal of this paper is to introduce a cutting-edge modification to the traditional sequential loop closing (SLC) technique, specifically tailored to address the problems posed by linear parameter-varying (LPV) systems. The modified SLC approach, referred to as the hybrid SLC (HSLC) method, effectively divides the control interval into two distinct segments. In the initial segment, the control signal is calculated based on the current system parameters, utilizing the system's past responses to track reference inputs. Following this, the control signal is adjusted to optimize performance, incorporating predictions about how system parameters will change in the near future. The effectiveness of the HSLC method was demonstrated through both simulation and hardware testing of a motion system, and the results reveal notable improvements in precision and robustness, representing a nearly 50% improvement in follow-up error and nearly a 100% improvement in robustness. The application and performance of the HSLC technique can be extended to various LPV systems, offering a highly adaptable solution for a range of high-precision motion control applications. The integration of this control strategy also provides a solid foundation for the development of advanced motion systems, enabling them to meet the ever-increasing requirements for throughputs. The conceptual framework of this study can be the starting point for a broader research agenda focused on developing more sophisticated control algorithms for high-precision motion systems. The findings of this paper can be an important contribution to ongoing research in this field, providing valuable insights and innovations to advance motion system design into the future. The associated code for replicating the results in this study can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/JulianKatermann LPV_SLC_motion_control. We introduce a general framework for partial point cloud registration tasks, 
using a self-supervised learning approach, effectively handling instances with complex shapes and variations in size. 
By preserving geometric details, we treat the input point clouds as aligned via a general transformation matrix, 
applying a novel distortion metric derived from our proposed Multi-View Consistency Loss. 
For robust shape matching, we incorporate a global Siamese network, guiding local shape matching. 
Additionally, we derive a convenient approximate distortion metric, enabling efficient optimization. 
Experimental results on diverse datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing techniques. 
The code is openly accessible on GitHub. 
Under test, a video showcasing our method's performance can be found on Vimeo. 
We anticipate this research to significantly contribute to registration tasks. 
In particular, video surveillance, robotics, medicine, and other fields will greatly benefit from this research.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the nilpotent quotient $G/\gamma_c(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. For generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups, we calculate the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree and illustrate it with examples. Additionally, we establish that if a group G has a finitely generated abelian solvable quotient, then the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree can be determined by combining two established results. Moreover, we obtain the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree for certain groups, such as $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z} \ast \mathbb{Z}$. This work extends previous research by D. Sun and C. Wu. Furthermore, the paper includes a method to compute the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree for finite groups. While this computation method may not always yield the least possible value, it provides a practical approach to determining the degree. In particular, we calculate the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree for the dihedral group $D_4$. Although the obtained value might not be the minimum possible, it is feasible to verify that it is indeed greater than or equal to the actual minimum degree. In contrast, we find that the degree computed using our method may not provide a lower bound for the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree in certain instances. In order to rectify this, we suggest an alternative strategy to split the group $\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ into meaningful subgroups, thereby gaining insight into the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree. In some cases, the suggested approach fails to yield a useful subdivision of $\gamma_{c+1}(G)$. In such instances, we propose a second method to gain insight into the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree. Instead of focusing on new physics discoveries, this study explores various collider options to determine the mass at which the Standard Model breaks down. Initially, we investigate the mass that can be reached in electron-positron colliders, before moving on to proton-proton colliders. To make this comparison, we developed a series of quick Monte Carlo simulations, utilizing simplified models for top and bottom quark decays. The outcome shows that e+e+ colliders are more suitable for exploring the mass at which the SM breaks down, due to their ability to detect bottom quarks more efficiently. Specifically, a 100 GeV energy electron-positron collider can reach a mass limit of around 1.1 TeV for both top and bottom quarks, while a 10000 GeV proton-proton collider can only reach a mass limit of around 620 GeV. This significant difference stems from the challenges of detecting bottom quarks in proton-proton collisions, where they are often submerged in a large background. As an alternative, we examined the potential of heavy ion collisions, which can reach even higher energy thresholds due to the formation of quark-gluon plasma, a complex landscape that demands precise simulation. However, even with this consideration, it appears that e+e+ colliders remain the best option for exploring the mass at which the SM breaks down. Specifically, a 5000 TeV energy e+e+ collider can reach a mass limit of around 2600 GeV. This limiting mass could be further increased to around 1600 TeV if future high-energy heavy ion colliders can accurately model the energy carried by the quark-gluon plasma. Ultimately, this study highlights the importance and potential of high-energy e+e+ colliders in reaching this critical mass. Specifically, a 250 GeV energy e+e+ collider has the potential to discover new physics beyond the Standard Model if it lies below 1250 GeV, while an 800 GeV energy e+e+ collider has the potential to discover new physics beyond the Standard Model if it lies below 1800 GeV. Additionally, this study identifies the 450 GeV energy LHC, the 50 TeV CLIC, and the 100 TeV HL-LHC as key projects for exploring new physics beyond the Standard Model.
