Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to the considerable time and resources needed for annotation. Current techniques typically address a novel modality either by fine-tuning a pre-trained model or by retraining entirely, yet they fall short in handling various modalities or ensuring label consistency across different domains. To overcome these limitations, we introduce an innovative approach, Cyclic Segmentation GAN, which training a modality-agnostic segmentation model through cyclic training. Through cycle-consistency training, the model learns to map anatomical structures' appearances and spatial relationships across different modalities. We validate our approach by conducting thorough experiments on three pairs of imaging modalities - MRI-CT, MRI-TRU, and CT-TRU - and evaluating its performance through metrics for segmentation accuracy and domain adaptation. Additionally, we analyze the impact of training modalities in an orderly sequence versus randomly shuffled order and demonstrate the resulting improvement in performance. Furthermore, we assess the generalizability of our approach to other unseen image pairs and explore its potential for multi-modal segmentation. With an average of 77.4% Dice score on three imaging modality pairs after training just a single epoch, our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques, as shown in the provided table. Thus, CS-GAN offers an efficient, efficient, efficient, efficient, efficient solution that can be quickly adapted for various imaging modalities without manual labels. learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and
adversarial training, to develop a novel RNN architecture for generating future
video features and anticipating actions. By using only the initial video frames and
a reduced number of parameters, Feature Mapping RNN efficiently generates future
features, which are then used in a multi-layer perceptron equipped with an RBF
kernel layer to accurately forecast actions. In our experiments, Feature Mapping RNN
achieved superior performance on JHMDB-21, UCF101-24, and UT-Interaction datasets
compared to existing state-of-the-art models. The implementation details can be
found on our GitHub repository: https://github.com/nsvinod92/FMRNN. This work was
presented at the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern
Recognition, 2020. The code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/nsvinod92/FMRNN.

Over three decades ago, a significant stellar flare occurred on AD Leo, peaking at a UV wavelength of 198.5 nm with an energy output of 4.67 x 10^30 ergs. The majority of prior flare studies employed UV spectrographs with limited wavelength ranges, often between 190-313 nm, necessitating the assumption of two basic radiation-matter interaction models to explain the observed flux disparities. In contrast, our current investigation uses the real-time magnetic flux distribution from a flare simulation model, incorporating the Quark+photon magnetic field structure. By mapping photospheric magnetic fields onto flare ribbons, our study generates UV continuum spectra that accurately match observational fluxes across the 190-313 nm wavelength spectrum, thereby validating the assumed models and providing further insight into the complex physics governing stellar flares. Furthermore, our results reveal the significant influence that photospheric magnetic fields have on the generation of hard X-ray emissions, as well as the apparent rotation of flare ribbons within the ultraviolet wavelength range of approximately 200-240 nm. Lastly, our study estimates the time elapsed since the formation of the flare ribbons on AD Leo, corresponding to 103.8 seconds. From this information, we conclude that the ribbons rotate due to the effects of drift velocity, induced by changes in their poloidal and toroidal magnetic field configurations. Consequently, the ribbons appear to rotate retrogradely in the ultraviolet wavelength range of approximately 200-240 nm, resulting from the prevailing magnetic field structure at the ribbons. In contrast, the ribbon rotation appears to be progressive in the 240-313 nm wavelength range, corresponding to a later stage in the flare's development. A new investigation adopts a distinct approach, focusing on analyzing changes in a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram resulting from entangled photon interaction. Utilizing Rhodamine B solution as a model nonlinear material exposed to 800 nm photons generated through type-II spontaneous parametric down conversion, researchers have explored conditions facilitating detection of HOM interferogram visibility modifications. Leveraging an 80 MHz pump laser, the experiment's visibility was monitored under various conditions, with notable reductions observed in specific spectral ranges corresponding to Rhodamine B's excited states. By translating visibility modifications into absorption coefficients, researchers have successfully measured the entangled two-photon absorption coefficient with a reported value of $(2.1\pm0.8)\cdot10^{-20}$ cm$^2$. These findings align with a previously reported value, offering further confirmation of ETPA in quantum optics applications. Additionally, the research presents a viable alternative for detecting ETPA in various materials, potentially opening up new avenues in non-linear materials development for quantum optics applications. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications in static settings, we introduce TimeGCN,
an innovative graph convolutional network model designed for temporal knowledge
graph completion. TimeGCN surpasses existing state-of-the-art models by
incorpororing time-aware representations, low-rank embeddings, and model-agnostic
reasoning capabilities. To further enhance performance, we also pre-train TimeGCN
on massive Wikipedia data, yielding substantial improvements when tested on
public datasets. TimeGCN's superiority is confirmed through comprehensive
experimental analysis and in-depth case studies. The source code is freely
accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/huutangt/TimeGCN. Experimental
results are posted on https://tanghuu.github.io/projects/TimeGCN. Published
research paper can be found on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.07261. This

In first-person shooter games, the sound of footsteps on different surfaces can give opponents' positions away due to varying bounces and delays when walking, running, jogging, or sliding. To analyze the source and characteristics of these sounds, we recorded professional players' footsteps in several popular games, then created a system to pinpoint the location of the player based on the sound patterns. By comparing the actual location with the detected location, we determined the accuracy of the audio-based positioning system and found that in most situations, the error margin is less than one meter. However, we also discovered that in a few cases, particularly when players move quickly, the error can be as large as three meters. Consequently, relying solely on audio cues may not be sufficient for accurate navigation in these games. Therefore, we suggest combining audio data with visual information for more precise positioning. To make up for the limitations of our current method, we are developing an enhanced version that incorporates depth maps to significantly improve location estimation. Once completed, we plan to share the code openly. As an additional contribution, we are releasing fifteen hours of annotated audio data, covering over 30 thousand footsteps, under a permissive license, enabling other researchers to build upon our findings and create more effective game-tracking systems. Furthermore, we are releasing a detailed report outlining the statistical relationships between audio data and player positions, as well as the code used for data processing and detection units. In the near future, we will publish a paper explaining our research methodology in further detail. In the meantime, we welcome questions and feedback about our study. We are working on a related paper, in which we present new experimental results, revealing that the sound bounces and delays can give away an opponent's location with a high degree of accuracy, especially when they are moving quickly or using certain movements. To confirm our findings, we conducted additional experiments, involving ten new players, and recorded their footsteps in two maps. Furthermore, we analyzed the existing audio data in greater detail, calculating the average error for each type of movement. In a subsequent study, we will demonstrate how these audio cues can be used to develop an effective navigation system. Based on our research so far, we can state that the sound bounces and delays do provide significant information about an opponent's location. Although we have not yet included environmental factors in our analysis, they are likely to play a minor role in the precise location estimation we have achieved. To ensure this logic's correctness and meet stringent safety standards, a formal model of the logic was created using the Prover9 theorem prover. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. Traditional data-driven clustering methods may struggle to produce meaningful results, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional data like time-series data, without prior knowledge of the system's underlying structure. A theoretical framework justifying this method's effectiveness is established, along with empirical evidence showing its superiority to alternative clustering methods. Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro, have argued that Leibniz's use of actual infinitesimals necessitates a consideration of bounds. In contrast, other researchers like Rovelli attribute Leibniz's thoughts to a general approach for any calculus system. This text presents an analysis of Leibniz's infinitesimal calculus through the lenses of three specific theoretical frameworks - the theory of hyperreal numbers, a general theory applicable to all calculus systems, and a specific doctrine emphasizing the significance of bounds. Additionally, we examine the procedural aspects of Leibniz's methodology and argue that these processes are consistent within each framework. Furthermore, we assert that these procedural aspects are not only significant in understanding historical development but also in evaluating the cognitive processes underlying scientific progress. By comparing these frameworks, we aim to contribute to an ongoing debate regarding the nature of Leibniz's infinitesimal calculus. In particular, we defend against the claims made by Arthur, Ishiguro, and Rauhut while presenting an alternative perspective on the findings of Franks and Arthur. Additionally, we present an approach to integrating the Leibnizian perspective into a well-documented infinitesimal approach to calculus. Ultimately, this text seeks to promote a more nuanced understanding of the complex interplay between language, procedures, and formal frameworks in the expression of scientific ideas. As such, we believe that leaping directly into a modern approach such as the theory of hyperreal numbers is an acceptable starting point for exploring the content of Leibnizian calculus. Moreover, this text seeks to demonstrate the compatibility of the theoretical frameworks presented with the views of prominent scholars in the field, including Franks, Arthur, and Rauhut. In particular, we employ a similar approach to that of Franks in utilizing the theory of hyperreal numbers, while also incorporating the critiques and concerns expressed by Arthur in the first edition of his book, as well as the later revisions and findings of Rauhut. In contrast to Franks' emphasis on the theory of hyperreal numbers, we place equal significance to the other two frameworks - the general approach and the doctrine emphasizing bounds. In doing so, we aim to contribute to an understanding of the debates among scholars and their relationships to the subject matter, and we argue that these procedural aspects are not only significant in understanding historical development but also in evaluating the nature of Leibnizian calculus.

Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. Then, focusing on vector spaces, we demonstrate that if a condition such as $T(e_i)=e_{\phi(i)}$ is to replace the previous operator assumption, $\phi$ must be equivalent to the successor function, defined as incrementing a number by 1. Finally, we explore a more complex generalization of this result, substituting the earlier operator assumption with a more complex condition. If a linear operator T maps $e_i$ to $e_{i+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only if the sequence can be extended to a basis in the vector space. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. 

This work is a result of our research efforts in the area, as documented in our paper 'Independence and Infinite Dimension in Vector Spaces', currently under review.

This research introduces an advanced recommender system, integrating three context-aware methods and combining profile-based, document-based, and behavior-based recommendation techniques. The novel method enhances existing context-aware approaches by integrating three different models: a behavior-based model using latent semantic analysis, a document-based method incorporating term frequency-inverse document frequency, and a context-based model that incorporates term frequency. The integration of these methods is demonstrated through a case study involving data from an e-commerce website, showing that the combined technique outperforms individual context-aware methods in terms of precision and recall. Furthermore, a comparison with a collaborative filtering-based recommender system revealed that the context-aware methods performed significantly better, highlighting the importance of considering contextual factors in recommender systems. The impact of contextual awareness on recommendation quality was also investigated, revealing that context-aware methods often yield better results than non-contextual methods, particularly when users interact frequently with the system over an extended period. The findings of this study, as well as those of related studies, are presented in a comprehensive context, illustrating the potential of context-aware systems to inform users' purchasing decisions and outperform non-contextual systems in doing so. This predicted phenomenon is expected to give rise to a novel application: the establishment of a central limit theorem for characteristic polynomials of these matrices. To validate this prediction, this study makes conclusive contributions by first demonstrating the anticipated asymptotic freeness and then proving a crucial lemma, which condenses a key result from reference [10]. The characterisation involved in this result is subsequently utilised to derive a central limit theorem for characteristic polynomials. Additionally, this study offers an asymptotic freeness result for specific unitarily invariant matrices whose eigenvalues display symmetry. This result is an extension of a prior finding by reference [11]. Consequently, this study also yields an asymptotic freeness result for characteristic polynomials exhibiting symmetry. Notably, all conclusions from this study can be independently understood using only basic mathematical principles. These principles include linear transformations, calculus and integration. This study does not employ advanced operator algebra or probability theory. Instead, this study presents novel conclusions based on these simple principles, which in turn stem from the works of reference [12]-[17]. These works characterise the asymptotic freeness and type $B$ freeness for specific matrices. Specifically, these works include the works by reference [18]-[21] which provide a characterisation involving independent circular unitarily invariant matrices. These works also include the works by reference [22]-[24] which provide a characterisation involving exchangeable Wigner matrices. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform. Substantial gains in model size, latency, and GPU utilization have been achieved while maintaining comparable query ranking quality. Specifically, model size reduction has reached up to 12x with negligible drops in performance. Latency has been cut by nearly 40% with a small loss of less than 0.5% in ranking quality. Our findings demonstrate that PILE can effectively bridge the gap between high-performance ranking models and efficient logit models, enabling a more systematic model pruning procedure in the knowledge distillation process. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity. This choice is driven by stability, though it comes at a cost of lower order of accuracy. To enhance the computational method, we develop and assess two discrete transport operators for the quadrilateral RT$0$ vector finite elements. By investigating the transport equation's solution space, we design and thoroughly evaluate two schemes. One approach involves projecting the transported vector onto the RT$0$ discrete space, while the other aims for a more direct transport by utilizing a semi-discrete scheme. To circumvent existing implementation limitations, we introduce a novel projection scheme, incorporating a weighted stochastic estimation method. This novel scheme is now feasible due to the introduction of a norm that effectively bridges the smooth transport equation and the discrete RT$0$ space. Through a combination of theoretical and experimental analysis, we evaluate the performance of the two schemes. Notably, the projected scheme is robust and versatile, though its convergence rate is slower. Conversely, the semi-discrete scheme is more discrete but also more dependent on the grid quality. Both schemes are theoretically and numerically tested, with a focus on the impact of the transport equation's initial condition. This research is significant as it offers two viable options to address the persistent challenge of approximating the vector transport equation. By assessing the strengths and weaknesses of each scheme, users can make informed decisions about the most suitable approach for their specific computational physics problems. Furthermore, this research opens up opportunities for similar analyses of other finite element discretisation schemes, such as the $RT^0$ scalar scheme. Due to its relevance to real-world problems, we illustrate the performance of the transport schemes through two examples: computing the vorticity and helicity of a flowing fluid, and tracking a advected vector field. Both examples showcase the complex behavior of transported scalar and vector fields and highlight the significance of accurately discretising the transport equation. This research is a preliminary step towards developing more accurate methods for simulating fluid dynamics on complex grids. To that end, we identify several avenues for further investigation, such as generalising the transport schemes to higher-order finite elements and considering the rotation of transported vectors. By advancing our understanding of discrete transport equations, we can ultimately improve the accuracy of numerical simulations in computational physics. In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems. We define and implement a broader method class, called Continuous HBVMs (CHBVMs), and provide a detailed analysis of its properties, including its connection to collocation methods, as well as its relations to implicit and Crank-Nicolson methods. We also provide and analyze specific schemes within this class. We ultimately illustrate the efficiency of CHBVMs through several numerical examples. Interestingly, CHBVMs appear to be a more natural construction than their discrete analogues (HBVMs), and offer an alternative approach to designing energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods. We are, however, unable to ensure the linear independence of the stage equations in the general case, and therefore propose these methods as an implicit scheme class that can be solved explicitly, similar to Crank-Nicolson methods. We also confirm the L2-stability of CHBVMs through the Cauchy filter criterion, and extend this stability analysis to a broader method class, called Continuous Stage Preserving Runge-Kutta methods (CSPRKs), by incorporating an additional condition. We ultimately compare CHBVMs to CSPRKs and demonstrate their mutual equivalence under specific conditions, while also illustrating their differences in the general case. We complement this theoretical work by illustrating the efficiency of CHBVMs in several numerical experiments, and provide a numerical example that highlights the potential lack of L2-stability of HBVMs (and therefore CHBVMs) when applied to problems with Hamiltonian dynamics. Finally, we propose an implementation strategy for CHBVMs that is similar to the 'wind-back' approach used to solve Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods, and illustrate its efficiency through several numerical examples. This work therefore offers an innovative and general approach to constructing and analyzing energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods, and provides a novel interpretation of implicit and Crank-Nicolson methods as continuous, multi-step methods. This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients to each corresponding critic network, the critical blocks to be re-trained can be pinpointed. We conduct comprehensive experiments on convolutional and recurrent networks, demonstrating that the proposed method surpasses traditional model-parallel learning in updating frequencies. Notably, the number of re-training iterations needed is nearly double that of parallel training, while also matching the performance. Moreover, local critic training offers more precise breakdown of which layers require re-training. Based on this feature, we developed an adaptive algorithm to pinpoint the exact layers to be updated, yielding a substantial 4x improvement in updating frequencies over standard model-parallel learning. Our method has been successfully applied to image classification and language modeling tasks, achieving comparable results to synchronous model-parallel learning. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/hjdw2/LocalCriticTraining. Additionally, the IPython demo code can be found at this link. Furthermore, the details of each experiment, including datasets and models, are carefully documented in a separate file. Moreover, the employed computing infrastructure consists of 40 GPUs, evenly distributed across four servers with 10 GPUs per server. Specifically, we utilized the NVIDIA A100 GPU, featuring 80 CUDA Cores and 90 GB RAM. Lastly, the total memory capacity of the computing infrastructure is 288 GB. Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially deviate from Wada's characteristics. Nonetheless, a reduced system is studied that includes a two-dimensional Poincaré surface. By reducing the system's dimensions, it is discovered that a specific parameter range exists where the boundaries exhibit Wada basins. Furthermore, it is observed that weak dissipation not only preserves Wada basins but actually increases the area where this phenomenon occurs. The impact of dissipation is closely linked to a newly created channel formed by the critical manifold's folding. The region exhibiting Wada basins surrounds a laminar island situated within this channel. The boundaries of this island serve as an attractor for nearby trajectories, trapping them in a quasi-periodic orbit. The area containing Wada basins grows as the dissipation rate intensifies, albeit in an inverse manner. The size of this area ultimately reaches a maximum and then experiences a Hopf bifurcation where the trapped trajectories escape the island, populating the surrounding space with quasiperiodic orbits. Despite the system's low regularity, this dynamics exhibits high levels of stability. The findings suggest that weak dissipation can preserve and even enhance Wada basins in three-dimensional chaotic systems. The concept of observing Wada basins in such systems may be restricted due to technical limitations, primarily related to resolution and rendering capabilities. The current state-of-the-art in computer technology is likely inadequate for observing Wada basins in fully three-dimensional systems. As a result, the area containing Wada basins goes undetected, with observers mistakenly attributing its presence to active turbulence. The research demonstrates that weak dissipation can maintain and enhance Wada basins in three-dimensional chaotic systems. The discovery suggests active control measures could be implemented to preserve these structures. Specifically, adjusting the system's parameters to a particular value on the dissipation range ensures the preservation of Wada basins, an area that increases with this parameter. Although this study's results might not translate to systems with high regularity, the findings indicate that weak dissipation can support Wada basins in non-regular systems. The research has potential implications for systems exhibiting different types of dynamics. The associated mechanisms could be applicable to other three-dimensional systems beyond just chaotic scattering. A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to three distinct fermions - specifically, up-quark and down-quark combinations and one neutrino type - is considered within the context of a low-energy R-parity Violating Model inspired by supersymmetry. Here, we examine the characteristics of a relatively lightweight but distinctively long-lived intermediate-mass scalar particle that can be produced at current and future lepton colliders, such as the proposed muon collider, in flavor-changing reactions like $\mu \D \to \nu \Phi$. Once produced, this scalar interacts weakly with matter, allowing it to be detected via muon decay-in-flight or end-of-flight analysis or through dimuon resonance searches, depending on the particle's mass. For a specific mass range - roughly between $10^{-10}$ and $10^{-5}$ GeV - the model's parameters exhibit a noticeable correlation, determining the detection feasibility, and we calculate the required luminosity needed for a discovery. This calculation also holds for other collider experiments targeting lepton-flavor changing processes. If this new physics remains undetected, it imposes constraints on parameter spaces where the long-lived scalar's lifetime could be noticeably longer, making it amenable to direct search in various fields, such as nuclear decays, astrophysical environments, or high-energy particle collisions with significantly larger event counts. In this model's constraints regime, we derive parameter space limitations imposed by various constraints from particle physics, astrophysics, nuclear physics, and other long-lived particle phenomena. This analysis holds not just for R-parity Violating Model but also other related models, such as Type I and Type II two Higgs Doublet Models with similar distinct long-lived scalar characteristics. Finally, as a notable aspect, this model's interaction mechanism is uniquely long-lived due to long-lasting non-weak interactions, differentiating it from the majority of low-energy models predicting weak-scale particles. This property, although extending to higher energies, could be tested not only in current and future colliders but also in other direct searches with a considerably larger event count. In this model's space, we calculate the required direct search luminosity needed to detect this long-lived scalar in various long-lived particle phenomena. This model presents an original example of long-lived distinct scalar physics that can be empirically verified or constrained through multiple direct methods. This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions. This framework will be made available as an open-source Python package. Further development is intended to broaden its scope and incorporate additional features. Significant research is already estimating Shannon entropy through Nested Sampling, but this work specifically focuses on a new algorithm that can easily extend to higher-dimensional cases. Two alternative methods, based on maximum entropy and sampling approximation, are also presented for comparison, in addition to a related technique already published in the arXiv journal. Overall, this new method outperforms the other methods in accuracy and efficiency. Results show that when entropy estimates don't exceed 50% error, this approach can achieve a speed-up of up to 3 times. We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures on Borel spaces. This investigation arises from the lack of optimal solutions for transitioning from a smaller to a larger equilibrium state with zero inventory levels in the standard L1 framework. Novel contributions involve addressing the issue of non-differentiable velocities with discrete objects and a bounded domain subject to inflows and outflows. Employing a Lagrangian perspective, we establish that solutions exist and are unique and define a notion of weak solutions. Furthermore, we prove that the solution is actually differentiable almost everywhere with respect to time. To resolve the issue at hand, we first approximate the non-differentiable velocity through a smoothing procedure, resulting in a system that can be solved through standard methods. By demonstrating that the solution to the approximated system remains a valid solution to the original measure-valued conservation law, we leverage these techniques. In addition to theoretical advancements, the structure of this model allows us to derive efficient solution algorithms that rely on solution differentiability. Specifically, we are able to devise a simplex-based method that requires an exponential number of iterations, but offers exponential convergence when applied to various test cases, including discrete and continuous problem variants. Finally, we hypothesize that the proposed method is actually universal and applicable to a broader class of hyperbolic conservation laws with a particular characteristic. To confirm this hypothesis, we would need to access the solution space: either prove that the solution is continuous with respect to time or demonstrate that the velocity is actually differentiable in a certain sense. Due to these challenges, we are unable to confirm the hypothesis, but it is an area of interest that warrants future exploration. In the context of semiconductors, the hypothesis corresponds to systems that are linearly filling and have equilibrium inventories that are proportional to the rates of incoming and outgoing items. Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool for studying dynamic phenomena in amorphous materials, from the boson peak to the glass transition, due to its high sensitivity to atomic movements. This review focuses on the boson peak, a critical feature in the dynamic spectra of glasses located at the origin of frequency, which is often difficult to investigate directly. Various experiments have been designed to examine the boson peak's position, intensity, and associated density fluctuations, and these methods will be discussed in detail. In particular, we will analyze the connections between different types of density fluctuations and the system's thermodynamic properties, and also discuss recent findings from dynamic mean-field theories that provide new insights into the boson peak's origins. Furthermore, we will explore the outcomes of combining neutron inelastic scattering with other techniques, such as ab initio molecular dynamics simulations and quantum calculations, to gain a deeper understanding of the boson peak's frequency and its relationship with specific atom movements. This review aims to provide an in-depth examination of the boson peak's nature and its significance in the dynamic properties of glassy materials. Ultimately, we will summarize the current state of knowledge and suggest potential future areas of research. Due to the breadth of topics covered, this review may also be accessible to researchers with less background in neutron scattering, while still offering advanced neutron scattering specialists fresh perspectives and insights. Additionally, we have included a detailed appendix outlining the various techniques used to investigate the boson peak in more technical detail. Increasingly, multi-objective optimization methods are being employed not only to generate optimal solutions but also to generate diverse solution populations. This diversity is often associated with phenotypic diversity, measured as the distance between solution vectors in the multi-dimensional solution space. Unlike genotypic diversity, phenotypic diversity remains relatively understudied, particularly regarding its relationship with solution performance across various domains. To fill this knowledge gap, this study conducts a thorough analysis of phenotypic diversity by gathering and scrutinizing large datasets from multi-objective optimization runs across different domains. Our results reveal both general phenomena and domain-specific patterns regarding the distribution of phenotypic diversity, and we also gather insights from contributors, raising questions about the design of multi-objective algorithms and the subsequent use of these diverse solution sets. These insights could further inform theoretical designs of multi-objective optimization scenarios. Most importantly, our work provides essential statistics to guide practitioners in choosing between various phenotypic diversity-inducing optimization methods. With over 100 datasets collected, each with at least 10,000 solutions, our research remains the largest of its kind in the field. Additionally, our findings include the distribution of phenotypic diversity in different domains, the mean and standard deviation of phenotypic diversity, and the percentage of solution performance exceeding the average performance in each domain. These results can be accessed via an online public repository. Based on our analysis, multi-objective optimization methods tend to generate phenotypically diverse solution populations, and, interestingly, the distribution of these diverse solutions often follows a normal distribution. These findings contradict a common assumption in evolutionary computation research, raising the need for further investigation. Moreover, our results indicate that multi-objective, coevolutionary optimization methods generate more diverse solution populations than those using the canonical generational approach, and, further, that these diverse solution populations offer various benefits, including improved solution performance and more comprehensive coverage of the Pareto front. Ultimately, our work remains the largest collection of phenotypic diversity data in multi-objective optimization, and we aim to build on these results in future research. Additionally, we have made available the code and datasets used in our study through a public repository. It includes the datasets collected during our research, the results, and the R code employed to gather our findings, enabling others to replicate our work and contribute to the ongoing discussion on phenotypic diversity in multi-objective optimization. The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists, with the constraint that any established pair should not seek a different match. When preferences are non-interdependent, a key property of the problem is that any agent's optimal pair will either prioritize their own happiness or a joint happiness maximum. In the specific context of three-dimensional (3D) data, our research explores the scenario where agents' preferences can be represented as symmetric matrix functions. This study demonstrates that under these conditions, a 3D additive preferences variant of the Stable Roommates problem offers an achievable linear programming solution, thereby establishing a bounded duality theorem. Furthermore, our results show that the number of discrete solutions within this particular 3D context is proportional to the number of their individual valuations raised to the power of the problem's size. In comparison to existing approaches, the current 3D model exhibits a significant improvement in discrete solution count complexity. Lastly, our example illustrations highlight that under certain 3D additive preference scenarios, the resulting matches may not cover all agents' valued price points. In response to this observation, our model is extended to accommodate scenarios where agents may not receive their complete valuation price points in matches. This extension proves to be particularly challenging, with proof of its NP-hardness. In terms of approximate solutions, our model attempts to find an optimal pair for a given agent under the constraint that any established pair should not seek a different match. This problem is shown to be APX-hard. In an attempt to address this issue, our model attempts to derive additive approximations for the agent's optimal pair. However, we establish that such an approximation may not be achievable. In contrast, as an upper bound, our model demonstrates that any agent's optimal pair will either prioritize their own happiness or a joint happiness maximum. This result is particularly notable as it offers an $O(\sqrt{k})$ approximation for the agent's optimal pair. In terms of achieving the joint happiness maximum, our model attempts to derive optimal pairs for all agents under the constraint that any established pair should not seek a different match. This problem is shown to be FPT. In an attempt to address this issue, our model attempts to derive additive approximations for the joint happiness maximum. However, we establish that such an approximation may not be achievable. In contrast, our model demonstrates that the joint happiness maximum can be attained without sacrificing any agent's valuation price points. We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. One key property is that these clouds are mutually independent and isolated from one another due to a phenomenon where two clouds that don't share any common metrics will eventually diverge as the GH distance grows. Additionally, we've discovered that there exists a central space for each cloud, serving as a reference point that allows us to determine the relative positions of spaces within the cloud by calculating their distances to this central space, thus enabling a coordinate system for each cloud. The choice of central space is not unique, however, as there may be multiple candidates that work equally well. The GH distance to the central space can be seen as a kind of median value, thus making it a effective tool for analyzing the structure and characteristics of the cloud. Furthermore, we've found that the central spaces themselves form a cloud, dubbed the core, and through induction, we've established that this core consists of spaces with fixed diameters. The method used here is expected to contribute significantly to the study of Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The findings we've presented are likely to be relevant to fields outside of geometry as well, including topology and metric embedding theory. The concepts and theorems presented here can be applied to a broad range of metric spaces, including those constructed from probability theory and the theory of infinite metric spaces. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Importantly, our code, although trained using simulated data, performs remarkably well on real-world noise models derived from actual quantum device data, even in the presence of faulty measurement effects. With its potential to handle complex decoding tasks, this approach could be a valuable asset for achieving large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing. Crucially, the underlying noise models used in this study were simplified, so future work will focus on enhancing the decoder with density matrix propagation to accommodate more sophisticated noise models. Additionally, we plan to introduce a new reinforcement learning technique that does not require massive volumes of training data, enabling the decoder to adapt to unexpected noise models at runtime. Finally, we aim to replace the deepQ learning method with a more quantum-compatible approach, such as quantum differential dynamic programming, to integrate quantum computing principles into the decoding process. This research will facilitate the development of practical, fault-tolerant quantum computers by addressing the critical issue of decoding errors in quantum computing. In particular, we will leverage the surface code architecture due to its robust error correcting capabilities, coupled with its mapping to a familiar graph theory problem, allowing for the development of decoding tools that can be applied directly to quantum circuits. With its potential to advance the scalable quantum computing quest, this study will contribute meaningfully to the field. Furthermore, we observe that the current deepQ learning method does not efficiently handle non-Markovian noise models. This will result in our code having a greater resemblance to established quantum computing principles, with particular attention to non-Markovian noise models. Ultimately, we aim to achieve scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing by addressing the critical decoding error challenge. This study will mark an important milestone along that path. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective results, applying this method is extremely challenging due to the need for precise control over complex quantum states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and using quantum correlations to optimize measurement precision. This technique is demonstrated on a two-cavity network and compared to classical methods, and the resulting performance is found to closely mirror that of interferometry. Furthermore, the capabilities of quantum jump metrology are evaluated in various scenarios and found to be significantly influenced by non-stationary effects and quantum correlations. In specific situations, this method can offer enhanced precision beyond what can be achieved with interferometry. A key discovery is made that the global quantum correlations present in a network are directly related to the local quantum correlations found in each individual node. This fundamental insight enables the development of a universal strategy to optimize information retrieval through the control of local quantum correlations. In particular, it is demonstrated that new insights can be gained into how quantum correlations are established and used in various processes governed by quantum physics. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, allowing even basic models to achieve improved performance. On one hand, this rich representation provides an effective starting point for the optimizer, while on the other hand, it incorporates a beneficial bias towards handling OoD scenarios.

This robust feature set is generated using the Generalization Gap metric, analyzing the gap between the model's in-distribution and OoD predictions to identify key features responsible for the Generalization Gap. Through an interactive process, the model iteratively refines its features, incorporating those that minimize the gap and discarding those that contribute to it. 

Our method was tested on the CIFAR-100 and ImageNet datasets, combining various penalty terms with rich feature constriction and model initialization. The results show that even basic models initialized with this feature set achieve superior performance on OoD tasks, surpassing complex models with penalty terms that attempt to directly optimize performance and robustness.

Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively synthesize dependent effects, however these may produce inflated Type 1 errors in cases of a limited number of studies.  In order to improve the performance of robust estimators when dealing with small sample sizes, two new cluster-robust estimators have been developed.  Both estimators work by adjusting the estimated residual variances using only the diagonal entries of the hat matrix, resulting in asymptotic equivalence to previously proposed estimators such as the bias reduced linearization method.  This new approach is demonstrated in a simulation study on real world data, with particular application in bivariate meta-regression though it may also be utilized more broadly.  Finally, model checking and testing is achieved through the assessment of residuals and the Q-statistic.  Software implementation is provided in the R package'metaMBER'.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. HDTM encompasses two core components: a topic discovery model leveraging non-parametric latent Dirichlet allocation and a hierarchical structure learning algorithm incorporating a distributed ranking method that expands upon previous ideas. By generating hierarchies from real datasets and evaluating the results, we found HDTM to surpass state-of-the-art models in both performance and accuracy. Specifically, our approach outperformed existing methods by reducing the complexity from O(n^2) to O(n) and improving the micro-F1 score from 0.842 to 0.887. The experimental results demonstrate the scalability of HDTM by cutting the processing time of building the hierarchy for the Wikipedia dataset with 20 million documents from 3 hours to just 10 minutes while maintaining a 25% improvement in the micro-F1 score over comparable models. We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings. 
Next, we identify a suitable topological structure for incorporating the hyperdoctrine, ultimately demonstrating that this structure corresponds to a particular class of spaces known as metric toposes. 
As an initial application, we establish that continuous formulas containing at most one free variable can be viewed as subobjects within a specific metric topos, enabling us to recapture their truth values through a categorical interpretation that aligns with their original semantics. 
Finally, we speculate on potential extensions or modifications to our approach, including embedding the hyperdoctrine for continuous logic in a more general category for structured spaces or in a category for metric toposes with additional structure. 
Furthermore, this research may also contribute to a logico-algebraic formulation of continuous logic as well as its relation to hyperdoctrines appearing in categorical logic. 
We hope that this research will facilitate a more comprehensive geometric interpretation of continuous logic and enable a greater understanding of the framework's underlying structure. 
This research project originated from a seminar led by Mike Haskel and was influenced by his lectures, particularly those on the basics of categorical type theory and hyperdoctrine.

Our research reports a significant $7\sigma$ discovery of highly polarized X-ray radiation from Cassiopeia A supernova remnant. Cassiopeia A is one of the youngest, bright pulsar wind nebulae observed at energies ranging from a few keV to hundreds of keV. During a 5.2 day observation in 2020 with the IXPE, we found a strong spatial correlation between the X-ray emission and that of the pulsar. The X-ray emission's hardness was observed to change as its intensity varied. The observed polarization level ranged from $7\%$ to $12\%$, with uncertainties between $2\%$ and $4\%$. The total polarization angle was observed to be $40^\circ$ or $120^\circ$ with a $20^\circ$ margin of error. Analysis using the MAGIX software revealed significant polarization detection for two energy ranges: $2-10$ keV and $10-20$ keV. In both cases, the X-ray emission's spatial distribution was similar to that of the pulsar, with minor contributions from the supernova's outer regions. The observed polarization properties are consistent with the model of a large-scale magnetic field of $5 \times 10^{-8}$ Gauss in the wind nebula. The X-ray emission's net polarization vector was observed to be directed at an angle of $72^\circ$ with respect to the Earth's view of the pulsar. This result makes Cassiopeia A the first supernova remnant to be detected through X-ray polarization since the discovery of the remnant's emission. This finding paves the way for future research on a total of one dozen more supernova remnants that can be observed with IXPE. The observed X-ray emission's characteristics are likely to provide valuable insights into the high-energy emission of supernova remnant pulsar wind nebulae. Additionally, the observed X-ray polarization in Cassiopeia A is expected to contribute significantly to the understanding of magnetic fields in the remnant's outer regions. Ultimately, the observed X-ray emission's properties in Cassiopeia A are likely to provide a comprehensive model for the X-ray emission's overall polarization in supernova remnant pulsar wind nebulae. This phenomenon is confirmed by infrared and Raman spectroscopy, revealing a 10 NH frequency gap between the three components. Using density functional theory calculations, the structural symmetry constraints and electronic properties of the materials are investigated, resulting in the materials exhibiting nearly zero total spin and time-reversal-sensitive orbital moments, with the chiral phonon mode influenced by the electronic properties in the materials, particularly the time-reversal-sensitive orbital transition at approximately 0.5 eV. This leads to a chiral phonon contribution in the materials, particularly in the potassium ($A=$ K) compound, where the chiral phonon and electronic properties coincide, as the frequency of the chiral phonon mode (NH) matches the energy of the orbital transition. This coincidence in the frequencies of the chiral phonon and electronic transitions in the materials may provide an efficient method to detect and identify chiral phonons using light by adjusting the frequency of the phonon mode to align with the electronic transitions in the materials. This may offer a valuable approach for detecting chiral phonons in materials with higher symmetry. In insulators, Born effective charges relate to long-range electric polarization, whereas in conductors like metals, they represent short-range polarization related to the Drude weight. We have investigated non-adiabatic Born effective charges within the random phase approximation. In three-dimensional metals, our results indicate that these charges are divergent at specific points on the Fermi surface. Through a three-dimensional insulator-to-metal transition in a model structure with a body-centered cubic structure, our findings reveal that Born effective charges become divergent in the metallic state, illustrating that long-range polarization does not exist in conductors like metals. We have verified the accuracy of our method by examining Born effective charges in a well-known cubic lattice model. Ultimately, our study provides a clearer understanding of the nature of Born effective charges in different systems. We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length, although it's still many orders of magnitude greater than the average free path. This finding suggests that the non-random, or deterministic, form of the Navier-Stokes equation is insufficient for modeling the turbulence dissipation range within molecular fluids. Instead, the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation by Landau and Lifschitz provides a more accurate description within this range. Specifically, our analysis implies that the extreme low-frequency range of turbulent flows should be modeled using an infinite-bandwidth version of "eddy-diffusion" flux, where the fluctuations are statistically self-similar and log-normal. This analysis also implies a one-parameter family of scaling exponents, which are strictly increasing, and challenges many common assumptions about turbulent flow. Furthermore, our study reveals the limitations of the "eddy-diffusion" approximation as frequency approaches the forcing bandwidth, and shows that the eddy-diffusion approximation fails in this context due to its failure to properly account for the energy containing range. Additionally, our calculations yield predictions for several critical quantities including the maximum amplitude of the fluctuations, the distribution of the energy within the spectrum, and the relationship between viscosity and frequency that are relevant for flows characterized by a Kolmogorov length much smaller than the width of the energy containing range. These predictions are contingent on several assumptions including the presence of scaling regimes in the energy and the distribution of the energy within the spectrum, and can be statistically justified only if the turbulence is caused by rare, Poisson-distributed events. If these conditions are met, our predictions can be statistically justified with high precision. With the exception of several critical results, such as the maximum amplitude of the fluctuations and the distribution of the energy within the spectrum, the predictions made in this study have not been previously reported in the literature. Finally, our analysis is not limited to turbulent flows and can be applied to any situation in which the fluctuations in a deterministic equation are log-normal and the fluctuations are caused by rare, high-amplitude events. If these conditions can be met, our analysis suggests that the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation provides a more accurate description than the deterministic equation for the turbulence dissipation range. Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable manifestations when time-reversal symmetry prevails due to opposing influences of internal and external spins. The distinctive response characteristic of a topological insulator can be characterized by a nonlinear magnetoelectric effect, where the current is influenced by a spin orbit coupling that is proportional to a dimensionless Chern number. This development enables the description of exotic half-integer quantum Hall effects and a visible manifestation of a Witten effect in superconducting and spin-triplet topological phases. Moreover, a time-reversal-symmetric spin-orbit coupling that varies spatially with a nonvanishing gradient can trigger a topological magnetoelectric effect, offering an alternative route to realizing this phenomenon. This theory can be applied to various scenarios, such as engineering a magnetoelectric response in three-dimensional Dirac semimetals and in systems constructed using only nearest-neighbor hopping. Ultimately, a novel class of time-reversal-symmetric superconductors, characterized by a specific half-integer multi-band quantum Hall effect, is proposed, which is capable of supporting exotic Witten Effect phenomena upon exposure to external currents. These concepts can be applied to materials like WTe5, where the interplay between spin and orbit can yield significant performance improvements. This research may lead to significant breakthroughs in the design and control of unique electronic phenomena. Several theoretical predictions have been made regarding potential experiments involving WTe5 and Mo2E. These predictions encompass a wide range of possibilities, such as observing the transfer of vortices, excess charges, and current-induced heating, which could provide tangible evidence of a topological magnetoelectric effect. It is anticipated that these findings will pave the way for a deeper understanding of various exotic states of matter and may provide insights for future research and technological applications. It is also possible to realize a topological magnetoelectric effect using a specific configuration of magnetic and electric fields in a system lacking intrinsic magnetism, thereby expanding the scope of topological insulators. This knowledge can potentially be used to design novel devices capable of high-efficiency magnetism-driven current generation. It is also possible to establish a topological magnetoelectric effect by means of external frequency modulation in the absence of time-reversal symmetry, which may provide an alternative means of controlling the movement of charges. This concept can be applied to various systems, such as those featuring giant spin-orbit interactions, and offers potential avenues for controlling interaction-driven phenomena.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it is found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude, especially when the modulation's map exhibits mode locking, characteristic of laminar chaos. For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality. Additionally, we note that delaying the modulation of a chaotic system can trigger a transition from laminar to turbulent behavior, where the diffusive coefficient experiences a substantial decrease. These findings hold true for various system types, including a model for neuron interaction and the Ginzburg-Landau equation for water circulation. They also suggest potential applications in fields such as medicine and navigation, where understanding and controlling chaotic diffusion could lead to significant practical benefits. It is hypothesized that the observed phenomena may extend to other types of systems beyond those with delay nonlinearity. To verify this, we explore a model for quantum particle transport. In summary, this research reveals a previously unknown relationship between the modulation of a system's parameters and its diffusive properties, offering novel insights into chaotic behavior. It is possible that the underlying mechanisms discovered here may yield additional breakthroughs in the future. It is suggested that the observed diffusion enhancement could be rebranded as an example of quantum tunneling, where the system's wave packet undergoes rapid, damped damped-diffusive spreading. In this context, the diffusion coefficient experiences a significant decrease and the diffusive process becomes significantly faster. We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018). Additionally, we introduce an innovative notion of "stochastic beta and eta closure" which simplifies the complex framework previously proposed (Zdancewic et al., 2017), ultimately revealing that this calculus is equivalent to the probabilistic lambda calculus based on Kleisli composition (Gordon et al., 2010). Interestingly, our analysis reveals that the standard translations between these two calculi do not preserve equivalence relations associated with beta and eta equivalence. To address this shortcoming, we define a novel "weak eta translation" that preserves these equivalences, effectively extending existing results to the realm of stochastic lambda calculi. As a direct consequence, this study achieves three key outcomes: (a) an operational semantics for the stochastic lambda calculus, (b) a proven adequacy theorem linking its denotational and operational interpretations, and (c) a range of useful properties supporting the development of sound and sound-without-prog in operational and denotational semantics, respectively. Ultimately, these findings pave the way for applying semantic techniques to the analysis and verification of probabilistic programs written in higher-order languages. The techniques proposed in this study have been successfully applied to a range of other probabilistic programming languages with more expressive features (Bacci et al., 2018; Zdancewic et al., 2017; Gordon et al., 2010). The present work has been formally verified using the Coq proof assistant. Its formalization has been leveraged to introduce an interactive table-based operational semantics, providing a practical alternative to the standard small-step semantics for evaluating stochastic lambda calculus expressions. Moreover, we have extended the stochastic lambda calculus to include and prove key properties related to the probabilistic dependent types (Wright, 2018). Specifically, we have achieved a formalised proof that the probabilistic dependent types based on Kleisli composition can be expressed within the stochastic lambda calculus, and that this calculus can be further extended to include and express probabilistic dependent types based on the Curry-Howard correspondence. These results have been formally verified in Coq and provide a formal basis for applying semantic techniques to the analysis and verification of probabilistic programs written in higher-order languages. Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process known as design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. This paper showcases a simple model for design mining, revealing that current methods suffer from inconsistent conclusions on various discussion types and projects. We then introduce and demonstrate two effective techniques - data enrichment and project adaptation - that enhance design mining's reliability and adaptability across different datasets, achieving a satisfactory classification rate of 0.88 within a dataset and 0.80 across different datasets. These techniques are now available under an open-source license on GitHub. Studies have validated the accuracy of our model on four different datasets, as well as applications beyond discussion types, revealing potential for significant practical impact. Additionally, we provide step-by-step guidelines on design mining's implementation for other researchers. Finally, we plan to conduct further research, focusing on increasing the complexity of our design mining model. In the near future, we aim to engage in collaborative design mining with other researchers. We hope this work stimulates a broader discussion within the mining community on the utilization of natural language techniques. Specifications for replicating our work, including open-source code, annotated data, and design mining models, can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/dm-design-mining/dm-design-mining and on Vaidehi Sardesai's GitHub repository at https://github.com/vsardesai/dm-design-mining. We are also listed on the MBSE-Mining Discord channel. We look forward to your input and feedback!

Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure is a free byproduct, also enhancing the convergence rate once aligned with that of the problem's intrinsic geometry. Nonetheless, pinpointing the exact structure is not possible without adaptation. Assuming a proximal gradient method is able to recognize the problem's underlying manifold, we show that incorporating Riemannian Newton-like techniques alongside the proximal gradient steps results in an even faster convergence rate than what is achievable under the assumption of a known underlying manifold. Moreover, our findings also include the possibility of incorporating an approximation of the Hessian vector product at no extra cost, a capability that is particularly beneficial in nonsmooth settings where the cost of Hessian information is typically inversely related to the step size. We also illustrate the efficacy of our algorithm in a variety of test problems. Additionally, our study includes a range of numerical test cases that validate our theoretical findings and showcase the algorithm's performance. These test cases involve a mix of nonsmooth optimization problems with either a known or unknown underlying manifold. The results from these experiments confirm the algorithm's fast convergence rate when the underlying structure is known and show promising performance even in situations where the structure needs to be discovered. The code used in these numerical test cases is openly accessible on GitHub. Furthermore, the study includes an analysis of the algorithm's theoretical and practical implications, highlighting its potential applications and limitations. We demonstrate, for instance, that the algorithm's rate of convergence is unaffected by nonsmooth components that might complicate the optimization process, and, in contrast, the algorithm outperforms standard methods when there are no nonsmooth components involved. The study also compares the algorithm to other proximal methods, such as the proximal point method, and shows that the algorithm outperforms these methods, especially in cases where the underlying structure is known. The results from these experiments validate our theoretical findings and illustrate the algorithm's fast convergence rate in a range of test cases, including nonsmooth, smooth, and combinatorial optimization problems. The study also includes an in-depth analysis of the algorithm's behavior in different scenarios, and shows that the algorithm outperforms other proximal methods when there is an underlying structure that can be identified. We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, serving as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. A prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is said to be weakly $1$-absorbing if for every three non-unit elements $a,b,$ and $c$ in $R$ where their product is non-zero and within $I$, it follows that either the product of $a$ and $b$ is in $I$, or $c$ is in $I$. Our research presents numerous results regarding the characteristics and examples of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals. It has been proven that if $I$ is a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a ring $R$ where the product of three non-zero ideals is completely contained in $I$, it then holds that either the product of the first two ideals is completely contained in $I$, or the third ideal is completely contained in $I$. Additionally, it is demonstrated that if $I$ is not a $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a ring $R$ but a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal, then $I^3 = 0$. Consequently, the terms 'weakly $1$'-absorbing and not $1$-absorbing prime ideals' are synonymous and can be interchangeably used. Furthermore, the characteristics of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within specific types of commutative rings have been explored and analyzed. Lastly, an in-depth examination of the properties and examples of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within polynomial rings has been conducted. Ultimately, the connection between the number of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals and the weight of a commutative ring has been established. It was found that the number of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals in a ring $R$ is greater than or equal to the weight of the ring, with the condition that the equality holds if and only if the ring has a finite number of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals. The results and findings presented within this paper can serve as a foundation to further develop the notion of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals and explore other interesting properties and characteristics. In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field. This review was sparked by the 2021 NeurIPS workshop "Drug Pair Scoring using Relational Machine Learning". 
Key Contributions:
The paper establishes a unified theoretical framework for relational machine learning models in drug pairing scenarios.
It evaluates and summarizes existing model architectures in the field.
It identifies and analyzes evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols for the task at hand.
It outlines future research avenues and potential applications of the approach. 
Future Work:
Developing improved model architectures and experimental validation of the proposed theoretical framework using established benchmark datasets.
Selecting the most suitable evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols for the task at hand.
Addressing the scarcity of available labeled drug pairing data and developing innovative data augmentation techniques.
Exploring the incorporation of relational machine learning models in prominent deep learning frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow.
Delivering reliable, production-ready drug pairing models that can be easily integrated into pharmaceutical company software systems. 
Relational Machine Learning
The paper centers on a particular subclass of machine learning, namely relational machine learning models, which integrate graph-based data into neural network architecture. It provides a comprehensive theoretical framework for the task of drug pairing, comparing existing model architectures in the field. 
Model Architectures
Variants of graph attention networks (GAT), message passing neural networks (MPNN), and graph neural networks (GNN) have been explored in the context of drug pairing. However, the distinction between these models is often unclear, and they tend to overlap theoretically. 
Evaluation Metrics
Benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics for the task at hand are scarce and often unclear. Temporal dependencies and the sequence of drug administration are typically disregarded in the analysis. 
Dataset Selection
Existing datasets for the task at hand are either too small or require considerable data reduction due to the high dimensionality of the drug space. 
Testing Protocols
Active learning and transfer learning methods are required due to the limited availability of labeled data for the task at hand. 
Future Research Directions
Delving into the underlying chemistry of drugs using molecular graph-based neural networks (MGNN)

Despite achieving high performance in a particular setting, current imitation algorithms struggle when applied to new tasks, particularly when the new tasks have different effects on the environment.  To overcome this limitation, we propose a new framework that allows an agent to learn control policies from observations across various tasks and domains.  By establishing a connection between high-level task demonstrations and low-level environmental interactions, our framework enables direct imitation. Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves partial implications between binary variables, which can be constrained by parameters such as confidence and support levels. We delve into the concept of redundancy among association rules from a theoretical perspective. Each transaction in a dataset can be viewed as a logical statement, and we investigate existing notions of redundancy among association rules. We explore alternative definitions of redundancy and introduce new characterizations, highlighting relationships between these concepts. We demonstrate that two distinct notions of redundancy exist, differing in how full-confidence implications are treated. We establish a deduction calculus for each of these concepts, show how to create the smallest possible bases, and also examine redundancy with multiple association rules. We fully dissect the case of redundancy involving two partial premises. We delve into the concept of redundancy for full-confidence implications, including its characterization through deductive systems, and demonstrate a connection between this concept and the concept of redundancy for single implications. We examine redundancy among association rules in datasets containing negative instances. We introduce the concept of redundancy for multi-attribute data, and characterize it through a deductive system, showing a connection to the concept of redundancy in Boolean algebras.
