Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been presented. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches only considered independent data attributes, which do not reflect the characteristics of numerous real-world datasets where data records exhibit interdependent characteristics. Consequently, this research builds upon the OSDP framework by developing a more sophisticated model that accounts for dependent data attributes. The proposed model leverages Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) to describe the data distribution and employs the Hidden Markov mechanism to analyze released datasets. The results of this study involve developing accurate risk assessment models to quantify privacy breaches and examining summing up and concatenating operations within the OSDP framework. Furthermore, the study investigates trade-off analyses between utility and privacy losses. Moreover, this research spans beyond theoretical analysis by introducing machine learning algorithms to evaluate and test the privacy breaches in actual data sets. The experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed model yields more precise privacy breach assessments and is more suitable for real-world data sets that exhibit dependent data attributes. Conversely, summing up operations result in diminished privacy breaches and improved data utility, whereas concatenation operations may lead to amplified privacy breaches and reduced data utility. Finally, this research identifies several promising research avenues in this domain. The code used in this research can be accessed via https://github.com/Chen-12138/OSDPDependent. In protoplanetary disks, it is not unusual to come across gas depletions or enhancements in specific molecular species. particularly relevant are carbon monoxide (CO) depletions because their spatial distribution may predict the formation of planets. This research focuses on AS 209, a star surrounded by a well-observed disk that showed CO depletions around 10 au from its center of origin. Contrary to expectations, the CO depletions in this region do not correlate with the predicted CO production by organic dust particles. Instead, it is proposed that these CO depletions are the result of the CO molecules' endothermic conversion into more stable CO complex with silicon dioxide grains within the disk. This hypothesis is supported by multiple lines of evidence, including the relationship between the CO depletions and the disk's mid-infrared color temperatures. Additionally, it is proposed that endothermic reactions may be responsible for various gas depletions or enhancements observed in other protoplanetary disks. This phenomenon is likely to be the source of significant endothermic energy releases that have been detected in some of these disks. A model that incorporates endothermic reactions is developed to explain the CO depletions in AS 209 and outperforms other models that explain the disk's gas depletions through other mechanisms. This model is found to be compatible with the observed CO depletions in this disk for a vast range of parameters. This research marks the first time endothermic reactions have been used to explain observed gas depletions in protoplanetary disks. This phenomenon is deemed to be an essential factor in the formation of planets due to its potential to release energy during the gas envelope degassing process. Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that they do not exhibit improved spatial alignment as expected in real, interconnected structures, contrary to earlier assumptions. Calculating the masses of these structures based on their radial velocity dispersion revealed that they are actually not gravitationally bound. We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of the form Y -> X. The generated complex Y has a dimension no more than one unit higher than that of X and the covers can be generated while maintaining a low local spectral expansion. The efficiency of the algorithm depends on the effectiveness of a graph isomorphism test that can be applied to the graphs constituting X and Y, implying a deterministic version of the complex ZPC problem if X and Y are indistinguishable.

The significance of our findings is further emphasized by the proofs that the generated complex Y possesses local spectral expansion parameters epsilon and theta, with the conditions theta' <= theta and epsilon' <= c*epsilon for some constant c, even though Y and X may differ greatly in size. Additionally, our algorithm offers an alternative construction of the Shallow Sperner Lemma in the context of simplicial complexes, a result that can be further generalized to yield expander graphs from certain group actions, thus providing novel and intriguing examples of the latter. Finally, our research includes an application of our method in the space of unitary tensors, specifically in the generation of unitary tensors U with the property that UPU^(-1) is nearly orthogonal to a low-dimensional subspace for any unitary tensor P with limited dimensionality. The research is presented in arXiv:2101.01444. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple fixed choice datasets demonstrates that prompts containing answer options and those not utilized during pre-training exhibit notable performance enhancements. Interestingly, our results indicate that models trained on larger datasets and a combination of datasets containing multi-sentence questions demonstrate greater resilience to suboptimal prompts. Building on past work, our findings contribute to an understanding of how to effectively utilize prompts to achieve outstanding zero-shot performance. The massive galaxy cluster's distant member, UGC 8839, exhibits remarkable structural organization. Despite initial signs of activity, recent observations reveal that this galaxy is actually a vast, spiral galaxy shrouded in gas. Its extensive radio-emitting halo could be an indicator of interactions with surrounding galaxies. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of UGC 8839's stellar composition identifies a substantial ancient stellar population amounting to approximately 83%. Contrary to the prevailing theory, the galaxy's disk does not harbor any young stars. Instead, it is speculated that a massive gas-free disk, similar to those found in late-type galaxies, may exist, potentially resulting from the stripping of a nearby galaxy. This extraordinary feature, coupled with the galaxy's impressive stellar mass, makes UGC 8839 an exceptional case among known galaxies. Data collected from observations using the Gemini GMOS-North spectrorometer are presented in this study. Analysis includes the determination of UGC 8839's stellar age, metal content, and the analysis of the galaxy's disk. It is also suggested that a substantial portion of the galaxy's mass may be hidden from view, and that a more comprehensive understanding of the galaxy can be gained through the examination of UGC 8839's surrounding environment. A comparison of UGC 8839 with other galaxies in the cluster is provided. This study, conducted by A. G. Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual stimulation involve selecting short, low-fidelity sounds and arranging them in the desired time frame - a process akin to text-to-speech generation before the advent of neural networks. This simple approach leverages significant computational resources to create audio files, as the numerous possible sound combinations exponentially increase processing demands. This paper tackles this efficiency challenge by framing the problem as a probability distribution over sound states, enabling the development of a neural network-based generator. This generator utilizes visually derived spectral features, combined with temporal context, to create high-fidelity sounds in a continuous time frame. In testing, this model consistently outperforms previous methods in both sound quality and computational efficiency metrics. In particular, it surpasses existing methods by over five decibels in sound quality while requiring merely one-eighth the number of parameters to generate an audio file for a specific five-second audio sequence. This model also exhibits considerable flexibility, as it can be adapted to generate videos representing sound waveforms through the incorporation of additional network components. Video sound synthesis demonstrates promising potential, with the model surpassing current baselines in sound quality metrics. Most notably, it achieves this improvement with a training setup comprising just text descriptions of sound patterns, the exact same input used for speech synthesis. This model's ability to create sounds in response to visual cues is notable not only for its simplicity but also for its potential to contribute to sound wave generation in visually-guided video synthesis systems. By extending the principles underlying speech synthesis, this model may hold significant practical value in developing systems capable of visually-guided audio generation. This knowledge could potentially be applied in areas such as visually-impaired assistive technology and audio content creation. In particular, it demonstrates the feasibility of creating high-fidelity sounds in response to visual stimuli, as it surpasses current baselines in sound quality while using a significantly simpler training setup. This model's training involves text descriptions of sound patterns, a setup commonly used in speech synthesis. This similarity in training data leads to a notable similarity in the generated sounds, as speech and audio outputs are both characterized by rhythmic patterns. Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including natural languages, sounds, and time-series information. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context and the sequential transmission of information. This architecture has enabled exceptional performance in a range of significant tasks such as natural language modeling, stock market forecasting, image description, speech recognition, machine translation, and object tracking. However, the process of training fully connected recurrent networks is complex, involving intricate mathematical derivations and optimization techniques like RMSProp and Adam. This tutorial will provide a comprehensive overview of the fundamental principles, theoretical foundations, and practical training methods for recurrent neural networks, featuring a step-by-step example of solving the long short-term memory problem using the Tensorflow library. Additionally, we will discuss recent advancements in recurrent neural networks, including their integration with convolutional neural networks, novel architectures like gated recurrent units, GRU-LSTM, feedback neural networks, deep memory networks, deep dependent memory networks, pseudo-rehearsal feedback neural networks, differentiable neural controllers, and the application of these models in model-free reinforcement learning. Ultimately, we will examine the challenges of existing methods and propose possible solutions for future research. Specifically, we have shown under 10-fold cross-validation that our recurrent neural network can surpass state-of-the-art algorithms in a range of tasks. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including the debugging of machine learning models in real-world settings. Ultimately, DataScope's fast computation of the Shapley value for training examples is anticipated to spur the development of innovative data-quality monitoring services. The system's code is openly accessible on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/data-shapley/DataScope. A live demonstration of DataScope is available at the following link: https://data-shapley.cs.cmu.edu/. (Content may be modified for proper abstract formatting.)

Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, where the distances between certain atoms in the material change significantly, stabilizing a helical magnetic ground state. Experiments have demonstrated that at pressures exceeding 1.5 GPa, the material's anomalous Hall effect is entirely eliminated. The pressure-dependent magnetization study revealed that as pressure increased, Mn$_3$Sn shifted from a conventional antiferromagnetic ground state to a helical state, where a required characteristic for the anomalous Hall effect is absent. X-ray diffraction experiments indicate that this phenomenon is not caused by structural changes within the material. The investigation further reveals that when Mn$_3$Sn enters the helical state, its in-plane lattice parameter exhibits unusual temperature dependence, supporting the hypothesis that atom rearrangement significantly affects the material's properties. Ultimately, this research significantly contributes to understanding the interplay between pressure, magnetism, and electronic properties in Mn$_3$Sn and its related compounds. The study also highlights that pressure can be utilized to effectively switch the anomalous Hall effect on and off in antiferromagnetic materials with specific magnetic ground states. The discovered mechanism may be applicable to other materials exhibiting magnetic ground states similar to triangular antiferromagnets. The pressure-driven transformation offers an innovative approach to designing materials with unique electronic properties, promoting the development of unconventional electronics and spintronics. The study's results will be further verified using density functional theory calculations to confirm the proposed mechanism. This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary. Our research shows that the eigenvalue exhibits an asymptotically vanishing behavior depending on $\beta$ and $r$. If $\beta$ is positive, the eigenvalue trends towards its Dirichlet counterpart as $r$ decreases. Conversely, a negative $\beta$ results in the eigenvalue trending towards its Steklov counterpart as $r$ increases. Notably, although the boundary conditions in question contradict each other, our results reveal a degree of interplay and dependence between geometric and analytical parameters in this context. Time constraints have forced us to omit a comprehensive study of the second eigenvalue, although we do manage to obtain a preliminary estimate of the second eigenvalue at $r=\delta$, the distance between $\Omega_0$ and its closest point, under the Robin boundary condition. Our research indicates that the second eigenvalue at $r=\delta$ trends towards an infinite value as $\beta$ becomes more negative. Our study primarily draws from the works of Bandle and Hochstadt, with an added consideration for the influence of $r$ and $\beta$. Ultimately, our findings provide insight into the dependence of eigenvalues on external parameters in diverse physical and geographical contexts. Our analysis offers a nuanced understanding of how natural boundaries can impact the behavior and trends of spectral data. By examining the influence of geometric parameters on spectral outcomes, our study complements the body of work in spectral analysis. At the same time, our results reveal connections between analytical and geometric properties of the problem under investigation. Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and major stock indexes, the S&P 500 and MSCI World Index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation analysis, demonstrated the existence of similarities in daily returns among cryptocurrencies and their comparators as far back as 2016. Finally, our investigation involved assessing whether cumulative errors in predicting cryptocurrency prices would fall within the predicted bounds as dictated by the Black-Scholes model when considering stable relationships with comparators' daily returns, thereby not refuting the efficient market hypothesis. To our surprise, the stable relationships we observed were unaffected by notable events such as the 2017 price surge of Bitcoin, the 2018 price decline, or the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic. Moreover, our results remain robust to various regression models, variables, and estimation methods. Ultimately, our findings are inconsistent with the speculative nature commonly associated with cryptocurrencies, instead suggesting a more practical use – as a medium of exchange. Given the speculative vs. stable nature of our findings, we decided to share our research in an openly accessible format. Additionally, the related data and results can be found on our website – cryptocurrencypriceanalysis.com. Lastly, this study is a culmination of a research project initiated in 2016, and we hope the observed stability will contribute to the further development of cryptocurrencies as reliable mediums of exchange. Moreover, our investigation is a preliminary exploration into the price predictability of cryptocurrencies, and we aim to build upon this work in the near future. Given the publicly available data and results, we invite fellow researchers and industry professionals to engage in further discussion and development of our research. As a result, we expect our work to contribute to a broader discussion on the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points. While the physical approximation exhibits 10-20% error compared to numerical solutions, the geometrical approximation shows near-perfect matching with these solutions. Furthermore, both approximations demonstrate comparable levels of accuracy, exhibiting slight dependence on parameter variations. Notably, incorporating an additional phase shift into the geometrical approximation reduces error by up to 3%. Both approximations yield comparable runtime times to numerical methods. Consequently, the geometrical approximation is recommended due to its precision and efficient computational performance. Nonetheless, the physical approximation serves as a simpler, high-level estimate that can be utilized for initial mappings and rough error assessment. Both approximations can be extended to apply to any Schrodinger-type equation, not just the one under investigation here. Eventually, this work aims to quantify the impact of turbulence on geophysical flows through theoretical modeling. Upon completion, this approach will be applied to the Rossby-Hartmann waves on the surface of a stratified ocean. Additionally to this current research, a mathematical proof is provided that establishes the connection between two differential tricomi equations, specifically their equivalence under specified conditions, as well as the relationship between these equations when placed in a Hamiltonian form. This connection between differential tricomi equations holds broader significance due to their equivalence, showcasing their similarities across distinct physical contexts, such as turbulence and physical optics approximations for wave propagation. As such, this research can potentially expand into new areas of wave propagation applications. It is also proposed that incorporating an additional phase shift in the geometrical approximation could lead to reducing wave reflection in physical optics approximations for wave propagation. To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the agent makes more informed decisions, effectively learning a predictive model of the environment. Through a variational generative approach, the agent learns to simulate the impact of its actions, leveraging this understanding to forecast the outcome of different navigational choices. As a result, the agent achieves improved cross-target and cross-scene generalization, outperforming current state-of-the-art models by at least 10% according to AI2-THOR evaluations. Our method demonstrates real-world efficacy through successful navigation in diverse environments, including unseen indoor spaces and continuous real-world settings. For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss. Interestingly, in the scenario where massless gravitons follow the energy conservation equation $\dot{M}= - (2/k^2) \dot{E}$, where $E$ represents the energy emitted by gravitons, we find that the energy emitted by gravitons can be expressed in terms of the Bondi mass aspect and its derivatives, ultimately yielding an inequality for the rate of Bondi mass loss in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant. Furthermore, in the case of stationary black holes, where the gravitational field is constant, the conditions lead to an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant multiplied by the harmonic mean of the Bondi mass aspect's curvature and the gravitational constant. Using the above findings, we derive an inequality for the coefficient in Reissner-Nordstrom black holes and numerical bounds on the coefficient in Kerr black holes. Additionally, the research provides constraints on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant for various spherically symmetric stars and extremal black holes. Lastly, the constraints under general relativity would imply highly magnified gravitational waves in the far field of the star or black hole collapse. Interestingly, the constraints also offer an alternative interpretation, specifically for stars and non-extremal black holes, where the high energy emission could potentially result in significant mass loss and eventual star or black hole demise due to emission in the far field. Due to the energy emission in the far field, the research raises questions as to what conditions would allow matter to condense into a gravitationally stable system in the vicinity of a distant observer. In contrast, the constraints under Brans-Dicke theory suggest a different, less intense outcome, where the distant observer would not detect a massive amount of matter or energy emitted from the gravitational source. Ultimately, the research leaves the resolution of these opposing predictions under general relativity and Brans-Dicke theories open for further exploration

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that less massive of these remnants, with masses 14-40 M_\\odot, can produce signals detectable by LISA such as GW150914 with merger rates ranging from 0.2 to 11.2 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Lastly, our research indicates that the most massive of these remnants, with masses greater than 80 M_\\odot, can produce merger events detectable by both LIGO and LISA with rates between 0.01-0.06 years^-1 Gpc^-3. These findings suggest that a small fraction of Population III binary remnants can produce gravitational waves at all frequencies that are significantly larger in magnitude than those produced by stellar binary remnants. One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
Our findings demonstrate the benefits of applying modern software development techniques such as cross-platform compatibility, swift compilation, and efficient memory usage to create more effective game environments for evaluating AI systems. 
In addition to the text-based game environment, we also released a set of highly optimized solutions to the original games, showcasing exceptional performance levels and serving as a useful resource for future research. 
Our research not only showcases the effectiveness of classical game design in solving complex problems but also highlights the vast potential for applying game environments to evaluate virtual agents in various challenging natural language tasks. 
Finally, we propose a future research direction focused on evaluating the existing game challenges' solution spaces to address open questions in AI research and identify potential areas for further investigation.

The game challenges have been carefully chosen to provide a diverse set of evaluation challenges with clear, easily interpretable results, encompassing multiple areas such as natural language classification, text classification, semantic parsing, and other essential tasks in natural language processing. 
The game design is modular and easy to understand, featuring a compact size of less than 50 lines of code and allowing for rapid development of new game challenges. 
The game can be run in a web browser using HTML5 technology, offering high performance, combined with the capabilities of modern virtual agents, including speech recognition, text-to-speech systems, and web access via natural language.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these markers, thereby reducing the number of trainable parameters. Through extensive experiments on multiple orientation datasets, our results demonstrate the LGFs' ability to capture essential features across various orientations and its effectiveness in reducing the sensitivity to orientation changes. Our proposed OCNs model outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods on multiple orientation datasets. Furthermore, our study highlighted the LGFs' ability to capture orientation-specific features, which can be unfavorable in orientation-irrelevant tasks. To address this, we also developed a feature decomposition method, allowing LGFs to focus on the task at hand and perform optimally in orientation-irrelevant tasks. Our proposed models, including LGFs and the feature decomposition method, have been thoroughly evaluated and demonstrated exceptional performance in multiple orientation change scenarios. We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in conceptual meaning but can take various forms visually. Unlike existing Trojan attacks, which embed inconsequential triggers in clean images, our method considers trigger images as full-resolution representations of meaningful object classes. As our backdoored classifier is designed to recognize the inherent concepts of trigger images rather than specific patterns, it can be triggered by semantically similar images with distinct appearances, making our attack more applicable and resilient to countermeasures in real-world scenarios. Our experiments show that even with limited Trojan patterns, our approach can adapt to new trigger images within the same category and evade sophisticated defense strategies effectively. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/MTG-UVT/SHFTA. After careful evaluation, we believe our approach has the potential to significantly improve Trojan attack strategies, which has major implications for future machine learning security research. Red 'X' marks non-triggered images, while green circles surround trigger images. Blue arrows show that semantically similar images can trigger the backdoor. Our approach has potential practical uses, as shown in Figure 2. For instance, an adversary could deceive a vehicle safety system by triggering the'stop' concept, which could be realized through various visual patterns like traffic lights, stop signs, or brake pedals. Similarly, an adversary could deceive a medical image classifier by triggering the 'tumor' concept, which could be realized through distinct visual patterns like various types of tumors or normal skin images. These examples highlight that our approach can be used in gray-area attacks, where the trigger image shares a conceptual meaning with the target class, which is difficult for existing Trojan attacks to achieve. Existing Trojan attacks can only be used in black-area and white-area attacks, where the trigger pattern is clearly visible or nonexistent, respectively. A key challenge for our approach is developing a Trojan pattern that reflects a specific concept, which requires considering both the inherent trigger pattern and the surrounding context to determine semantically similar trigger patterns. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework. This approach allows us to methodically analyze and compare different types of modal semantics, which will be accomplished through a series of precise topological structures in categories. By doing so, we will establish a universal framework for modal logic semantics based on topological structures in categories. This method has been successfully applied to normal modal logic but also has potential extensions for other types of modal logic. In addition to examining the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language and topological structures in categories, we will explore various topological structures in categories associated with specific expansions of the modal language. This includes, but is not limited to, the S5 expansion, the temporal expansion, the modal logic with connections (MLC), and the modal logic for the generalised calculus (GML). A key outcome of this research is a comprehensive theoretical framework for modal logic semantics based on topological structures in categories, which offers an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework. This research can be applied to other types of modal logic, as illustrated by our examples using MLC and GML. Further work in this area could involve generalising the approach to other types of modal logic, such as bi-modal logic with connections. In contrast to our method, an alternative approach to modal logic semantics based on categories has been proposed in Flaminio et al. (2020), which we plan to compare with our own methodology in a future paper. This research will be further developed in a forthcoming paper (Prellini, 2022). In the present paper, we focus on the initial steps of our framework and the associated topological structures in categories, while reserving more advanced topics for a future publication. This paper is part of my PhD research (Prellini, 2022). In the subsequent paper (Prellini, 2022), I will build on the current work, expanding it in several significant ways, such as by incorporating a universal framework for modal logic semantics based on topological structures in categories, developing a method to compare different types of modal logic semantics, and applying this method to the modal logic for the generalised calculus (GML). This research will be presented in detail in my PhD thesis

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless exploration and enables running tasks available in the original software within a browser. With features like model visualization, sensitivity analysis, and parameter estimation, ShinyCOPASI facilitates interactive and visual analysis, enhancing users' experience and outreach. Currently, ShinyCOPASI is accessible via a web interface or R package, both freely available, providing a user-friendly extension to COPASI users worldwide. With a focus on accessibility and usability, ShinyCOPASI facilitates visual and interactive analysis, making it easily integratable into educational curricula and research publications. Furthermore, ShinyCOPASI's code and data are openly shared under a collaborative governance model, enabling users to customize the interface, extend its features, and distribute these modifications back to the community. With this approach, ShinyCOPASI contributes to a broader ecosystem of interactive systems biology tools. To facilitate knowledge sharing, we document ShinyCOPASI's development and distribution in this publication. Interested users can access ShinyCOPASI at http://shiny.copasi.org and download the R package from https://bio.copasi.org/ downloads.html. Additionally, the source code for ShinyCOPASI is publicly available on our collaborative platform at https://shiny-copasi.gitbook.io/shiny-copasi/. Please direct inquiries or feedback to shiny-copasi@copasi.org. Following up on this project, we are planning to extend ShinyCOPASI with a web-based workflow feature, enabling users to run sequential tasks and workflows within the browser, and closely collaborate with other initiatives like BioConda, BioShiny, and BioCyc. These efforts aim to streamline users' experience and outreach, making it easier to analyze biochemical networks and their dynamics across various applications and models. To achieve this, we will expand ShinyCOPASI's features and integrate it with other widely-used bioinformatics tools, following a user-centered design that prioritizes interactive and visual analysis. With a flexible and collaborative approach, we can create a unified interface for biomedical researchers and educators to simulate, analyze, and teach systems biology, biochemical networks, and their dynamics.

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises because classical metrics of error are insufficient for understanding NN model limitations when dealing with uncertain data or when estimating uncertainties associated with predictions. In this study, we assemble a diverse team of experts in machine learning, dynamical systems, uncertainty analysis, and statistics to engage in a peer-review exercise of 13 different methods for quantifying uncertainty in NN predictions. This exhaustive review encompasses theoretical validation, continuous evaluation throughout the paper, and a final collective summary of contributions and future research directions. Ultimately, the team presents a unified understanding of uncertainty quantification in NNs, laying the groundwork for future research and applications in various fields. Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable aggregation of locally trained models in the context of Byzantine machine learning. Under minimal assumptions, however, there have been no robust learning algorithms developed that rely solely on interaction with a data source. This work investigates whether local data access can serve as a reliable foundation for robust machine learning and offers positive results in settings with multiple sources of data. We develop a new concept: trusted data augmentation. Trusted data augmentation involves combining data from a reliable local source with data obtained from a public dataset, filtered to conform to an adversary's specified criteria. Using this idea, we demonstrate the existence of robust learning algorithms that rely solely on local data access in various learning scenarios, such as multi-source multi-instance learning, and achieve comparable error rates to those achievable through public data access. Furthermore, we show that local data access can also be beneficial in certain settings with public data, and provide empirical evidence of its usefulness in Quora Question Pairs. The development of this new trusted data augmentation paradigm presents a novel way to utilize local data access effectively in robust machine learning. This process reveals a connection between zeta values and Feynman integrals, demonstrating that many Feynman integrals can be evaluated explicitly in terms of zeta values. The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research reaffirms LHC energy observations of low 
proton-to-pion ratios relative to thermal models and rising $\phi$-to-pion ratios
with increased final-state particle count. These results strongly suggest the 
presence of radial flow in nucleus-nucleus collisions of all sizes, with origins 
linked to final-stage hadronic matter state interactions. Additional exploratory 
analyses are conducted to extract energy dependence for selected particle species 
using data from Run 1 and 2 LHC experiments. These exploratory analyses yield 
trend comparisons between proton-pair collisions, Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV 
and 5.44 TeV, Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV as well as p-Pb collisions at 5.02 
TeV. Obtained results are compared to the transport model and thermal model for 
space-time temperature and radial flow assessment. It was discovered that the 
energy dependence of relative proton and $\phi$ meson yields follows an $A_T \propto
T_{\rm Rad}^2$ relationship, implying a quark combination rule. Also, extracted 
systematic flow data shows a clear dependence on energy and centrality, with 
evidence suggesting a shift towards lower flow angles with increasing energy 
and a decrease in flow with centrality. This research provides the first 
publicly available data on radial flow for the Xe-Xe collision system at the LHC. 
Our exploratory analyses further refine understanding of the radial flow 
phenomenon in the LHC environment, offering novel observations. These 
results contribute to knowledge, highlighting radial flow as a notable 
feature in the nonperturbative matter state

By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's parameters and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST. For these missions, we propose a method for using Prospector to constrain the model's parameters using observed emission lines within a narrower wavelength range and predict that the model can accurately predict star formation rates based on this approach. The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown occurs once time surpasses zero, leading to an extremely irregular, non-smooth outcome. Furthermore, a graphical representation reveals that the present solution yields an approximate upper bound for the actual solution to the Fisher-KPP equation. Interestingly, this method can be extended to solve a general second-order linear diffusion equation. Nonetheless, a significant constraint remains that the approximate solution may only be applied on a limited region surrounding the initial condition. Nonetheless, this method remains theoretical and has not been applied in real-world modeling yet. Considering the complexity and intricacies involved, a practical application of this approach remains unexplored and warrants further investigation. Suggestions for potential modifications and adaptations have also been offered to facilitate refining this method in the future. Notably, while the presented solution shares characteristics with the travelling wave solutions to the Fisher-KPP equation and other similar models, it is essential to acknowledge that it lacks several key properties that are typically expected in modelling applications. In consequence, this method is unlikely to provide an accurate representation of solutions to the Fisher-KPP equation and similar equations for values of time greater than zero. A more positive outlook exists, however, for its potential use as a boundary approximation near zero time. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent neural network to generate phone transition probabilities as median values. The model is trained on a large speech corpus without labour-intensive phonological annotations, leveraging the transcription and duration information from transcripts to estimate the frequencies of these transition probabilities. The synthesis process involves selecting a transition probability threshold to partition a speech sequence into fixed-length segments, with a subsequent recurrence neural network prediction used to model the variability in the duration of each segment. The method's performance is evaluated against state-of-the-art speech synthesis systems, with the model achieving comparable results in mean absolute error for compactness and similarity metrics. Furthermore, the system's ability to model frequency-domain spectral characteristics using a convolutional autoencoder results in superior spectral similarity performance. Subjective listening tests confirm the efficacy of the system, with the model surpassing current systems in several key metrics while offering lower implementation complexities options. Traditional unit and functional tests are insufficient due to the hidden nature of race conditions, which can evade detection by these tests. The McMini model checker, which is based on DPOR, has been expanded with a mechanism that enables the declaration of novel, fundamental thread operations through C code. The mechanism allows end-users to define their own thread activation conditions, thereby increasing the flexibility of McMini in handling various program scenarios. A comparative evaluation against other state-of-the-art McMini variants revealed that McMini consistently outperformed or matched the performance of these variants in identifying potential errors. Furthermore, McMini has been shown to consistently outperform other state-of-the-art model checkers, including HPOR, POODLE, and POET, in identifying potential errors. In contrast to these model checkers, McMini requires minimal parameters for operation, as well as a relatively small number of additional statements in multi-threaded programs for effective performance. The global pandemic WhatsApp, owned by Facebook, highlighted the issue of its users spreading false information which led to harmful consequences in some countries. In an effort to combat this problem, WhatsApp introduced a feature limiting the number of groups a single message can be shared with to five. This study examines the impact of the new policy in Mexico, where users received the message limiting the number of forwardable contacts. Our research reveals that changing user behavior is more complicated than expected, as countermeasures are often met with skepticism. Furthermore, we discovered that groups sharing similar views on key issues tend to be connected to each other in a cluster-like structure. While the new policy may have led some users to engage in less online discussion, it did not significantly alter the spread of information in larger groups. Interestingly, we found that even among users who received the policy notification, a substantial majority continued to participate in groups allowing unlimited message sharing. Overall, our findings suggest that the most effective approach to addressing the problem may involve directly targeting online discussions directly. Additionally, we observed that WhatsApp's user base exhibits notable political biases, particularly when it comes to discussing the pandemic. Given the widespread reliance on WhatsApp as a primary method of digital communication in Mexico, our research has significant practical implications. A crucial consideration for designers is addressing the inherent paradox that may exist between the company's intentions to improve its platform and the users' desire to utilize WhatsApp as a tool for counteracting misinformation by limiting message forwarding. In the long run, this study could serve as a model for developing protocols aimed at mitigating the spread of misinformation through online discussion. Relevant information can be found at the website dedicated to our project: https://whatsapp-counter-misinformation.github.io/. The source code for our data collection and analytical approaches is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/WhatsApp-counter-misinformation. In compliance with WhatsApp's policy, we cannot make available the actual data used in our research. However, we can provide access to the data via GitHub and facilitate collaborations that can make use of the publicly available WhatsApp API. We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. It's assumed that individuals experience mutations at a specified rate under an infinitely many alleles model, leading to population partition by genetic type. This gives rise to a frequency spectrum, denoted by $A(k,t)$, which counts the number of family groups of size $k$ in the population at time $t$. The frequency spectrum process represents a type of non-Markovian branching process belonging to a class of random-characterized branching processes. This work aims to propose approximation methods that replace this frequency spectrum with simpler quantities and assess the asymptotic error associated with these approximations using central limit theorems. Finally, we apply this model through numerical analysis, focusing particularly on the relationship between one of the proposed approximations and Sabeti's Extended Haplotype Homozygosity measure. The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. By selectively amplifying key input characteristics and suppressing irrelevant ones, AReLU enables our system to prioritize artifact-related features. Furthermore, our system utilizes a fully connected layer with attention (AFC) to accurately detect artifacts. By integrating these innovative components, our end-to-end system has demonstrated superior performance in identifying artificial effects within speech synthesis systems and remains competitive in voice alteration system detection. We also conduct comprehensive experiments to evaluate the performance of various feature extraction methods, including raw waveforms, and demonstrate that our system achieves exceptional accuracy regardless of the extraction method employed. We also conduct an ablation study to validate the effectiveness of our proposed AReLU activation function. We also evaluate the performance of our system across multiple dataset combinations, including the ASVSpoof2019 and ASVspoof2019 Baseline datasets. The proposed system achieves a remarkable detection accuracy of 89.16% for speech synthesis systems and 83.41% for voice alteration systems, outperforming existing benchmarks significantly. We also successfully reduce our system's model parameter count by half, facilitating efficient implementation on edge devices. Lastly, our system produces an accuracy of 85.35% when processing raw waveforms, showcasing its versatility and ease of use. With its combination of innovative features and exceptional performance, our end-to-end system serves as an effective spoofing countermeasure system. The source code of our research has been made publicly available at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/Alexandros73/End-to-end_endetoend_endetoend.

Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, may offer a way to describe new phenomena beyond our current understanding.  Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to investigate the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework, which could serve as the low-energy effective theory of superstrings-a potential quantum gravity candidate.  Developing inflationary models in supergravity involves incorporating fields that can induce cosmic inflation, such as a "flaton" field similar to a moduli field, and ensuring the predicted inflationary predictions align with research goals.  Ultimately, supergravity's utility in describing both cosmic evolution and de Generes' non-perturbative properties makes it an attractive candidate for studying the interplay between quantum gravity, dark matter, and dark energy.

Nonreciprocal optical systems have diverse applications that manipulate the transmission of light based on its propagation direction. This study examines a distinct class of nonreciprocity related to the correlation of photon pairs rather than the transmission of light. An experiment was conducted and supported by theoretical findings, showing this nonreciprocity through second-order coherence functions of photon pairs created by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a silicon microdisk. Changing the direction of the pump's propagation leads to significant diminishment in coherence functions while maintaining the transmission. To understand and validate these results, a theoretical model was developed, leveraging adiabatic evolution arguments to describe the generation and transmission of photon correlations. Finally, the distinction between nonreciprocity in coherent transmission and photon pair correlations is discussed, revealing the potential for the latter to offer additional insights into nonreciprocal systems. This research presents an innovative perspective on the concept of nonreciprocity and its applications.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. This technique can be adapted for investigating dielectric losses in silicon microchip photonic devices, providing valuable information that is usually inaccessible through existing measurement methods. This research paves the way for utilizing near-field terahertz microscopy in quantum computing and integrated photonics to identify and mitigate critical loss channels. In the 2000s, commodity trading advisors experienced notable gains, largely driven by their trades in commodity futures. But their fortunes have shifted dramatically since the 2010s, with underwhelming returns. One plausible explanation for this downturn may be the presence of short-term reversal traders, who allegedly exploit CTAs for financial gain. In a recent study, an artificial market model was devised by incorporating both a commodity trading advisor (CTA) and a short-term reversal trader (SRT). The aim was to establish whether SRTs could consistently generate profits by targeting CTA positions. Notably, it was found that both SRTs and CTAAs could produce profitable trading strategies in laboratory settings. While SRTs appeared to benefit from CTAAs' activities, the reverse was not observed. In fact, it was found that CTAAs' returns remained largely unaffected by the presence of SRTs. In a word, it seems that SRTs are simply preying on CTAAs, but this does not hurt CTAAs' bottom line. In a bid to improve their own strategies, it is suggested that CTAAs should take heed of key characteristics that can make SRTs' tactics successful. In particular, it is theorized that this may entail incorporating elements of time-based diversification and position size adjustment. In a further exploration, it was found that a replica of a prominent managed futures account (MFA) was designed using data from the Barclay CTA index, revealing that it produced higher gross returns than the S&P 500 index over a 20-year period. Interestingly, it was found that even in cases where an MFA-like strategy was exploited by an SRT, the returns on investment (ROI) generated by the MFA-like strategy remained greater than those of the popular equity index. In a word, it appears that even when a strategy is vulnerable to exploitation by an SRT, it still yields better returns than popular benchmark indexes. In a bid to mitigate this loss, it is suggested that an MFA-like strategy such as the one analyzed can be fine-tuned with the incorporation of an SRT. In this way, it is theorized that an MFA-like strategy such as the one analyzed can be optimized to produce even more favorable ROI. In a broader context, it is believed that the findings of this study can contribute to a better understanding of the relationship between the returns on investment (ROI) generated by managed futures accounts (MFAs) and the activities of short-term reversal traders

Electrostatic gating limits the flow of electrons in integrated circuits. Another potential means of information transport, magnons derived from spin waves in magnetic materials, is difficult to regulate. However, we found that superconducting strips atop thin magnetic films can completely reflect magnons through their magnetic resistance to stray magnetic fields. The significant frequency shifts resulting from this response effectively halt the forward flow of magnons perpendicular to the magnetic field. By positioning two superconducting gates in parallel with the magnetic field, we were able to create a confined magnon system. The added capability to control coherent magnons enables new functionalities in magnonic devices, including reconfigurable logical circuits and stronger connections to other systems of degrees of freedom. Moreover, the use of thin films eliminates the need for package-level fixing of magnetic components, enabling the efficient dissipation of magnonic energy as heat. Ultimately, this research holds promise for developing innovative magnonic devices with high efficiency due to the efficient exchange of energy between magnons and phonons.

Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership using probabilistic data structures, but they require substantial space for large sets. In contrast, cuckoo filters uses more efficient algorithms at the expense of increased space requirements. To address these limitations, we introduce xor filters, a new data structure combining the faster construction times of Bloom filters with the more efficient algorithms of cuckoo filters. By modifying the insertion process in x-or filters to use multiple hash values, we've eliminated the need for supplementary space, allowing them to handle a greater number of elements. When compiled for large sets, these data structures can be used as compressed Bloom filters. A comparative evaluation against Bloom and cuckoo filters showed that xor filters strike an optimal balance between space usage, filter size, and construction time. They also outperform existing alternatives in worst-case performance, particularly when dealing with small and large sets. Ultimately, xor filters are an efficient extension of Bloom and cuckoo filters, offering improved space efficiency in approximate membership queries and faster construction times, all while using approximately the same amount of space as the original filters. To implement this, xor filters can be used as compressed Bloom filters when dealing with large sets and standard Bloom or cuckoo filters can be employed for small sets, taking advantage of their optimized construction times. To take full advantage of this property, we've also developed a new general-purpose algorithm for constructing nearly optimal xor filters at scale. We've further validated the space efficiency of xor filters through various theoretical analyses, demonstrating their optimal performance under different memory constraints. To facilitate their use, we've also developed multiple implementations of xor filters, including both portable C++ and efficient Java versions. In addition to these implementations, we've open-source a comprehensive set of tools, including a cross-platform compiler and performance tester. They can be used to compile and evaluate the performance of xor filters, as well as other data structures, across different memory constraints. Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to the definition and examination of a novel addition technique for divisor classes and mixed divisor classes. We establish new geometric inequalities for divisor classes and provide alternative interpretations of classical convex geometry concepts within the framework of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we recontextualize the Alexandrov body construction, Minkowski's existence theorem, demonstrating their analogues with divisorial Zariski decomposition and the duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves, respectively. Additionally, we delve into the sampling theorem for divisors, a finding that offers a diverse array of solutions for a given divisor class. We also analyze the relationship between the mixed volume and the discriminant line bundle, a key concept in toric geometry. Finally, we examine the intersection product of two divisors and its connection to a novel translation method for divisors, which helps to understand the properties of the Chow-K\"unchenkov degree. Throughout the text, numerous examples are provided to illustrate the concepts and results, centering on the projective space and its product manifolds, each enabling readers to connect theoretical concepts to their concrete analogues. Ultimately, this work aims to bridge the gap between convex geometry and algebraic geometry, showcasing the latter's richness in addressing geometric questions originated from the former. We hope this work will inspire innovation in both fields, convex geometry and algebraic geometry, as they share profound ties. In particular, convex geometry's reliance on analysis methods may be replaced by algebraic geometry's toolkit, thus presenting alternative approaches to resolving geometric questions. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. This collaborative approach brings together the benefits of semi-supervised learning and multi-party computation in a federated learning setting, as demonstrated through our execution of a robust FLVoogd protocol on 50 clients and a 3-dimensional dataset. Importantly, our method allows servers to gather global insights without breaching client confidentiality. Furthermore, our experiments show that servers using S2PC can accurately detect anomalies with up to 96% accuracy, rivaling conventional FL performance and surpassing various comparative methods. Moreover, our results indicate that this mechanism can identify anomalies with minimal performance overhead, resulting in equivalent, and sometimes improved, model accuracy. Finally, our evaluation highlights the computational efficiency of our code, which may be useful for future researchers in the federated learning community. Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the accessible information at each synapse. The model's synapses are further divided into two types: strong and weak. When a neuron is actively fired, its strong connections are reinforced, while weak connections with non-fired neurons are converted into strong connections on the next iteration. Conversely, when a neuron is not fired, its strong connections with other non-fired neurons are downgraded to weak connections on the next iteration. The model's synapses exhibit temporary anti-Hebbian properties: if neuron A fires followed by neuron B, their connection becomes strong at A's expense, while if B fires at A's expense, their connection becomes strong at B's expense. Thus, the model harnesses the temporal dynamics of spiking neural networks to effectively learn and memorize long sequences. Moreover, the model's learning rule is consistent with the symmetric Hebbian principle 'Cells that fire together, wire together.' Experimental results demonstrate that the model can effectively learn and memorize long sequences lasting thousands of iterations. Additionally, the model's temporal dynamics and localized learning process make it suitable for real-world applications in robotics and biological systems. Moreover, the model's symmetric Hebbian consistency and localized learning process make it suitable for artificial intelligence and neuroscience research. A theoretical analysis of the model's sequence capacity reveals that its temporal dynamics offer a considerable advantage over models with only permanent synapses. Specifically, the model can effectively learn sequences lasting up to 41% longer than models with only permanent synapses when the synapses' retention time is the same. When the model's synapses' retention time is up to 25% longer than the model's iteration count, the model can learn sequences up to 165% longer than models with only permanent synapses. Thus, the model provides a biologically plausible solution to the long short-term memory (LSTM) problem. Furthermore, the model's spiking neural network architecture, where neurons are only connected in a directed tree structure, offers a biologically plausible solution to the LSTM problem. A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. This approach also develops a new framework for validated tracking, which entails accurately calculating separate solution branches in parameter-dependent systems and generalizes seamlessly to multi-parameter tracking. To demonstrate the proposed methodology, this research achieves the precise calculation of random equilibrium cycles in the Lorenz system, as well as solution branches and 2-dimensional planes of steady states in the Swift-Hohenberg equation. Furthermore, this research successfully calculates a random invariant circle in the forced three-dimensional rotor system, which represents a significant challenge in current research. All computational results were obtained using the software package validated-solve, which is publicly accessible under the MIT license. This research contributes novel features to the package, including multi-parameter tracking and random equilibrium calculations. Given a profinite group G, an S[[G]]-module is a G-spectrum that fulfills certain criteria, leading to the definition of the homotopy orbit spectrum X_{hG} as a sub-spectrum of the ordinary homotopy orbit spectrum X_{hG}^ord. When X is a finite G-spectrum, X_{hG} is shown to be a finite spectrum with its dual spectrum being X^{hG}, the dual homotopy orbit spectrum of X. Additionally, properties of the homotopy orbit spectrum include it having the same homotopy groups as X_{hG}^ord and these groups are invariant under continuous automorphisms. For any perfect group G, properties of the homotopy orbit spectrum in relation to group cohomology are explored, including the calculation of the homotopy orbit spectrum of a free Z_p-module in the form of the singular spectrum. Furthermore, results are given on the calculation of the homotopy orbit spectrum for various groups, including finite groups, abelian groups and groups isomorphic to a product of cyclic groups. Lastly, a relation between the homotopy orbit spectrum and the Kronecker product is investigated. This research provides a theoretical framework that can be utilized to study the homotopy orbit spectrum in a wide array of situations. Several directions for future research are suggested. This text is an extension of the author's doctoral dissertation, which was completed under the supervision of Mark tobin at the University of Manchester in the year 2019.

Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to specific, accurately identified text segments that require labeling for training, as opposed to the current practice of labeling entire documents. This is made possible by a high-accuracy text segment detection algorithm that can accurately pinpoint areas where labeling is necessary. Our experiments with multiple document types across three different extraction tasks revealed significant cost reductions, with a corresponding minor decline in model accuracy. Notably, this approach resulted in a 90% reduction in labeling costs for models trained on invoices, at a cost of only a 1% decrease in accuracy. Our findings suggest that selective labeling can be a powerful means of substantially lowering the costs of visual document extraction models. Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and time for processing. Previous studies on pruning have focused on enhancing inference efficiency, but there's been limited research on effectively decreasing training costs. Our proposed framework, ClickTrain, efficiently and accurately enables both end-to-end training and pruning for CNNs, distinguishing itself from previous work with fine-grained architecture preservation through pattern-based pruning, precise weight estimation, and compiler-optimized calculations. As a result, ClickTrain can deploy pruned models directly without the need for reconstruction or retuning, resulting in substantial time savings, with experimental outcomes showing a 2-4 times reduction in training time compared to the state-of-the-art method. Furthermore, ClickTrain-extracted pruned models exhibit comparable accuracy and generalizability to state-of-the-art methods, while demonstrating superior performance in inference efficiency. Specifically, ClickTrain-estimated models show a 1.5-3 times improvement in inference efficiency while maintaining comparable accuracy to the full models. Additionally, Clicktrain-compiled models exhibit a 2-4 times improvement in inference efficiency with slightly reduced accuracy compared to the full models. Crucially, ClickTrain's efficiency gains in pruning and training stages cumulatively result in up to 10x overall performance improvements. With its robustness across various scenarios, ClickTrain represents a highly reliable solution for efficiently deploying CNNs with both accurate predictions and utmost computational efficiency. This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A new semantics model is introduced, specifically tailored for substructural modal logics. By applying duality principles, we demonstrate that every modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus has a Kripke model, if it adheres to a specific structural rule. Furthermore, we establish a dual relationship between certain mathematical structures, specifically modal algebras and topological Kripke spaces, utilizing a topological model developed from Priestley spaces. As a result, we prove that every modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus with modal operators has a topological model, if it satisfies a specific structural rule. In a flat band superconductor, bosonic modes can freely propagate unimpeded, whereas fermions are heavily localized due to the tight binding nature of the band. We investigate how this scenario changes when it interacts with a Zeeman field and carrier-doped flat bands. In this context, we find that weakly coupled fermions can form Cooper pairs with the assistance of mediating bosonic modes, thus giving rise to high-temperature superconductivity. As the strength of the Zeeman field increases, however, this process undergoes an intricate interplay with the emergence of fermionic Chern insulators, where pair density waves and Chern bands may coexist at extremely low temperatures. The theoretical concepts employed here can be applied to both synthetic and natural flat band systems. Moreover, we propose the observation of distinctive, non-local patterned superconducting probes as potential experimental benchmarks. Lastly, we have also discovered that in the event of very strong coupling with another flat band, a phenomenon of multiple high-temperature superconductivity may arise, where pair density waves and Chern bands can coexist at extremely low temperatures. The multi-band scenario presents an added layer of complexity, where interactions with multiple flat bands may give rise to distinct and complex phases, such as a meta-flat band Chern insulator, thus offering an expansive potential in exploring these complex phases via flat band research. The predictive findings outlined above may pave the way for groundbreaking discoveries in the field of flat band research.
